\title{\textbackslash{}'Etale Fundamental Groups -- a geometric and topological approach to fundamental groups in algebraic geometry}
\author{Loris De Vos}

\noindent\textbf{Source:} \href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23906}{arXiv:2606.23906} \quad \textbf{Field:} math.AG\\

\section*{TL;DR}
The thesis presents a systematic pedagogical exposition of fundamental groups across three domains: classical covering space theory and Galois theory (Chapter 1), the étale fundamental group of schemes (Chapter 2), and the Tannakian approach connecting all three (Chapter 3). The technical\_correctness specialist (confidence 0.70) rated the work mostly\_sound with only minor presentational errors and no headline claim found false; TC13 flags a major absence---no machine-checked formalization of any load-bearing result. The reproducibility specialist (confidence 0.88) assigned a score of 0.22, citing two critical-severity concerns: absence of a proof repository and lack of a formal proof artifact for the headline étale-vs-topological comparison theorem, plus two major concerns for the Tannakian and Nori comparisons. The novelty specialist (confidence 0.75) assigned 0.08 with verdict marginal, finding the thesis reproduces constructions from SGA 1, Szamuely, Schauenburg, and Nori without novel mathematical content. The citation specialist (confidence 0.72) flagged two missing references central to the Tannakian chapter---Deligne--Milne 'Tannakian Categories' (1982) and Saavedra Rivano 'Catégories Tannakiennes' (1972)---along with reliance on an unpublished student thesis (Horosiewicz 2022) as a primary Chapter 2 proof source. Specialists are in agreement: the exposition is clear and mostly correct, but the thesis lacks novel contributions, lacks formal proof artifacts, and under-references its core Tannakian framework. The paper's field (math.AG) is code-amenable under the recommendation gate, and both technical\_correctness (TC13, major) and reproducibility (critical) flagged missing proof-as-code artifacts, mandating major\_revision.

\textbf{Recommendation:} Major revision \quad \textbf{Confidence:} 82\%\\

\section*{Strengths}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item Self-contained, pedagogically clear exposition unifying three foundational frameworks---topological covering theory, étale fundamental groups, and Tannakian duality---within a single coherent narrative.
  \item All headline theorems are technically correct as stated; the technical\_correctness specialist found only minor presentational errors and no false claim across Chapters 1--3.
  \item Bibliography is appropriately anchored in primary sources (SGA 1, EGA IV, Hartshorne, Szamuely, Serre's GAGA), with stable-tag Stacks Project citations that will not rot.
  \item The comparison between the étale and topological fundamental groups over ℂ is carefully set up via GAGA and transcendental methods, providing a useful bridge for readers coming from topology.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Weaknesses}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item The thesis contains no novel mathematical contributions: every construction---étale fundamental group (SGA 1 / Szamuely), Tannakian reconstruction (Schauenburg), Nori fundamental group scheme (Nori 1982)---is reproduced from existing literature, yielding a novelty score of 0.08.
  \item No machine-checked proof artifact accompanies any load-bearing claim; both technical\_correctness (TC13, major) and reproducibility (critical) identify this absence as a significant gap for a math.AG thesis whose central results (Galois correspondence, étale--topological comparison, Tannakian reconstruction) are formalizable in Lean/Mathlib.
  \item The Tannakian chapter omits the two canonical foundational references---Deligne--Milne 'Tannakian Categories' (1982, LNM 900) and Saavedra Rivano 'Catégories Tannakiennes' (1972, LNM 265)---leaving the precise fibre-functor framework employed without its primary citations.
  \item Multiple proofs contain presentational defects that impede verification: notation collision in Theorem 34 (\ensuremath{\delta} used for two distinct objects), conflation of group elements with deck transformations in Proposition 21, reversed natural-transformation direction in Theorem 75, and typographic errors throughout.
  \item Reliance on the unpublished student thesis Horosiewicz (2022) as a primary proof source for 'many of the following proofs and concepts' in Chapter 2 is unusual and reduces verifiability; the extent of adaptation versus original presentation is not delineated.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Open Questions}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item What, if any, is the novel mathematical contribution beyond pedagogical synthesis? Is there a result, comparison, or construction the author claims as original?
  \item Would the author provide a companion Lean/Mathlib or Coq formalization of at least the headline comparison theorem (étale \ensuremath{\pi}₁ ≅ profinite completion of topological \ensuremath{\pi}₁ for connected finite-type ℂ-schemes)?
  \item Why are Deligne--Milne 'Tannakian Categories' (1982) and Saavedra Rivano 'Catégories Tannakiennes' (1972) absent from the bibliography, given that they are the foundational references for the neutral Tannakian framework employed throughout Chapter 3?
  \item Can the author clarify which proofs in Chapter 2 are direct adaptations of Horosiewicz (2022) and which represent independent presentations, and can published sources be substituted where available?
  \item The Chow citation uses the 2018 reprint but the text attributes the result to 'Chow 1949'; can the bibliography be corrected to cite the original Amer. J. Math. 71 (1949), 893--914 publication?
\end{itemize}

    "text": "\#\# Introduction\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe aim of this thesis is threefold. It is first to give an overview of\textbackslash{}nGrothendieck's interpretation of topological covering spaces and the\textbackslash{}nfundamental group of a topological space. Then, to show how it led to\textbackslash{}nthe realisation of similar concepts within the category of schemes. And\textbackslash{}nfinally, to link this approach to the classical results of Tannaka and\textbackslash{}nKrein.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nThe fundamental group of a topological space is an object which occupies\textbackslash{}na central place in mathematics and, more precisely, in algebraic\textbackslash{}ntopology because it provides one of the first ways of translating\textbackslash{}ngeometric phenomena into algebraic language. In the first chapter of\textbackslash{}nthis dissertation, we will study the fundamental group through the scope\textbackslash{}nof the theory of covering spaces. This approach is well-suited for the\textbackslash{}ndevelopments appearing later in the thesis because it reveals a deep\textbackslash{}nanalogy between topology and Galois theory. Indeed, covering spaces\textbackslash{}nbehave in many respects like field extensions: automorphism groups of\textbackslash{}ncoverings resemble Galois groups, universal covers play the role of the\textbackslash{}nalgebraic closures, and the classification of coverings mirrors the\textbackslash{}nclassical correspondence between intermediate field extensions and\textbackslash{}nsubgroups of its Galois group. We will then discuss a generalisation by\textbackslash{}n*Krull* of classical Galois theory for infinite field extensions, which\textbackslash{}ntakes advantage of the topology endowed on profinite groups. This\textbackslash{}nperspective emphasises the fact that the essential structure underlying\textbackslash{}nclassical Galois theory is not tied specifically to fields, but rather\textbackslash{}nto discrete sets equipped with an action of a Galois group. From there,\textbackslash{}nwe will explain how covering spaces fit into this broader framework by\textbackslash{}nshowing a similar reformulation for the classification of covering\textbackslash{}nspaces. The first chapter will end with a triple interpretation of\textbackslash{}ncovering spaces, as locally constant sheaves and as representations of\textbackslash{}nthe fundamental group. This chapter will serve as both a review of\textbackslash{}nclassical material and a conceptual foundation for the remainder of the\textbackslash{}nthesis.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nOne of Grothendieck's deepest insights was that an analogy similar to\textbackslash{}nthe one between Galois theory and covering spaces could be transported\textbackslash{}ninto algebraic geometry. But the difficulty in doing so lies in the fact\textbackslash{}nthat schemes do not possess a sufficiently rich topology. Indeed, for\textbackslash{}nthe Zariski topology, many schemes become topologically simply\textbackslash{}nconnected, making the resulting fundamental group trivial. Consequently,\textbackslash{}na new notion of topology had to be introduced. It led to the *étale\textbackslash{}ntopology*, for which coverings are no longer given by open subsets, but\textbackslash{}nby families of étale morphisms. One possible axiomatic approach we could\textbackslash{}nhave taken in this work was to study the *Galois category* of finite\textbackslash{}nétale morphisms over connected schemes. The étale fundamental group\textbackslash{}nwould then appear as the automorphism group of a certain fibre functor.\textbackslash{}nThis is done in [@SGA] and in [@Lenstra]. In this second chapter, we\textbackslash{}nchose to follow a more direct approach, also presented in [@Szamuely],\textbackslash{}nwhere the goal is to construct the algebraic counterpart of the theory\textbackslash{}ndeveloped for topological spaces. This will allow us to define an object\textbackslash{}nanalogous to the fundamental group of topological spaces called the\textbackslash{}n*étale fundamental group*. This can only be done after a thorough\textbackslash{}ninvestigation of étale morphisms. Here the reader will contemplate how\textbackslash{}nour approach of the fundamental group through covering spaces from the\textbackslash{}nfirst chapter bears its fruits. The techniques we use to describe the\textbackslash{}nétale fundamental group are almost equivalent to the ones used to\textbackslash{}ndescribe its topological counterpart. For the sake of accuracy, we then\textbackslash{}npresent an approach that allows us to compare our two analogue\textbackslash{}nfundamental groups. It uses techniques called transcendental methods.\textbackslash{}nThese show that the étale fundamental group of a connected scheme of\textbackslash{}nfinite type over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$, is the profinite completion of the\textbackslash{}ntopological fundamental group of the analytification of that scheme,\textbackslash{}nprovided we fix compatible base points. We finish by giving a few\textbackslash{}nstructure theorems for the étale fundamental group, further deepening\textbackslash{}nthe bridge between algebraic geometry, topology and arithmetic.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nWe end our investigation by a linearisation of the above concepts,\textbackslash{}nreplacing coverings by linear algebraic data. This idea originates from\textbackslash{}nthe work of Tadao Tannaka and Marc Krein, and goes as follows; rather\textbackslash{}nthan studying a (locally) compact group directly, one studies the\textbackslash{}nmonoidal (tensor) category formed by its representations and attempts to\textbackslash{}nrecover the group from this category and an associated fibre functor\textbackslash{}nalone. Later, Grothendieck and Saavedra Rivano extended the theory to\textbackslash{}naffine group schemes. The third chapter aims to introduce the basic\textbackslash{}nmachinery of Tannakian categories and explain how we can define a\textbackslash{}nTannakian fundamental group scheme via the automorphism group of the\textbackslash{}nfibre functor. One of the remarkable aspects of this theory is its\textbackslash{}nunifying character, étale fundamental groups, topological fundamental\textbackslash{}ngroups (and actually differential Galois groups and motivic Galois\textbackslash{}ngroups) all arise naturally within the Tannakian framework. This\textbackslash{}nhighlights the *motivic* character of the Tannakian fundamental group.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# Notations and Conventions \{\#notations-and-conventions .unnumbered\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Most of the notations we use in this thesis are defined in the\textbackslash{}n  Appendices, for example every schemes are assumed to be separated.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Categories are usually represented by calligraphic capital letters\textbackslash{}n  such as \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ or bold abbreviations such as\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Set\}\}\}\$, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Rng\}\}\}\$,\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\$, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dots\$\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- When considering group actions, we always assume that they act on a\textbackslash{}n  set from the left.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- All rings are considered to be commutative.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- We denote the algebraic closure of a field \$k\$ by \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}\$, this\textbackslash{}n  is not to be confused with the geometric point \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\$ when\textbackslash{}n  \$s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in S\$ for \$S\$ a scheme.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- And in the context of algebraic geometry all schemes are assumed to be\textbackslash{}n  Noetherian.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- When \$A\$ is a local ring, we denote its (unique) maximal ideal with a\textbackslash{}n  fraktur symbol, such as \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{p\}\$ or \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- When \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ is a morphism of schemes,\textbackslash{}n  \$f\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\#\}: A \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow B\$ is the induced homomorphism of rings for the\textbackslash{}n  affine morphism \$f:U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow V\$ with\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: B = U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$ and\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A = V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset Y\$ such that \$f(U)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset V\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Other notations are defined in the Appendices.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\# Topological Covering Spaces and Galois Theory\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe fundamental group is a core object from algebraic topology; it is an\textbackslash{}nalgebraic invariant for topological spaces. It is usually defined via\textbackslash{}nhomotopy of closed paths, and many powerful tools can be used to compute\textbackslash{}nthem, such as the *Seifert-Van Kampen theorem* or *deformation\textbackslash{}nretracts*. However, in this thesis we will focus on a method which lies\textbackslash{}nwithin the theory of covering spaces. In this chapter, we describe how\textbackslash{}nfundamental groups arise as automorphism groups of certain covering\textbackslash{}nspaces and present theorems classifying these covering spaces.\textbackslash{}nInterestingly enough, the theory of covering spaces is in some sense\textbackslash{}nparallel to the theory of separable field extension; it has a certain\textbackslash{}n''Galois flavour\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" to it.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# The Fundamental Group in Topology\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe start by defining what homotopies and homotopy groups are. Let \$X\$ be\textbackslash{}na topological space, two paths on \$X\$ are said to be *homotopic* if it\textbackslash{}nis possible to continuously deform one into another. Formally:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 1**. A **homotopy of paths** in \$X\$ starting at \$x\_0\$ and\textbackslash{}nending at \$x\_1\$ is a family of paths \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_t:[0,1]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$\textbackslash{}nindexed by \$I\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- the endpoints are fixed : \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_t(0) = x\_0\$, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_t(1)=x\_1\$ , and\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- the map \$H:I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times[0,1]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ ; \$(t,s)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_t(s)\$ is\textbackslash{}n  continuous.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nTwo paths \$f\$ and \$g\$ are said to be **homotopic** if there is a\textbackslash{}nhomotopy of paths between them and we write \$f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}simeq g\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIt is a straightforward verification to see that the relation\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}"\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_1\$ is homotopic to \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_2\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" is an equivalence relation.\textbackslash{}nLet's denote \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Sigma(X,x)\$ the set of loops in \$X\$ based at \$x\$, now\textbackslash{}npath-homotopy of loops defines an equivalence relation on \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Sigma(X,x)\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 2**. A continuous map \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ is called a\textbackslash{}n**homotopy equivalence** if there exists a continuous map\textbackslash{}n\$g:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ such that \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}simeq  \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{id\}\}\_X\$\textbackslash{}nand \$f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}simeq \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{id\}\}\_Y\$. In this case, the spaces\textbackslash{}n\$X\$ and \$Y\$ are said to be **homotopy equivalent**.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 3**. The **fundamental group** of \$X\$ based at \$x\$, denoted\textbackslash{}nby \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$, is the set of homotopic classes of loops based at \$x\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe fundamental group is also often called the first homotopy group. The\textbackslash{}nsubscript \$1\$ in the fundamental group notation hints at the existence\textbackslash{}nof higher homotopy groups \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_n(X,x)\$, which are similarly considered\textbackslash{}nas sets of homotopy classes based on maps \$f:(S\^{}n,s)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow(X,x)\$.\textbackslash{}nThese higher homotopy groups ''detect\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" higher-dimensional ''holes\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" and\textbackslash{}nthe situation becomes much more complicated. In this thesis, we focus on\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$, which already gives us a very rich theory.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nThe set of loops equipped with the homotopy equivalence relation is\textbackslash{}nindeed a group with its operation being the concatenation of paths\textbackslash{}ndenoted by \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bullet\$ and its inverses correspond to reversing the\textbackslash{}ndirection of paths. Given two paths\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_1,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_2 : [0,1] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ with\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_1(1) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_2(0)\$ we define their concatenation\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bullet\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_2 : [0,1]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ by \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{equation*\}\textbackslash{}n  \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bullet\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_2 =\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{cases\}\textbackslash{}n      \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_1(2t) \& \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{for \$t\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in [0,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}frac\{1\}\{2\}]\$\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n      \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_2(2t-1) \& \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{for \$t\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in [\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}frac\{1\}\{2\}, 1]\$\}.\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{cases\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{equation*\}\$\$\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe say that a topological space is **simply-connected** if and only if\textbackslash{}nits fundamental group is trivial.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 1**. Let \$f:(X,x)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow (Y,y)\$ be a continuous map between\textbackslash{}npointed topological spaces such that \$f(x)=y\$, then we denote by\textbackslash{}n\$f\_*:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y)\$ the induced homomorphism, obtained\textbackslash{}nby composition, \$f\_*([\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]) := [f \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\$ for any\textbackslash{}n\$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAs expected, the fundamental group is a topological invariant :\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 4**. *Homeomorphic spaces have isomorphic fundamental\textbackslash{}ngroups. If \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ is a homeomorphism, then\textbackslash{}n\$f\_ *:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,f(x))\$ is an isomorphism.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* If \$f\$ is a homeomorphism, then\textbackslash{}n\$(f\^{}\{-1\})\_*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f\_* = (f\^{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f)\_* = (id\_X)\_* = id\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\}\$.\textbackslash{}nSimilarly, \$f\_* \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ (f\^{}\{-1\})\_*\$ is the identity on \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,f(x))\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nSimilarly, one proves the following.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: corollary\textbackslash{}n**Corollary 5**. *Two homotopic equivalent spaces have the same\textbackslash{}nfundamental group. If \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ is a homotopy equivalence, then\textbackslash{}n\$f\_ *:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,f(x))\$ is an isomorphism.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nOne thing to notice is that if \$X\$ is not path-connected, the\textbackslash{}nfundamental groups based at points in different path-connected\textbackslash{}ncomponents don't have any relation to each other. Therefore, it is\textbackslash{}ncustomary to consider path-connected topological spaces when studying\textbackslash{}nfundamental groups. The next proposition tells us that in a\textbackslash{}npath-connected space, the fundamental group is insensitive to changes of\textbackslash{}nbase points. Thus, when this is clear, we will sometimes omit to write\textbackslash{}nthe base point.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#fund\_grou\_base\_pt .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 6**. *If \$X\$ is a path-connected topological space, then\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X, x\_0)\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X, x\_1)\$ are isomorphic for any\textbackslash{}n\$x\_0,x\_1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Since two points \$x\_0\$ and \$x\_1\$ may be joined by a path\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\$ starting at \$x\_0\$ and ending at \$x\_1\$, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x\_0)\$ is\textbackslash{}nnon-canonically isomorphic to \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x\_1)\$ via\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bullet \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bullet \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\^{}\{-1\}\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: example\textbackslash{}n**Example 7**. Of course, since \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{R\}\^{}n\$ is contractible, any loop\textbackslash{}nis homotopic to the constant loop, so \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{R\}\^{}n,x) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$\textbackslash{}nfor any base point \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{R\}\^{}n\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nComputing non-trivial fundamental groups such as \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(S\^{}1)\$ is already\textbackslash{}nharder. An alternative is to use the theory of covering spaces and\textbackslash{}nlifting of paths. The calculation of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(S\^{}1)\$ however, has many\textbackslash{}napplications. It allows one to give a proof of the *Fundamental Theorem\textbackslash{}nof Algebra*, to show the *Brouwer's fixed-point theorem in dimension\textbackslash{}n\$2\$* or even to prove the *Borsuk-Ulam theorem in dimension \$2\$* (these\textbackslash{}ntheorems with their proofs can be found in [@Hatcher] as Theorem \$1.8\$,\textbackslash{}n\$1.9\$ and \$1.10\$ respectively).\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nIn the language of categories, the fundamental group is a covariant\textbackslash{}nfunctor which assigns to each pointed topological space \$(X,x)\$ its\textbackslash{}nfundamental group based at \$x\$, and to each pointed continuous map\textbackslash{}n\$f:(X,x)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow(X',x')\$ with \$f(x)=x'\$ its induced homomorphism\textbackslash{}n\$f\_\{*\}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X',f(x))\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Covering Spaces and their Galois structure \{\#fund\_grp\_cov\_spaces\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn this section, we introduce the theory of covering spaces. Then we\textbackslash{}nshow that it exhibits a structure that behaves similarly to that of\textbackslash{}nfield extensions. Later on, we will prove the existence of a so-called\textbackslash{}nuniversal covering that is deeply related to the fundamental group.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n[]\{\#covering\_spaces label=\textbackslash{}"covering\_spaces\textbackslash{}"\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#def\_cover .definition\}\textbackslash{}n**Definition 8**. A **covering** of a topological space \$X\$ consists of\textbackslash{}na topological space \$Y\$ and a map \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ with the following\textbackslash{}nproperty : for any \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$ there exists a neighbourhood \$U\$ of \$x\$ such\textbackslash{}nthat\textbackslash{}n\$\$p\^{}\{-1\}(U) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigsqcup\_\{y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\} V\_y  \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{ and \} p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_\{V\_y\}:V\_y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow U \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{ is a homeomorphism\}\$\$\textbackslash{}nfor each \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in p\^{}\{-1\}\$. The sets \$V\_y\$ are called sheets of the\textbackslash{}ncovering. We define a morphism between the covers \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$q:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ to be a continuous map \$f:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ making the\textbackslash{}nfollowing diagram commute, \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{tikzcd\}[column sep=small]\textbackslash{}n        Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[rd,\textbackslash{}"p\textbackslash{}"'] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[rr,\textbackslash{}"f\textbackslash{}"]   \&   \&Z \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[ld,\textbackslash{}"q\textbackslash{}"]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n          \& X      \textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{tikzcd\}\$\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThis makes a category over the topological space \$X\$, whose objects are\textbackslash{}ncovers of \$X\$ and morphisms are morphisms of covers of \$X\$, called the\textbackslash{}ncategory of covers of \$X\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#connected\_constant\_sheets .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 2**. In the following, we will assume that \$X\$ is\textbackslash{}n(path)-connected, otherwise we can simply consider coverings of\textbackslash{}nconnected components individually. The definition yields that each fibre\textbackslash{}n\$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ is a discrete set for any \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$, since each sheet \$V\_y\$\textbackslash{}ncontains a unique point of \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$, namely \$y\$. If this set is\textbackslash{}nfinite for any \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$, then the number of sheets \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\#p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ is\textbackslash{}nconstant over \$U\$ and (since \$X\$ is connected) constant over \$X\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nFor the purposes of our thesis, we further assume that all our\textbackslash{}ntopological spaces are locally path-connected and semi-locally\textbackslash{}nsimply-connected. These assumption can be understood as the technical\textbackslash{}nbedrock for covering space theory to hold.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nHowever, as our first example shows, we do not require that the above\textbackslash{}ncovering space must be connected :\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#example\_covering .examples\}\textbackslash{}n**Examples 9**.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Let \$I\$ be a non-empty discrete topological space and form the\textbackslash{}n  topological product \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times I\$. The projection on the first component\textbackslash{}n  \$p:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ turns \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times I\$ into a cover of \$X\$ with\textbackslash{}n  fibre \$I\$. We call this the **trivial cover**.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Consider the circle \$S\^{}1\$, with a map \$p:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{R\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\^{}1\$\textbackslash{}n  defined by \$p(t)=e\^{}\{2\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi i t\}\$. This map is clearly a connected\textbackslash{}n  covering of \$S\^{}1\$, locally \$S\^{}1\$ is homeomorphic to \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{R\}\$, and\textbackslash{}n  it is even an infinitely sheeted covering. An insightful picture is to\textbackslash{}n  think about the covering as an infinite helix above the circle.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn this sense, every covering space can be characterised as being\textbackslash{}nlocally trivial. And if \$X\$ is connected, the fibres of \$p\$ are all\textbackslash{}nhomeomorphic to the same discrete space \$I\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nOf course the composition of two coverings maps is still a covering map\textbackslash{}nwhere the number of sheets might be greater. We also have the following\textbackslash{}nproposition about composition of coverings. We say that a cover is\textbackslash{}n*connected* is the covering space is connected.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#composition\_covers .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 10**. *Let \$q:Z \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be a connected cover and\textbackslash{}n\$f:Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ be a continuous map. If the composition\textbackslash{}n\$q\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f:Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is a cover, then so is \$f:Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* We first show that for any open neighbourhood \$V\$ of \$z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Z\$,\textbackslash{}nits preimage by \$f\$ is a disjoint union of open sets such that each of\textbackslash{}nthem map homeomorphically onto \$V\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nLet \$x= q(z)\$ and \$U\$ be an open neighbourhood of \$x\$ such that its\textbackslash{}npreimages by \$q\$ and \$p=q\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f\$ are \$q\^{}\{-1\}(U) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigsqcup\_i V\_i\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$p\^{}\{-1\}(U) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigsqcup\_j W\_j\$ as in the definition of covering maps. So,\textbackslash{}nfor each \$W\_j \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset Y\$, its image \$f(W\_j)\$ is a connected subset of\textbackslash{}n\$Z\$ mapped by \$q\$ onto \$U\$, hence there is some \$i\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\$f(W\_j)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset V\_i\$. Which is actually a homeomorphism since both\textbackslash{}n\$f(W\_j)\$ and \$V\_i\$ are homeomorphically mapped onto \$U\$ by \$q\$. This\textbackslash{}nshows that the preimage of any \$V\_i\$ by \$f\$ is a disjoint union of\textbackslash{}n\$W\_j\$'s.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nNow we show that \$f\$ is surjective. First notice that the argument above\textbackslash{}nimplies that \$f(Y)\$ is open in \$Z\$. Since \$Z\$ is connected it is enough\textbackslash{}nto now prove that \$Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}backslash f(Y)\$ is also open. If\textbackslash{}n\$z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}backslash f(Y)\$ and \$U\$ is a neighbourhood of \$x=q(z)\$ as above,\textbackslash{}nthen the whole component \$V\_i\$ of \$q\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ containing \$z\$ must be\textbackslash{}ndisjoint from \$f(Y)\$, otherwise the whole component would have to be\textbackslash{}ncontained in \$f(Y)\$ which is a contradiction. This shows that \$f\$ is\textbackslash{}nsurjective, concluding the proof. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nPowerful tools in the study of covering spaces are the following lifting\textbackslash{}nlemmas:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#unique\_lift .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 11** (Lifting (Homotopy) Property). *Let \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be a\textbackslash{}ncover, \$y\$ a point of \$Y\$ and \$x=p(y)\$.*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *Given a path \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma:[0,1]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ starting at \$x\$, there is a\textbackslash{}n  unique lift \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}:[0,1]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ with\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}(0)=y\$ and \$p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\$.*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *For each homotopy \$h:I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times [0,1]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ such that\textbackslash{}n  \$h(t,0) = x\$ for all \$t\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$, there is a unique lift\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{h\}:I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times [0,1]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ such that\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{h\}(t,0) = y\$ for all \$t\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Hartshorne] (Prop.1.30 and 1.34). ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#lift\_criterion .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 12** (Lifting Criterion). *Let \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be a connected\textbackslash{}ncovering and \$f:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be a continuous map. Then a lift\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{f\}: Z \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ of \$f\$ exists if and only if\textbackslash{}n\$f\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Z,z))\$ is a subgroup of \$p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y))\$ for\textbackslash{}n\$(y,z)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times Z\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Hartshorne](Prop. 1.33). ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe following lemma is the universal property for continuous maps with\textbackslash{}nthe quotient topology.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#univ\_ppty\_lift .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 13**. *Let \$X\$ and \$Y\$ be topological spaces and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sim\$ be an\textbackslash{}nequivalence relation on \$Y\$. Let \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be a continuous map\textbackslash{}nsuch that for all \$y,y'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\$, \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sim y' \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Rightarrow p(y)=p(y')\$. Then\textbackslash{}nthere exists a unique continuous map\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{p\}: Y/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sim \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ with \$p=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{p\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\$ for\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sim\$ the natural projection*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@munkrs], Theorem \$II.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:22.2\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAs the above lifting properties suggest, there is an intimate connection\textbackslash{}nbetween covering maps and fundamental groups. The key to further\textbackslash{}nunderstanding this connection is a natural action on each fibre of a\textbackslash{}ncovering by the fundamental group of the base called the *monodromy\textbackslash{}naction*.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 14** (The Monodromy Action). *Let \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be a\textbackslash{}nconnected covering and \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$. There is a transitive left action of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$ on the fibre \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ called the **monodromy action**,\textbackslash{}ngiven by \$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_y(1)\$ for\textbackslash{}n\$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$, \$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_y\$ the\textbackslash{}nunique lift of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\$ in \$Y\$ starting at \$y\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Let any \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$, then the path-lifting property\textbackslash{}n[11](\#unique\_lift)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"unique\_lift\textbackslash{}"\}\textbackslash{}nassociates to every loop \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\$ based at \$x\$ in \$X\$ a unique lift\textbackslash{}nwhich is a path \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_y\$ starting at \$y\$ and finishing at\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_y(1)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$. By lifting of homotopies we have\textbackslash{}nthat if \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_1 \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sim \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_2\$, then\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_1\}\_y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sim \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_2\}\_y\$, so\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_y(1)\$ depends only on the path-class of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\$\textbackslash{}n(\$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y\$ is now well defined). Let us prove that this is\textbackslash{}nindeed a group action. Since the constant path is the unique lift of the\textbackslash{}nconstant loop \$[c] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{c\_y\}(1) = y\$. Suppose \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\$\textbackslash{}nand \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta\$ are two loops based at \$x\$ and let\textbackslash{}n\$z = [\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_y\}(1)\$, then\textbackslash{}n\$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot ([\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta\_z\}(1)\$. And\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta\_z\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bullet \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_y\}\$ being the lift of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bullet\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\$ at \$y\$, we associativity as follows:\textbackslash{}n\$\$([\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bullet[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma])\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y = [\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bullet\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y = (\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta\_z\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bullet\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_y\})(1) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta\_z\}(1) = [\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot ([\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y)\$\$\textbackslash{}nAnd finally since \$Y\$ is path-connected, any two points \$y, y'\$ in\textbackslash{}n\$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ are joined by a path \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega\$ in \$Y\$. Setting\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma = p \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega\$ (\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega\$ becomes a loop when its endpoints\textbackslash{}nare collapsed together by \$p\$), we see that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega\$ is actually a lift\textbackslash{}nof \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\$ and therefore by monodromy action \$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y = y'\$.\textbackslash{}nThe action is transitive on \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nBelow we prove a theorem that is a direct consequences of the lifting\textbackslash{}nproperties.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#property\_morphism\_covers .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 15**. *Let \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ and \$q:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be two\textbackslash{}ncoverings.*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *If two morphism of coverings from \$p\$ to \$q\$ agree at one point of\textbackslash{}n  \$Y\$, then they are equal.*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *Fixing \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$, any morphism between the coverings \$p\$ and \$q\$\textbackslash{}n  restrict to a \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$-equivariant map from \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ to\textbackslash{}n  \$q\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ (with respect to the monodromy action).*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* A morphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ of covers can also be seen\textbackslash{}nas a lift of \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$. Thus uniqueness follows from uniqueness\textbackslash{}nof the lifting property proving \$a)\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nSuppose \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ is a morphism of covers (from \$p\$ to\textbackslash{}n\$q\$). By definition, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\$ maps \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ to \$q\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$. Now,\textbackslash{}ngiven \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$, \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ and \$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$, we need to\textbackslash{}nshow that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi([\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y)= [\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi(y)\$. Let\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_y\$ be the lift of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\$ to a path in \$Y\$ starting\textbackslash{}nat \$y\$, and consider the path \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_y\$ in \$Z\$.\textbackslash{}nIts initial point is \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_y(0) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi(y)\$\textbackslash{}nand it satisfies\textbackslash{}n\$q\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_y = p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_y\$,\textbackslash{}nso \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_y\$ is the lift of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\$ to \$Z\$\textbackslash{}nstarting at \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi(y)\$. Therefore, by the monodromy action,\textbackslash{}n\$\$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi(y) = (\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_y)(1) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_y(1)) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi([\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y).\$\$ ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nA clever way of retrieving new covering spaces from existing ones, is to\textbackslash{}nconsider their quotient by some group action. Let us define the\textbackslash{}nappropriate group action needed in this case :\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#properly\_discontinuous .definition\}\textbackslash{}n**Definition 16**. A group \$G\$ acting on a topological space \$X\$ by\textbackslash{}nhomeomorphisms (here we may understand by automorphisms) is said to act\textbackslash{}n**properly discontinuously** if for each \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$, there exist an open\textbackslash{}nneighbourhood \$U\$ of \$x\$ such that \$(g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot U)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap U = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}emptyset\$ for\textbackslash{}nall \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\$ and \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}neq 1\$. Properly discontinuous actions are also\textbackslash{}ncalled covering space actions.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#quotient\_cover .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 17**. *Let \$Y\$ be a connected topological space and let\textbackslash{}n\$G\$ act on \$Y\$ properly discontinuously. Then the quotient map\textbackslash{}n\$p\_G : Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y/G\$ is a covering.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* The map \$p\_G\$ is surjective and moreover each \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y/G\$ has an\textbackslash{}nopen neighbourhood of the form \$U = p\_G(V)\$ with \$V\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap (g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot V)=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}emptyset\$ for all \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\$ with \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}neq 1\$. And \$U\$\textbackslash{}nsatisfies the conditions of Definition\textbackslash{}n[8](\#def\_cover)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"def\_cover\textbackslash{}"\} so that \$Y\$\textbackslash{}nbecomes a covering of \$Y/G\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe now introduce a particular group which has the property of acting\textbackslash{}nproperly discontinuously on covering spaces.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 18**. Let \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be a covering. A **deck\textbackslash{}ntransformation** is a homeomorphism \$d:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ such that the\textbackslash{}nfollowing diagram commutes. \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{tikzcd\}[column sep=small]\textbackslash{}n                Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[rd,\textbackslash{}"p\textbackslash{}"'] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[rr,\textbackslash{}"d\textbackslash{}"]   \&   \&Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[ld,\textbackslash{}"p\textbackslash{}"]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n                                        \& X                        \textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{tikzcd\}\$\$ Together with composition, the set of deck\textbackslash{}ntransformations forms a group denoted \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Deck\}\}(p)\$ or\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\$ \$(\$the second notation may be familiar to\textbackslash{}nthe reader, as it resembles the notation used to describe Galois\textbackslash{}ngroups\$)\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nNotice that for any \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$, the automorphism group\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\$ sends all of \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ to itself. We\textbackslash{}nfurther assume that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\$ acts on \$Y\$ by the\textbackslash{}nleft.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#corollary\_property\_morphism\_covers .corollary\}\textbackslash{}n**Corollary 19**. *A homeomorphism \$d\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\$ of\textbackslash{}na connected covering \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ having a fixed point must be\textbackslash{}ntrivial.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* This is immediate from Theorem\textbackslash{}n[15](\#property\_morphism\_covers)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"property\_morphism\_covers\textbackslash{}"\} if we take one (auto)morphism of\textbackslash{}ncovers to be the deck transformation \$d\$ and another one to be the\textbackslash{}nidentity. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 20**. *If \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is a connected covering, the\textbackslash{}naction of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\$ on \$Y\$ is properly\textbackslash{}ndiscontinuous.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Let \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\$ and set \$x = p(y)\$. Let \$U\$ be a connected open\textbackslash{}nneighbourhood of \$x\$ such that \$p\^{}\{-1\}(U)\$ is a disjoint union of open\textbackslash{}nsets \$V\_i\$ as in the Definition [8](\#def\_cover)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"def\_cover\textbackslash{}"\}, where one of these opens, let's say \$V\_i\$,\textbackslash{}ncontains \$y\$. For \$d\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\$ non-trivial, \$d\$\textbackslash{}nmaps \$V\_i\$ isomorphically onto some \$V\_j\$ by definition of a deck\textbackslash{}ntransformation. Since \$Y\$ is connected, we can apply Corollary\textbackslash{}n[19](\#corollary\_property\_morphism\_covers)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"corollary\_property\_morphism\_covers\textbackslash{}"\} and since \$d\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}neq id\_Y\$,\textbackslash{}nwe must have \$i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}neq j\$. This satisfies the condition of properly\textbackslash{}ndiscontinuity. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nOne more thing can be said about the group \$G\$, acting properly\textbackslash{}ndiscontinuously on the connected topological spaces \$Y\$ and the\textbackslash{}nassociate quotient map \$p\_G:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y/G\$ from Proposition\textbackslash{}n[17](\#quotient\_cover)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"quotient\_cover\textbackslash{}"\}:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#G\_is\_aut\_group .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 21**. *If \$G\$ is a group acting properly discontinuously\textbackslash{}non a connected space \$Y\$, the automorphism group of the covering\textbackslash{}n\$p\_G:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y/G\$ is precisely \$G\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Since \$G\$ acts by homeomorphism on \$Y\$ and \$p\$ sends any\textbackslash{}n\$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\$ to \$p(y)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y/G\$, then \$p(y) = p(g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y)\$ by properly\textbackslash{}ndiscontinuity of the action of \$G\$ onto \$Y\$, therefore \$G\$ is a subgroup\textbackslash{}nof \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|(Y/G))\$. Now, let\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y, (Y/G))\$, and \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\$. Since the fibres\textbackslash{}nof \$p\_G\$ are exactly the orbits of \$G\$ (we quotient \$Y\$ by it), we may\textbackslash{}nfind \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\$ such that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi(y) = g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y\$. Now applying Corollary\textbackslash{}n[19](\#corollary\_property\_morphism\_covers)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"corollary\_property\_morphism\_covers\textbackslash{}"\} to the homeomorphism\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ g\^{}\{-1\}\$, we get \$g=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFrom the previous propositions, it is now obvious that for a connected\textbackslash{}ncovering \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$, we have the following decomposition\textbackslash{}n\$p = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{p\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ p\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\} : Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow\{p\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\}\} Y/ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{p\}\} X\$.\textbackslash{}nWhere \$p\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\}\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{p\}\$ are continuous\textbackslash{}nmaps and \$p\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\}\$ is a now a *subcovering* of\textbackslash{}n\$p\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 22**. We say that a covering \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is\textbackslash{}n**Galois** or **Normal** if \$Y\$ is connected and if the map\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{p\}\$ defined above is a homeomorphism.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe previous proposition already gives us an example of Galois\textbackslash{}ncoverings. These types of coverings will turn out to be important in the\textbackslash{}nclassification of covering spaces (Theorem\textbackslash{}n[26](\#clasification\_of\_covers)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"clasification\_of\_covers\textbackslash{}"\}), playing a similar role to Galois\textbackslash{}nfield extensions in the Main Theorem of Galois.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#Galois\_free .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 3**. If \$Y\$ is a connected Galois covering of \$X\$, then\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\$ acts freely on \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ for any\textbackslash{}n\$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$. This follows by Corollary\textbackslash{}n[19](\#corollary\_property\_morphism\_covers)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"corollary\_property\_morphism\_covers\textbackslash{}"\}, indeed for any two\textbackslash{}npoints \$y\$ and \$y'\$ in \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$, there is an automorphism\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\$ mapping \$p(y)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto p(y')\$.\textbackslash{}nSuppose that there exists another such automorphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi'\$. Then we can\textbackslash{}nconstruct a map \$d:= \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\^{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi'\$, fixing \$p\$. By the corollary\textbackslash{}nit must be the identity and thus \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi'\$, meaning that the action\textbackslash{}nis not only transitive but also free.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFinally, we will give equivalent characterisations of Galois covers. But\textbackslash{}nfirst, we need two lemmas\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#induced\_subgroup .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 23**. *Let \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be a connected covering and\textbackslash{}n\$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$. For each \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$, the stabiliser of \$y\$ under the\textbackslash{}nmonodromy action is \$p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y)) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}leq \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$. And as \$y\$ varies\textbackslash{}nover the fibre \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$, the set of induced subgroups\textbackslash{}n\$p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y))\$ is exactly one conjugacy class in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Let \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ be arbitrary, and suppose that \$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\$\textbackslash{}nis in the stabiliser of \$y\$. This means that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_y(1) = [\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y = y\$ (by the monodromy\textbackslash{}naction), hence \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\$ is actually a loop in \$Y\$ and thus\textbackslash{}nrepresents an element in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y)\$. And by uniqueness of lifts we\textbackslash{}nhave that the induced map \$p\_* : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x\$ sends\textbackslash{}n\$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_y]\$ to \$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\$, so \$p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y))\$.\textbackslash{}nConversely, if \$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y))\$, then there is a loop\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta\$ in \$Y\$ based at \$y\$ such that \$p\_*([\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta]) = [\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\$, which\textbackslash{}nmeans that \$p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\$ are homotopic equivalent. Denote\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma' = p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta\$, then \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma'\}\_y\$ by\textbackslash{}nuniqueness of lifts and\textbackslash{}n\$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y = [\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma']\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma'\}\_y(1) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta(1) = y\$,\textbackslash{}nwhich means that \$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma]\$ is in the stabiliser of \$y\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nThe last statement follows from Theorem\textbackslash{}n[264](\#Cameron\_1\_3)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"Cameron\_1\_3\textbackslash{}"\} on the\textbackslash{}nclassification of transitive \$G\$-spaces by conjugacy classes subgroups\textbackslash{}nof \$G\$ and quotients by stabilisers. As \$y\$ varies over \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$, the\textbackslash{}nset of stabilisers of \$y\$ is exactly one conjugacy class in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$\textbackslash{}n(recall that the monodromy action is a transitive action). ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe following lemma is actually a criterion for deciding whether the\textbackslash{}nmorphism of coverings of Theorem\textbackslash{}n[15](\#property\_morphism\_covers)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"property\_morphism\_covers\textbackslash{}"\} is actually an isomorphism.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#isomorphism\_conjugate .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 24**. *Let \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ and \$q:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be two\textbackslash{}nconnected coverings.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n\$Y\$ and \$Z\$ are isomorphic if and only if, for some \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$ the\textbackslash{}nconjugacy classes of subgroups of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$ induced by \$q\_1\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$q\_2\$ are the same.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* First assume that \$Y\$ and \$Z\$ are isomorphic. For any \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$,\textbackslash{}nthis isomorphism restrict to a \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$-equivariant bijection from\textbackslash{}n\$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ to \$q\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ as in Theorem\textbackslash{}n[15](\#property\_morphism\_covers)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"property\_morphism\_covers\textbackslash{}"\}. So the sets of stabilisers of\textbackslash{}npoints in \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ and in \$q\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ are in the same conjugacy class\textbackslash{}nsubgroup as Theorem [264](\#Cameron\_1\_3)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Cameron\_1\_3\textbackslash{}"\} suggests. And since these groups are exactly\textbackslash{}nthe induced subgroups \$p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y))\$ and \$q\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Z,z))\$ form Lemma\textbackslash{}n[23](\#induced\_subgroup)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"induced\_subgroup\textbackslash{}"\}, they must be conjugate.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nNow suppose that \$p\$ and \$q\$ induce the same conjugacy class of\textbackslash{}nsubgroups for some \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$. Choosing \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\$ arbitrarily, by Lemma\textbackslash{}n[23](\#induced\_subgroup)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"induced\_subgroup\textbackslash{}"\}, there is some \$z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Z\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\$p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y)) = q\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Z,z))\$. By the Lifting Criterion, there\textbackslash{}nexist homomorphism of coverings \$f : Z \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$g: Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ (since they are essentially lifts) with \$f(z) = y\$\textbackslash{}nand \$g(y)=z\$. The composites \$f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ g\$ and \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f\$ are covering\textbackslash{}nhomomorphism fixing \$z\$ and \$y\$ respectively, so by Corollary\textbackslash{}n[19](\#corollary\_property\_morphism\_covers)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"corollary\_property\_morphism\_covers\textbackslash{}"\}, they are identities,\textbackslash{}nthere is an isomorphism of coverings between \$p\$ and \$q\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFinally we get to the following characterisation,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#caracterize\_Galois\_cov .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 25**. *Let \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be a connected covering.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nThe following conditions are equivalent :*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *\$p\$ is a Galois covering.*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *\$Y\$ is connected and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\$ acts transitively\textbackslash{}n  on the fibre \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ for any \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$.*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *The stabiliser \$p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y))\$ is a normal subgroup of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$\textbackslash{}n  for any \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* \$a) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Leftrightarrow b)\$ ; by definition, the underlying set of\textbackslash{}n\$Y/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\$ is the\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\$-orbits of \$Y\$. So the map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{p\}\$ is\textbackslash{}none to one precisely when each such orbits is equal to a whole fibre of\textbackslash{}n\$p\$ or equivalently that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\$ acts transitively\textbackslash{}non each fibre. And since \$X\$ is connected, all fibres are homeomorphic\textbackslash{}nto the same discrete space.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\$b) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Leftrightarrow c)\$ ; fix \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$. Combining Lemmas\textbackslash{}n[23](\#induced\_subgroup)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"induced\_subgroup\textbackslash{}"\} and\textbackslash{}n[24](\#isomorphism\_conjugate)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"isomorphism\_conjugate\textbackslash{}"\}, we have that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\$ acts transitively on \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ if and\textbackslash{}nonly if the subgroups \$p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y))\$ are the same for all \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\$.\textbackslash{}nAnd since they are conjugacy classes, it is equivalent to saying that\textbackslash{}n\$p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y))\$ is a normal subgroup of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe now touch upon the classification of topological covering spaces,\textbackslash{}nwhich is surprisingly similar to the Galois correspondence of field\textbackslash{}nextensions, here, Galois covers play the role of Galois field\textbackslash{}nextensions, the Galois groups are automorphism groups of covers, and as\textbackslash{}nwe will see later, universal coverings are separable closures.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#clasification\_of\_covers .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 26** (Main Classification of Coverings). *Let \$X\$ be a\textbackslash{}nconnected topological space, \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be a Galois cover and\textbackslash{}n\$G\$ the group automorphisms of \$p\$. If \$q:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is a connected\textbackslash{}ncover such that \$p = q\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f\$ for \$f:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$, then \$f\$ is a\textbackslash{}nGalois cover and \$Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong Y/H\$ (where \$H=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|Z)\$ is a\textbackslash{}nsubgroup of \$G\$). The maps \$H\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto Y/H\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|Z)\$ induce a bijection between the\textbackslash{}nsubgroups of \$G\$ and the intermediate covers \$Z\$ as above. The cover\textbackslash{}n\$q:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is Galois if and only if\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|Z)=H\$ is a normal subgroup of \$G\$ (in that\textbackslash{}ncase, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Z|X) = G /H\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* By hypothesis, the map \$p\$ factors as the composite\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{p\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ p\_H\$ with \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{p\}= Y/H\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$p\_H:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y/H\$ for \$H\$ a subgroup of \$G\$. Since \$p\$ and \$p\_H\$\textbackslash{}nare coverings (Proposition [17](\#quotient\_cover)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"quotient\_cover\textbackslash{}"\}), then \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{p\}\$ is continuous.\textbackslash{}nMoreover, \$p\$ is a covering, so by definition, there exists an open set\textbackslash{}n\$U\$ in \$X\$ such that \$p\^{}\{-1\}(U) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times I\$ and the subgroup \$H\$ of\textbackslash{}n\$G\$ acts on \$I\$. So we have that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{p\}\^{}\{-1\}(U)\$ is open subset\textbackslash{}nof \$Y/H\$ with \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{p\}\^{}\{-1\}(U)=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times J\$ where \$J\$ is the\textbackslash{}nset of \$H\$-orbits of \$I\$. Hence \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{p\}\$ is a cover since locally\textbackslash{}n(for a sufficiently small open set) it is a trivial cover.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nNow suppose that \$q:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is a connected cover with\textbackslash{}n\$p=q\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f\$ as above. Then by Proposition\textbackslash{}n[10](\#composition\_covers)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"composition\_covers\textbackslash{}"\}, \$f:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ is a covering map as\textbackslash{}nwell. To see that it is moreover a Galois cover, by the characterisation\textbackslash{}n[25](\#caracterize\_Galois\_cov)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"caracterize\_Galois\_cov\textbackslash{}"\} of Galois coverings, we need to\textbackslash{}ncheck that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|Z)\$ acts transitively on a fibres of\textbackslash{}n\$f\$. Let \$z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Z\$ and \$y\_1,y\_2\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in f\^{}\{-1\}(z)\$. Then\textbackslash{}n\$y\_1,y\_2\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in p\^{}\{-1\}(q(z))\$ because \$f\^{}\{-1\}(z) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset p\^{}\{-1\}( q(z))\$.\textbackslash{}nSince \$p\$ is a Galois covering, there exists\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\$ such that \$y\_1 = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi(y\_2)\$. We are\textbackslash{}ndone if we show that actually \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|Z)\$, which\textbackslash{}nis equivalent to saying that the set \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid f(y)=f(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi(y))\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$\textbackslash{}nis equal to the whole of \$Y\$. But this follows from Theorem\textbackslash{}n[15](\#property\_morphism\_covers)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"property\_morphism\_covers\textbackslash{}"\}, so we have that \$f = f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\$\textbackslash{}nand \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid f(y)=f(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi(y))\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\} = Y\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|Z)\$. The above two constructions being\textbackslash{}ninverse to each other, only the last statement is left to prove.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nOne implication is easy. Since \$p\$ is a Galois covering, if \$H\$ is a\textbackslash{}nnormal subgroup of \$G\$, then \$G/H\$ acts transitively on fibres of \$q\$ in\textbackslash{}n\$Z=Y/H\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset Y\$. Making \$q:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ a Galois cover.
