And by\textbackslash{}ndefinition of Galois covers and Proposition\textbackslash{}n[21](\#G\_is\_aut\_group)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"G\_is\_aut\_group\textbackslash{}"\},\textbackslash{}n\$Z/(G/H) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong X\$ and so \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Z|X)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong G/H\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nFor the other implication, assume that \$q:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is a Galois\textbackslash{}ncovering. What we want to show is that each\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X)\$ induces an automorphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\$\textbackslash{}nof \$Z\$ over \$X\$, which in term induces a group homomorphism\textbackslash{}n\$h : G \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Z|X)\$ given by\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\$. Let \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\$ with \$x = p(x)= (q\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f)(y)\$. Since\textbackslash{}n\$q\$ is a covering, \$f(y)\$ and \$f(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi(y))\$ are in the same fibre\textbackslash{}n\$q\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ of \$q\$. \$q\$ being moreover Galois, there is an automorphism\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Z|X)\$ with \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi(f(y))=f(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi(y))\$\textbackslash{}nby transitivity of automorphism groups of Galois covers. Our group\textbackslash{}nhomomorphism \$h\$ is well-defined since \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\$ is unique, for if\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Z|X)\$ was another such automorphism, by\textbackslash{}nTheorem [15](\#property\_morphism\_covers)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"property\_morphism\_covers\textbackslash{}"\}, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\$. By the same\textbackslash{}nargument, the maps \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f\$ and \$f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\$ are equal making\textbackslash{}nthe following diagrams commute \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{tikzcd\}\textbackslash{}n        Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[r,\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\textbackslash{}"] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d, \textbackslash{}"f\textbackslash{}"'] \& Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d,\textbackslash{}"f\textbackslash{}"] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n        Z \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[r,\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\textbackslash{}"] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d,\textbackslash{}"q\textbackslash{}"'] \& Z \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d,\textbackslash{}"q\textbackslash{}"]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n        X \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[r, \textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{id\}\}\textbackslash{}"'] \& X\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{tikzcd\}\$\$ And since the kernel of the morphism \$h\$ is simply\textbackslash{}n\$H = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Z|X)\$, we have that indeed \$H\$ is a normal\textbackslash{}nsubgroup of \$G\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe end our discussion on covering spaces and actions with the following\textbackslash{}ntwo results linking deck transformations and monodromy actions. Below,\textbackslash{}nwe denote for \$H\$ a subgroup of \$G\$, the *normaliser* of \$H\$ in \$G\$ as\textbackslash{}n\$N\_G(H) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid gH=Hg\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#th\_link\_aut\_fund .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 27**. *Let \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be a covering map and fix\textbackslash{}n\$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\$ and \$x = p(y)\$. Then we have the following isomorphism\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}frac\{N\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\}(p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y)))\}\{p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y))\}  .\$\$*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Intro\_manifolds], Theorem \$12.7\$ ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#co\_link\_aut\_fund .corollary\}\textbackslash{}n**Corollary 28**. *For \$X\$, \$Y\$, \$x\$ and \$y\$ as in Theorem\textbackslash{}n[27](\#th\_link\_aut\_fund)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"th\_link\_aut\_fund\textbackslash{}"\}. If the covering \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is a\textbackslash{}nGalois covering, then\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|X) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}frac\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\}\{p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y))\}.\$\$*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Follows from Theorem\textbackslash{}n[27](\#th\_link\_aut\_fund)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"th\_link\_aut\_fund\textbackslash{}"\} since \$p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y))\$ is a normal\textbackslash{}nsubgroup of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$ (Theorem\textbackslash{}n[25](\#caracterize\_Galois\_cov)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"caracterize\_Galois\_cov\textbackslash{}"\}). ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 4**.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Recall from Theorem [27](\#th\_link\_aut\_fund)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}n  reference=\textbackslash{}"th\_link\_aut\_fund\textbackslash{}"\} and Corollary\textbackslash{}n  [28](\#co\_link\_aut\_fund)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}n  reference=\textbackslash{}"co\_link\_aut\_fund\textbackslash{}"\} that the Main Classification of\textbackslash{}n  Coverings for \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ Galois can be restated in terms of\textbackslash{}n  fundamental groups \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$ and induced subgroups\textbackslash{}n  \$p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y))\$ as follow:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n  **Theorem :** *Let \$X\$ be a connected topological space and \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$\textbackslash{}n  is any base point. There is a one-to-one correspondence between\textbackslash{}n  isomorphism classes of coverings of \$X\$ and conjugacy classes of\textbackslash{}n  subgroups of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$. The correspondence associates each covering\textbackslash{}n  \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ with the conjugacy class of its induced subgroup\textbackslash{}n  \$p\_*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(Y,y))\$.*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- From the classification of covering spaces, it is now direct that if\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$ is abelian, every covering of \$X\$ is a Galois covering.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Universal Cover and Fundamental Group \{\#universal\_cover\_section\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn the previous section, we discussed the concept of subcovers, or\textbackslash{}ncovers that cover other covers. We now introduce a new type of covering\textbackslash{}nspace, which can be thought of as the covering of all coverings,\textbackslash{}ninherently called the universal cover.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 29**. Let \$X\$ be a path-connected, locally simply-connected\textbackslash{}ntopological space and pick a base point \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$. The covering\textbackslash{}n\$q: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is called an **universal cover** if\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x\$ is simply-connected.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIt is important to note that universal covers do not exists in general.\textbackslash{}nBut for sufficiently nice topological spaces (path-connected, simply\textbackslash{}npath-connected) they always exists, for more on this, we refer to\textbackslash{}n[@Hatcher] page \$63\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: construction\textbackslash{}n**Construction 30**. For \$X\$ path-connected and locally\textbackslash{}nsimply-connected, there is a way to construct a **simply-connected\textbackslash{}ncover** \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x\$ of \$X\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nThe points of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x\$ are homotopy classes of paths on \$X\$\textbackslash{}nstarting from \$x\$. That way, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x\$ has a canonical point\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{x\}\$ corresponding to the constant path on \$x\$. This\textbackslash{}nconstruction is motivated by the fact that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x\$ has to be\textbackslash{}nsimply-connected, thus any two points of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x\$ can be joined\textbackslash{}nby a unique homotopy class of paths. The projection\textbackslash{}n\$q: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is defined as follows: take a point\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{y\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x\$ consider its representing path\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma:[0,1]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ starting at \$x\$ and ending at \$y\$, and set\textbackslash{}n\$q(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{y\})=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma(1)=y\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nSimply-connected covers constructed that way are endowed with the\textbackslash{}nfollowing topology: consider as a basis of open neighbourhoods of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{y\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x\$, the sets \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{U\}\$. Thus as above\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\$ sends the path\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot r\_n(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_m)\$ defined by the\textbackslash{}nendpoint \$n+m\$ to its image under \$p\$, which is the homotopy class of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_m\$. So \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma(n+m) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma(n)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma(m)\$,\textbackslash{}nmaking \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\$ a morphism of groups.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nConsider a loop \$f\$ in \$S\^{}1\$ with base point \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in S\^{}1\$ that represents\textbackslash{}nan element of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(S\^{}1)\$. Again, by the path-lifting property, there\textbackslash{}nexist a unique lift \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{f\}\$ that starts at \$0\$ and ends at \$n\$\textbackslash{}nsince \$p(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{f\}(1)) = f(1) = x\$ and \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Z\}\$.\textbackslash{}nTherefore by our reconsiderations above, we have that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma(n) = [p(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{f\})] = [f]\$, so \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\$ is surjective. Now\textbackslash{}nsuppose that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma(n) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma(m)\$, implying that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_n \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}simeq\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_m\$. Let \$h\$ be the homotopy between \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_n\$\textbackslash{}nand \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\_m\$. By the homotopy lifting property\textbackslash{}n[11](\#unique\_lift)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"unique\_lift\textbackslash{}"\}, there\textbackslash{}nis a unique homotopy lift \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{h\}\$ between the paths\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_n\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_m\$. Moreover it implies\textbackslash{}nthat \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_n \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}simeq \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}gamma\}\_m\$ which means that\textbackslash{}n\$n=m\$, proving that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\$ is injective. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe finish our introduction on covering spaces and topological\textbackslash{}nfundamental groups by invoking a result about compact manifolds.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 38**. *A compact manifold is homotopy equivalent to a CW\textbackslash{}ncomplex.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Hatcher], Corollary \$A.12\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAnd as consequence of the Van Kampen Theorem, we have the following\textbackslash{}napplication for CW complexes:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 39**. *The fundamental group of a CW complex is finitely\textbackslash{}npresented.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Hatcher], Chapter \$1.2\$, Applications to Cell\textbackslash{}nComplexes. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFrom this, for every compact manifold \$M\$, its fundamental group\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(M)\$ is finitely presented.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# A Reformulation of Classical Galois Theory\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn this section, we present a reformulation of the famous classification\textbackslash{}nof field extensions by Galois-correspondence. It was an idea originated\textbackslash{}nby Grothendieck who recognised that the Galois correspondence was really\textbackslash{}na statement about group action and sets, we shall refer to such\textbackslash{}nrealisations with the French expression ''à la Grothendieck\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}". This\textbackslash{}nreformulation could be seen as a genesis for this thesis since this idea\textbackslash{}nmotivated Grothendieck to develop an analogous theory for the\textbackslash{}nclassification of topological covering spaces. With these two\textbackslash{}nreformulations at hand, Grothendieck, in his more than influential\textbackslash{}n*Séminaires de Géométrie Algébrique* [@SGA] developed the theory of\textbackslash{}nfinite étale covering for algebraic spaces, which sits above the\textbackslash{}nintersection between field extensions and covering spaces.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nGrothendieck's idea was to study field extensions through the prism of\textbackslash{}ncategory theory, by showing the existence of a category equivalence\textbackslash{}nbetween separable field extensions and sets on which the *absolute\textbackslash{}nGalois group* acts in a certain way. For that, we need a stronger result\textbackslash{}nwithin the theory of Galois, related to infinite field extensions and\textbackslash{}nprofinite groups. This theorem was proven by *W. Krull* in the 1930's,\textbackslash{}nfor that he introduced a topological structure on Galois groups.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nIn the following, the requisite background for classical Galois theory\textbackslash{}nis assumed. However, for the sake of clarity, we recall the Main Theorem\textbackslash{}nof Galois theory, which provides the definitive classification of\textbackslash{}nseparable field extensions.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#galois\_finite\_field .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 40** (Main Theorem of Galois Theory). *Let \$L|k\$ be a finite\textbackslash{}nGalois extension with Galois group \$G\$. The maps \$H\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto L\^{}\{H\}\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$M \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(L|M)\$ yield an inclusion-reversing\textbackslash{}nbijection between the set of subgroups of \$G\$ and the set of\textbackslash{}nintermediate fields between \$L\$ and \$k\$ \$(\$for \$H\$ a subgroup of \$G\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$M\$ an intermediate field between \$L\$ and \$k)\$. Moreover the extension\textbackslash{}n\$L|M\$ is always Galois and the extension \$M|k\$ is Galois if ans only if\textbackslash{}n\$H\$ is a normal subgroup of \$G\$\textbackslash{}n(\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(M|k)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong G/H\$).*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* The material needed and the proof itself of the main theorem of\textbackslash{}nGalois can be found in [@Lang\_algebra] (Chapter \$VI.\$ \$1\$) . ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFrom classical Galois theory for field extensions, we obtain the\textbackslash{}nfollowing lemma (mostly from the primitive element theorem, Theorem\textbackslash{}n\$4.6\$ in [@Lang\_algebra])\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#embed\_finite\_subextension .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 41**. *Let \$K|k\$ be a Galois field extension (possibly\textbackslash{}ninfinite). Then each finite subextension of \$K|k\$ can be embedded in a\textbackslash{}nfinite Galois subextension of \$K|k\$ called the Galois closure.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* By the *theorem of the primitive element*, each finite\textbackslash{}nsubextension is simple (of the form \$k(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha)\$) and we may embed\textbackslash{}n\$k(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha)\$ into the splitting field of a the minimal polynomial of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\$ which is Galois over \$k\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# Profinite Groups\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAs the name suggests, the notion of a topological group is one of the\textbackslash{}nmost natural bridges between group theory and topology. A topological\textbackslash{}ngroup \$G\$ is a topological space for which the underlying set is also a\textbackslash{}ngroup. We also require that the group operations and the inversion maps\textbackslash{}nare continuous. A homomorphism of topological groups is defined to be a\textbackslash{}ncontinuous group homomorphism \$G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow H\$. Together they form a\textbackslash{}ncategory. Since topological groups are still groups, they can act on all\textbackslash{}nkinds of sets, below we give a necessary and sufficient condition to\textbackslash{}ndetermine whether an action of a topological group on a discrete\textbackslash{}ntopological space is continuous or not.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 42**. We say that an action of a topological group \$G\$ on a\textbackslash{}ntopological space \$X\$ is a **continuous group action** if the map\textbackslash{}n\$m :G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X ; (g,x) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot x\$ is a continuous\textbackslash{}nmap.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#continuous\_open\_stabiliser .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 43**. *Let \$X\$ be a discrete topological space, and \$G\$ a\textbackslash{}ntopological group acting on \$X\$. We say that \$G\$ has a continuous action\textbackslash{}non \$X\$ if and only if for each \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$, the stabiliser \$G\_x\$ is open.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Suppose that \$G\_x\$ is open. Since \$X\$ has the discrete\textbackslash{}ntopology, every \$x\$ is open and\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n\$U\_x = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{(g,y)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times X \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid gy=x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ is their preimage by our\textbackslash{}naction. And \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{equation*\}\textbackslash{}n        U\_x = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigsqcup\_\{y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{(g,y), g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid gy = x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\textbackslash{}n            = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigsqcup\_\{y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot x\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{(g,y), g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid gy=x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{equation*\}\$\$ since if \$y\$ is not in the \$G\$-orbit of \$x\$,\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{(g,y) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid gy = x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}emptyset\$. Now, for all \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot x\$, take\textbackslash{}n\$g\_y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\$ such that \$g\_yx = y\$, then \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{equation*\}\textbackslash{}n        U\_x  = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigsqcup\_\{y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot x\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{ (g,y), g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid gg\_yx=x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\textbackslash{}n            = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigsqcup\_\{y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot x\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times G\_x g\_y\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{equation*\}\$\$ which is open by assumption. The previously defined\textbackslash{}naction \$m:G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is then continuous. Now suppose that\textbackslash{}nthe above map is continuous, then \$G\_x\$ is the preimage of \$x\$ by the\textbackslash{}ncomposition \$m\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}iota\_x\$ where \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}iota\_x : g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto  (g,x)\$\textbackslash{}ncontinuously. Hence, for every \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$, \$G\_x\$ is open by assumption ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAn important class of topological groups are profinite groups. Profinite\textbackslash{}nobjects arise in category theory as the inverse limit of an inverse\textbackslash{}nsystem of finite objects.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 44**. A **profinite group** is a group that is isomorphic\textbackslash{}nto the inverse limit of an inverse system of discrete finite groups. An\textbackslash{}ninverse system consists of a directed set \$(I, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}leq)\$, an indexed family\textbackslash{}nof finite groups \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{G\_i \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid i \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ and a family of homomorphisms\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_\{ij\} :G\_j\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow G\_i \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid i,j\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I , i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}leq j\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_\{ii\}\$ is the identity map and the collection satisfied\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_\{ij\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_\{jk\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_\{ik\}\$ whenever \$i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}leq j\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}leq k\$. The\textbackslash{}ninverse limit is then the set,\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varprojlim G\_i = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Bigl\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{(g\_i)\_\{i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod\_\{i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\}  G\_i \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_\{ij\}(g\_j)=g\_i \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{ for all \} i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}leq j   \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Bigr\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#prof\_are\_top .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 5**. We can endow a profinite group with a natural topology as\textbackslash{}nfollows: let \$G\$ be an inverse limit of the system of finite groups\textbackslash{}n\$(G\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\} , \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}beta\})\$ and endow \$G\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\}\$ with the\textbackslash{}ndiscrete topology, their product with the product topology and the\textbackslash{}nsubgroup \$G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod G\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\}\$ with the subspace topology.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nWith this in mind, we see that the projection homomorphisms\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{pr\}\}\_i:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varprojlim G\_i \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow G\_i\$ are continuous,\textbackslash{}nand their kernels form a basis of open neighbourhoods of \$1\$ in \$G\$ (the\textbackslash{}nlast statement holds since for every non-trivial element \$g\$, there\textbackslash{}nexists some coordinate \$i\$ such that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{pr\}\}\_i(g)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}neq 1\$\textbackslash{}nby definition of the inverse limit).\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nAnd by translations, we can then obtain a basis of open normal subgroups\textbackslash{}nof neighbourhoods of any elements \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\$ (note that translations are\textbackslash{}nhomeomorphisms)\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAnother famous characterisation of profinite group is the following:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#profinite\_groups\_other .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 45**. *Profinite group are equivalently groups for which the\textbackslash{}nunderlying set is compact, totally disconnected and Hausdorff.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Ribes] (Theorem \$2.1.3\$) ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#closed\_profinite\_subgroup .corollary\}\textbackslash{}n**Corollary 46**. *Closed subgroups of profinite groups are again\textbackslash{}nprofinite.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Since closed subsets of a compact Hausdorff space are precisely\textbackslash{}nthe compact subsets and subsets of totally disconnected Hausdorff spaces\textbackslash{}nare again totally disconnected and Hausdorff. Closed subgroups are again\textbackslash{}nprofinite by the above characterisation. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#open\_subgroup\_profinite .corollary\}\textbackslash{}n**Corollary 47**. *A subgroup of a profinite groups is open if and only\textbackslash{}nif it is closed and of finite index.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Every open subgroup \$U\$ in a topological group is closed.\textbackslash{}nIndeed, for topological groups, translations are homeomorphisms, so\textbackslash{}n\$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto gU\$ is a homeomorphism and since the complement of \$U\$ is\textbackslash{}ngiven by the disjoint union of open cosets \$gU\$, it is also closed. By\textbackslash{}ncompactness, the number of these cosets must be finite hence the\textbackslash{}nsubgroup is of finite index. Conversely, a closed subgroup of finite\textbackslash{}nindex is open, being the complement of the finite disjoint union of its\textbackslash{}ncosets, which are closed by homeomorphism. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#trivial\_intersection\_normal\_subgroups .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 48**. *Let \$G\$ be a profinite group. Then the intersection of\textbackslash{}nall open normal subgroups of \$G\$ is trivial.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Since \$G\$ is Hausdorff, for any element \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\$, there exist\textbackslash{}ntwo open sets \$U\$ and \$V\$ in \$G\$ with \$1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in U\$ and \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in V\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap V = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}emptyset\$. But since \$U\$ contains \$1\$, from the basis of\textbackslash{}nnormal open neighbourhoods \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{U\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ (from Remark\textbackslash{}n[5](\#prof\_are\_top)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"prof\_are\_top\textbackslash{}"\}),\textbackslash{}nthere exists an open normal subgroup \$U\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset U\$ which contains \$1\$.\textbackslash{}nThus \$U\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap V=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}emptyset\$, so \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}notin \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigcap\_\{i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\}U\_i\$. Hence the\textbackslash{}nonly element that lies in every neighbourhood of \$1\$ is \$1\$ itself. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#lemma\_profinite .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 49**. *Let \$G\$ be a profinite group, and \$H\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset G\$ a closed\textbackslash{}nsubgroup.*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *The intersection of the open subgroups of \$G\$ containing \$H\$ is\textbackslash{}n  exactly \$H\$.*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *Given an open subgroup \$V'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset H\$, there is an open subgroup\textbackslash{}n  \$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset G\$, with \$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap H = V'\$*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* For the first statement, given \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}backslash H\$, we shall\textbackslash{}nfind an open subgroup of \$G\$ containing \$H\$ but not \$g\$. Since \$H\$ is\textbackslash{}nclosed, and \$G\$ is Hausdorff, there exists an open neighbourhood \$U\$ of\textbackslash{}n\$g\$ such that \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap H = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}emptyset\$. From Remark\textbackslash{}n[5](\#prof\_are\_top)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"prof\_are\_top\textbackslash{}"\}, by\textbackslash{}ntranslation we can take an open subgroup \$N\$ in \$H\$, normal in \$G\$ such\textbackslash{}nthat \$gN\$ is a basis element of the neighbourhood system at \$g\$, this\textbackslash{}ngives us \$gN\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap H = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}emptyset\$. Then the open subgroup\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{pr\}\}\_N\^{}\{-1\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{pr\}\}\_N(H))\$ is such a\textbackslash{}nsubgroup, with \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{pr\}\}\_N: G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow G/N\$ the natural\textbackslash{}nprojection.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nFor the second statement, we use that \$V'\$ is closed in \$G\$ and by the\textbackslash{}nfirst statement, we write both \$V'\$ and \$H\$ as the intersection of the\textbackslash{}nopen subgroups of \$G\$ containing them. But since \$[H:V']\$ is finite (by\textbackslash{}nthe above corollaries), we find finitely many open subgroups\textbackslash{}n\$V\_1,...,V\_n\$ in \$G\$ containing \$V'\$ but not \$H\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\$V'= V\_1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:...\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: V\_n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap H\$. Thus \$V = V\_1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap...\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:V\_n\$\textbackslash{}nproves the last statement. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nSometimes, we want to endow a group with a profinite group structure (in\textbackslash{}nthe sense of Theorem [45](\#profinite\_groups\_other)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"profinite\_groups\_other\textbackslash{}"\}) even when it is not possible. For\textbackslash{}nexample, the group \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Z\}\$ cannot be seen as a profinite group; we\textbackslash{}ncannot endow it with a topology that is simultaneously compact, totally\textbackslash{}ndisconnected and Hausdorff. When this is the case, we can ''force\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" a\textbackslash{}nprofinite group structure by considering the profinite completion of a\textbackslash{}ngroup.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 50**. Given an arbitrary group \$G\$, the **profinite\textbackslash{}ncompletion** \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}hat\{G\}\$ of \$G\$ is defined as the inverse limit of the\textbackslash{}ngroups \$G/N\$, where \$N\$ runs through the normal subgroups in \$G\$ of\textbackslash{}nfinite index (these normal subgroups are partially ordered by inclusion,\textbackslash{}nwhich makes them into an inverse system of natural homomorphisms between\textbackslash{}nthe quotients).\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#finite\_generated\_prof\_grp .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 6**. While it is not always the case that the profinite\textbackslash{}ncompletion of a finitely presented group is finitely presented, it is\textbackslash{}nthe case that the profinite completion of a finitely generated group is\textbackslash{}ntopologically finitely generated (see [@Ribes], Section \$2.12.2\$). We\textbackslash{}nsay that a profinite group is topologically finitely generated if it\textbackslash{}ncontains a dense finitely generated subgroup.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe next proposition realises Galois groups of Galois extensions as\textbackslash{}nprofinite groups\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#Galois\_groups\_are\_profinite .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 51**. *Let \$K|k\$ be a Galois field extension (possibly\textbackslash{}ninfinite). The Galois groups of finite Galois subextensions of \$K|k\$\textbackslash{}ntogether with the homomorphisms\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_\{ML\}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(M|k)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(L|k)\$\textbackslash{}nform an inverse system whose inverse limit is isomorphic to\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(K|k)\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* By the main theorem of Galois theory, we can quickly check that\textbackslash{}nthe above data forms an inverse system, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_\{ML\}\$ are the canonical\textbackslash{}nsurjections and we have \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_\{NL\}=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_\{ML\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_\{NM\}\$ for \$N\$ a\textbackslash{}nfinite Galois subextension containing \$M\$. We only have to prove the\textbackslash{}nisomorphism part of the statement.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nLet us define a group homomorphism \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{equation*\}\textbackslash{}n        \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{split\}\textbackslash{}n            \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(\&K|k)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}longrightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod\_\{L\}  \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(L|k)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{ \} ; \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{ \}\textbackslash{}n            \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}longmapsto \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod\_\{L\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_L\textbackslash{}n        \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{split\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{equation*\}\$\$ For \$L\$, finite Galois extensions of \$k\$. We first\textbackslash{}nprove that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\$ is injective by contraposition: if \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma\$ does not\textbackslash{}nfix an element \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\$ of \$k\_s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset K\$ (for \$k\_s\$ the separable\textbackslash{}nclosure as in Definition [53](\#separable\_closure)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"separable\_closure\textbackslash{}"\}), then its restriction to a finite Galois\textbackslash{}nsubextension \$L\$ containing \$k(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha)\$ (which always exists via Lemma\textbackslash{}n[41](\#embed\_finite\_subextension)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"embed\_finite\_subextension\textbackslash{}"\}) is nontrivial. And then show\textbackslash{}nthat \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\$ is also surjective. From the *main theorem of Galois\textbackslash{}ntheory*, the image of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\$ is contained inside\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varprojlim \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(L|k)\$ since the chaining inclusions\textbackslash{}nmake the correct sequences. We define the **separable closure** of \$k\$ in\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}\$ as the compositum of all separable extensions of \$k\$. k\_s\$. Take any \$a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in L\$, we want to show that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_1(a) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_2(a)\$ in \$L\$. For all \$f:M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow k\_s\$,\textbackslash{}n\$f(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_1(a)) = f(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_2(a))\$, so \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_1(a)\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_2(a)\$ have the same image under embeddings\textbackslash{}n\$f :M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow k\_s\$. Thus \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_1(a) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_2(a)\$ implies that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_1=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_2\$. This shows injectivity. Let\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(M,k\_s) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(L,k\_s)\$\textbackslash{}nbe a \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$ equivariant map. Pick\textbackslash{}n\$j\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(M,k\_s)\$ and set \$i=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi(j)\$ two\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-embeddings. For \$g\$ an element of \$U\_j\$ the stabiliser of \$j\$ in\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$, we have\textbackslash{}n\$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot i = g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi(j) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi(g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot j) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi(j) = i\$ so\textbackslash{}n\$U\_j \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset U\_i\$ (the stabiliser of \$i\$ in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$).\textbackslash{}nHence\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k\_s| j(M)) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k\_s|i(L))\$,\textbackslash{}nthus \$i(L)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset j(M)\$ as subfields of \$k\_s\$, and so\textbackslash{}n\$j\^{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ i:L\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow M\$ is a well-defined \$k\$-homomorphism. We\textbackslash{}ndenote \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi:=j\^{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ i\$. Since \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$ acts\textbackslash{}ntransitively on \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(M,k\_s)\$, then for any\textbackslash{}n\$f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(M,k\_s)\$, \$f = g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot j\$ for some\textbackslash{}n\$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$. And\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi(f) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi(g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot j) = g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi(j) = g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot i\$ while\textbackslash{}n\$f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi = (g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot j) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ (j\^{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ i) = g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot i\$, so\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi(f) = f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\$ for any \$f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(M,k\_s)\$.\textbackslash{}nWe have shown essential surjectivity.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nThe last statement is now direct from Corollary\textbackslash{}n[55](\#Galois\_normal\_reformulation)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Galois\_normal\_reformulation\textbackslash{}"\}. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# Étale and Separable Algebras\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe end this section with an important generalisation of the previous\textbackslash{}nreformulation theorem, which makes use of *étale algebras*, a natural\textbackslash{}nreplacement for finite separable extensions (for commutative algebras).\textbackslash{}nIt allows one to consider sets with a continuous but not necessarily\textbackslash{}ntransitive \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$-action.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 57**. A finite-dimensional commutative \$k\$-algebra \$A\$ is\textbackslash{}nsaid to be **étale** (over \$k\$) if it is isomorphic to a finite direct\textbackslash{}nproduct of separable extensions of \$k\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 8**. Morphisms of finite étale \$k\$-algebras are simply\textbackslash{}nmorphisms of \$k\$-algebras. From this we can consider the category of\textbackslash{}nfinite étale \$k\$-algebras \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{F\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}acute\{e\}Al\}\}\}\_k\$. And\textbackslash{}njust as before, for \$A\$ an étale \$k\$-algebra, the\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$-action on the separable closure \$k\_s\$ induces\textbackslash{}na left action on the set of \$k\$-algebra homomorphisms\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(A,k\_s)\$. Allowing us to consider the functor\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\_,k\_s)\$ with domain\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{F\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}acute\{e\}Al\}\}\}\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#equivalence\_catgory\_etale\_algebra .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 58**. *Let \$k\$ be a field with separable closure \$k\_s\$. Then\textbackslash{}nabove functor \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k( , k\_s)\$ mapping a finite étale\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-algebra \$A\$ to the finite set \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(A,k\_s)\$ gives\textbackslash{}nan anti-equivalence between the categories\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{F\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}acute\{e\}Al\}\}\}\_k\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$-\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{FCSet\}\}\}\$. Here\textbackslash{}nseparable field extensions give rise to sets with transitive\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$-actions and Galois extensions to\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$-sets isomorphic to quotients of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* This theorem follows from the previous one by noticing that,\textbackslash{}ngiven a finite decomposition \$A = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod\_i L\_i\$ into a product of fields\textbackslash{}nand an element \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(A,k\_s)\$, the maps\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\$ induces the injection of exactly one \$L\_i\$ in \$k\_s\$. Indeed, if\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi(L\_i)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}neq 0\$, being a field extension, \$L\_i\$ injects into \$k\_s\$,\textbackslash{}nand on the other hand, a product \$L\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times L\_j\$ cannot inject into\textbackslash{}n\$k\_s\$ since \$k\_s\$ has no zero-divisors. Thus we have the decomposition\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(A,k\_s) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigsqcup\_i \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(L\_i,k\_s)\$.\textbackslash{}nFor a similar reason, given another finite étale \$k\$-algebra\textbackslash{}n\$A' = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod\_jL\_i'\$, a morphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi:A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow A'\$ is given by a\textbackslash{}ncollection of morphisms \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_\{ij\}:L\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow L\_j'\$, for each\textbackslash{}n\$i,j\$. And these correspond bijectively to morphisms of the\textbackslash{}ncorresponding \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$-sets by the previous theorem. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nÉtale algebras will also play an important role later in this thesis.\textbackslash{}nFor that reason, we give another characterisation of finite étale\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-algebras. For that, we first need the next lemma.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#finite\_dimensional\_direct\_sum\_reduced .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 59**. *A finite-dimensional commutative algebra \$A\$ over a field\textbackslash{}n\$k\$ is isomorphic to a direct sum of finite field extensions of \$k\$ if\textbackslash{}nand only if \$A\$ is reduced.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* The ''only if\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" part is obvious, one just has to notice that\textbackslash{}nfields are already reduced.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nTo prove the other direction, by decomposing \$A\$ into a finite direct\textbackslash{}nproduct of indecomposable \$k\$-algebras, we may assume that \$A\$ is\textbackslash{}nindecomposable. Under this restriction \$A\$ can have no idempotent\textbackslash{}nelements other than \$0\$ and \$1\$, indeed, if \$e\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}neq 0,1\$ is an\textbackslash{}nidempotent, then \$A \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong Ae \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times A(1-e)\$ would be a non-trivial\textbackslash{}ndirect product decomposition since \$e(1-e)=e-e\^{}2=0\$. The lemma follows\textbackslash{}nif we show that every non-zero element \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in A\$ is invertible making it\textbackslash{}na field. Since \$A\$ is finite-dimensional, it is Artinian, i.e. the\textbackslash{}ndescending chain of ideals\textbackslash{}n\$(x)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}supset (x\^{}2)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}supset\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: ... \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}supset (x\^{}n)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}supset\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:...\$ must\textbackslash{}nstabilise. And thus for some \$m\$, we have \$x\^{}n = x\^{}\{n+1\}y\$ for some\textbackslash{}n\$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in A\$. By iteration we get \$x\^{}n = x\^{}\{n+i\}y\^{}i\$ for \$i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{N\}\$\textbackslash{}nuntil \$x\^{}n = x\^{}\{2n\}y\^{}n\$, thus \$(x\^{}ny\^{}n)=(x\^{}ny\^{}n)\^{}2\$, an idempotent. If\textbackslash{}n\$x\^{}ny\^{}n=0\$, then \$x\^{}n = (x\^{}n)(x\^{}ny\^{}n) = 0\$ which is a contradiction\textbackslash{}nsince \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}neq 0\$ by assumption. So \$x\^{}ny\^{}n=1\$ and \$x\$ is invertible. \$A\$\textbackslash{}nis reduced. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#etale\_algebras .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 60**. *Let \$A\$ be a finite-dimensional commutative\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-algebra. Then the following are equivalent :*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *\$A\$ is étale*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *\$A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_k \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}oplus\^{}n\}\$*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *\$A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_k\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}\$ is reduced.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Let us first show that \$a)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Rightarrow b)\$:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nWe may restrict to finite separable extensions \$L\$ of \$k\$. Then of\textbackslash{}ncourse, we have \$L = k[x]/(f)\$ for some polynomial\textbackslash{}n\$f(x)=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod\_i(x-\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\_i)\$ in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}\$. We can conclude by the\textbackslash{}nChinese Remainder Theorem as follows :\textbackslash{}n\$\$L\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_k\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}[x]/(f) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}[x]/(x-\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\_1)...(x-\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\_n)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod\_\{i=1\}\^{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}[x]/(x-\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\_i) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod\_\{i=1\}\^{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}.\$\$\textbackslash{}nNow to prove that \$b)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Rightarrow a)\$, consider\textbackslash{}n\$A\_r = A/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Nil\}\}(A)\$, then \$A\_r\$ is reduced and the\textbackslash{}nprevious lemma implies that \$A\_r\$ is the direct sum of finite field\textbackslash{}nextensions of \$k\$. Since \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}\$ is reduced as a field, each\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-homomorphisms \$A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow
