The assumption of \$b)\$\textbackslash{}nimplies that the set\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}\}(A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_k\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\})\$\textbackslash{}nhas \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dim\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}\}(A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_k\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\})\$ elements and actually\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dim\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}\}(A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_k\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dim\_k(A)\$, proving the\textbackslash{}nequivalence.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nFinally, \$b)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Rightarrow c)\$ is immediate, again fields are automatically\textbackslash{}nreduced.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nAnd \$c) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Rightarrow b)\$ follows by applying the previous lemma to the\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}\$-algebra \$A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_k\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe have discussed so far a generalisation of separable field extension\textbackslash{}nthrough étale algebras, and seen that it allows to refine the\textbackslash{}nclassification field extensions. Another plausible and useful\textbackslash{}ngeneralisations of separable field extension is the notion of *separable\textbackslash{}nalgebras*, it can be considered a broader generalisation than the étale\textbackslash{}ncase since it allows to consider non-commutative algebras.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 61**. An algebra \$A\$ over a field \$k\$ is called\textbackslash{}n**separable** if there exists a map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta : A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_k A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow A\$\textbackslash{}nwith \$m(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(a))=a\$ and \$a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(b) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(ab) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(a)b\$, for\textbackslash{}n\$a,b\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in A\$ and \$m\$ the usual multiplication of \$A\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#commut\_separable\_is\_etale .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 62**. *Commutative separable algebras and finite étale\textbackslash{}nalgebras coincide over fields.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Corollary \$4.5.8\$ in [@Sep\_al] says that such a commutative\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-algebra \$A\$ is a separable algebra if and only if \$A\$ is isomorphic\textbackslash{}nto a finite direct sum of fields \$L\_1 \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}oplus ... \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}oplus L\_n\$ where each\textbackslash{}n\$L\_i\$ is a finite separable field extension of \$k\$. But this is exactly\textbackslash{}nthe definition of finite étale \$k\$-algebras. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFor \$m:A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_k A \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow A\$ the multiplication map of a\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-algebra \$A\$, denote its kernel \$I\$. Notice that if \$A\$ is a\textbackslash{}ncommutative algebra, \$A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_kA\$ is a commutative algebra in its own\textbackslash{}nright, and \$I\$ is an ideal in this algebra because it is an\textbackslash{}n\$A\$,\$A\$-bimodule : for all \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$, \$(a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes b)x = axb \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$ for\textbackslash{}n\$a,b\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in A\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#lemma\_splitting\_exact\_sequence\_separable .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 63**. *An algebra \$A\$ over a commutative ring is separable if\textbackslash{}nand only if this short exact sequence of \$A\$,\$A\$-bimodules splits\textbackslash{}n\$\$0\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow[]\{\} I \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow[]\{i\} A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_kA \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow[]\{m\} A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow 0\$\$\textbackslash{}nfor \$i\$ the inclusion.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* We use the splitting lemma (in [@Lang\_algebra], Proposition\textbackslash{}n\$3.2\$). We can define a map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta: A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes A\$ so that\textbackslash{}n\$m\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{id\}\}\_A\$. And \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta\$ is an\textbackslash{}n\$A\$,\$A\$-bimodule map if and only if\textbackslash{}n\$a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(b) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(ab)= \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(a)b\$. But this is precisely the\textbackslash{}ndefinition of a separable algebras.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Another Classification of Covering Spaces \{\#equivalence\_fibre\_functor\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nSimilarly as in Galois theory, there is a formulation ''*à la\textbackslash{}nGrothendieck*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" of the classification of covering spaces in terms of\textbackslash{}nequivalence of categories via a fibre functor.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#covering\_reformulation\_1 .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 64**. *Let \$X\$ be a connect topological space and \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$ a\textbackslash{}nbase point. The fibre functor \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_x\$ induces an\textbackslash{}nequivalence of the categories between \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Cov\}\}\}(X)\$\textbackslash{}nand \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$-\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Set\}\}\}\$. Connected covers\textbackslash{}ncorrespond to \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$-sets with transitive action and Galois covers\textbackslash{}ncorrespond to coset spaces of normal subgroups.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* We check that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_x\$ is fully faithful and\textbackslash{}nessentially surjective.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nLet \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ and \$q:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be two covers of \$X\$. We\textbackslash{}ncan assume that \$Y\$ and \$Z\$ are connected since (otherwise, we can just\textbackslash{}nrun the following argument on pairs of connected components). We want to\textbackslash{}nshow that the \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$-equivariant map\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_x(Y),\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_x(Z))\$\textbackslash{}ncomes from the unique morphism of covers \$f: Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$. Consider\textbackslash{}nthe maps \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_y: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_z:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ corresponding to the points\textbackslash{}n\$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_x(Y)\$ and \$z:=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi(y)\$ respectively as in\textbackslash{}nProposition [32](\#representable\_fibre\_functor)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"representable\_fibre\_functor\textbackslash{}"\}. Since the universal covering\textbackslash{}n\$r:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is Galois\textbackslash{}n([33](\#unive\_cov\_galois)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"unive\_cov\_galois\textbackslash{}"\}) and by the above classification of\textbackslash{}ncovering spaces, the maps \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_y\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_z\$ are Galois\textbackslash{}ncoverings and \$Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}/H\_y\$ and \$Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}/H\_z\$\textbackslash{}nfor each stabilisers \$H\_y=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x|Y)\$ of\textbackslash{}n\$y\$ and \$H\_z=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x|Z)\$ of \$z\$. So we can\textbackslash{}nwrite\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_x (\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}/H\_y) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_x(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}/H\_z)\$.\textbackslash{}nSince this map is \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$-equivariant, it induces a map\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_x (\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\})/H\_y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_x(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\})/H\_z\$,\textbackslash{}nwhich implies that there is a map between the stabilisers\textbackslash{}n\$H\_y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow H\_z\$ via \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\$. Hence,\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_z: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ induces a map\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x / H\_y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x/H\_z \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow[]\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sim\} Z.\$\$\textbackslash{}nComposing this with the homeomorphism \$Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\_x/H\_y\$,\textbackslash{}ngives us the desired map\$f:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$, thus\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_x\$ is indeed fully faithful.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nTo show essentially surjective, consider \$S\$ any \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$-set, we\textbackslash{}nwant to find a covering map whose fibre is exactly \$S\$. Assume that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$ acts transitively on \$S\$ and take \$s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in S\$. Let\textbackslash{}n\$H=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\_s\$ be the stabiliser of \$s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in S\$, again by Theorem\textbackslash{}n[264](\#Cameron\_1\_3)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"Cameron\_1\_3\textbackslash{}"\}, we\textbackslash{}nhave that \$S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)/H\$ the coset. Thus we wish to construct a\textbackslash{}ncovering map whose fibre is this exact coset. Consider\textbackslash{}n\$q:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ the universal cover, by Proposition\textbackslash{}n[33](\#unive\_cov\_galois)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"unive\_cov\_galois\textbackslash{}"\} it is Galois, thus\textbackslash{}n\$X \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$. Let \$Y:= \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}/H\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ a covering space, then we have on the quotients that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}/H\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$ is a covering map.\textbackslash{}nRecall that from Corollary [36](\#fibre\_univ\_cov)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"fibre\_univ\_cov\textbackslash{}"\}, we have\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_x(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\}/H) =\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_x(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\})/H \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)/H \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong S\$.\textbackslash{}nFor \$S\$ not transitive, we decompose \$S\$ into disjoint union of orbits\textbackslash{}n(into transitive components) and define a covering\textbackslash{}n\$p\_i:Y\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ for each orbit. Then, taking the fibre of the\textbackslash{}ndisjoint union yields a \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$-equivariant bijection from the\textbackslash{}ndisjoint union of these fibres to the disjoint union of orbits of \$S\$,\textbackslash{}nand thus a \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$-equivariant bijection to \$S\$ itself.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nFinally the last statement of the theorem follows from the previous\textbackslash{}nargument combined with the above classification of covering spaces. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe can state a refinement of the previous theorem. It applies the\textbackslash{}ntheorem to our previous discussion on Galois groups being profinite.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 9**. Earlier, we have shown that Galois groups of Galois\textbackslash{}nextensions are profinite, however fundamental groups of topological\textbackslash{}nspaces are generally not profinite; a prime example of this is the\textbackslash{}nfundamental group of the circle \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(S\^{}1) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Z\}\$ which cannot\textbackslash{}nbe seen as profinite.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nNotice that this refinement is much closer to Grothendieck's formulation\textbackslash{}nof Galois theory for finite field extensions (Theorem\textbackslash{}n[56](\#Grot\_reformulation\_Galois)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Grot\_reformulation\_Galois\textbackslash{}"\}). Since the subsequent chapter\textbackslash{}nwill mostly focus on finite coverings (over algebraic spaces), this\textbackslash{}nrefinement is quite fitting. The ''new\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" tool we use here is the\textbackslash{}nprofinite completion of groups defined in the previous section.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 65**. We say that a covering space \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{finite\}\$ if it has finite fibres. For a connected topological\textbackslash{}nspace, these fibres have the same cardinality, called the **degree** of\textbackslash{}nthe covering.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn order to prove the next theorem, we first need the following lemma.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: lemma\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 66**. *Let \$G\$ be a group and \$H\$ a subgroup of finite index.\textbackslash{}nThen there exists a normal subgroup \$N\$ of \$G\$ contained in \$H\$*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Suppose the index of \$H\$ in \$G\$ is \$[G:H]=n\$, and consider the\textbackslash{}nrepresentation of \$G\$ on the left coset space of \$H\$, so\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho:G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Sym\}\}(G/H) = S\_n\$ is a group\textbackslash{}nhomomorphism whose kernel \$N=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}ker\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\$ is\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigcap\_\{g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\} gHg\^{}\{-1\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{core\}\}\_G(H) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subseteq H\$.\textbackslash{}n(or exercise \$I\$ \$9.(a)\$ in [@Lang\_algebra]) ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#covering\_reformulation\_2 .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 67**. *Let \$X\$ be a connect topological space and \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$ a\textbackslash{}nbase point. The functor \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_x\$ induces an equivalence\textbackslash{}nbetween the category of finite covers of \$X\$ and the category of finite\textbackslash{}ncontinuous \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\}\$-sets. Connected covers correspond to\textbackslash{}nfinite \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\}\$-sets with transitive action and Galois\textbackslash{}ncovers to coset spaces of open normal subgroups.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* First, notice that for a finite connected cover\textbackslash{}n\$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$, from the classification of coverings, the action of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$ on \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ factors through finite quotients, so\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\}\$ also acts on \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$. By orbit stabiliser and\textbackslash{}nsince the covering is finite, the stabiliser of each point \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\$ is a\textbackslash{}nsubgroup of finite index. Thus, by the above lemma, it must contain a\textbackslash{}nnormal subgroup of finite index. Since those normal subgroups of finite\textbackslash{}nindex are the kernels of the projection maps \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{pr\}\}\_N\$,\textbackslash{}nthey must be open, and being contained in the stabiliser of \$y\$, the\textbackslash{}nstabiliser can be seen as a union of cosets of an open normal subgroup.\textbackslash{}nHence, this stabiliser is open, and by Lemma\textbackslash{}n[43](\#continuous\_open\_stabiliser)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"continuous\_open\_stabiliser\textbackslash{}"\}, this means that the action is\textbackslash{}ncontinuous. Conversely, a continuous action of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\}\$ on\textbackslash{}na finite set factors through continuous actions of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$ on\textbackslash{}nfinite quotients and by Theorem\textbackslash{}n[64](\#covering\_reformulation\_1)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"covering\_reformulation\_1\textbackslash{}"\}, gives rise to a finite cover. The\textbackslash{}nlast two statements are proven similarly as in the proof of Theorem\textbackslash{}n[64](\#covering\_reformulation\_1)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"covering\_reformulation\_1\textbackslash{}"\}, by factoring through quotients.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Classification of Locally Constant Sheaves\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe theories of *locally constant sheaves* and covering spaces are\textbackslash{}nclosely related. In this section, we show that they are, in fact,\textbackslash{}nequivalent. The reader may find all the necessary preliminaries to\textbackslash{}nsheaves in Appendix [6.1](\#review\_sheaves)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"review\_sheaves\textbackslash{}"\}. Let us now introduce the main objects of\textbackslash{}nthis section.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 68**. Let \$X\$ be a topological space and \$S\$ be a discrete\textbackslash{}nset. We define a sheaf of sets \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_S\$ on \$X\$ by taking\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_S(U)\$ to be the set of continuous functions\textbackslash{}n\$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$. But since \$S\$ is discrete, the sections of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_S\$ are just constant functions, thus \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_S(U) = S\$\textbackslash{}nand we call this sheaf the **constant sheaf** with values in \$S\$. A\textbackslash{}nsheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ on \$X\$ is then said to be **locally constant** if\textbackslash{}nthe restriction \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_U\$ is a constant sheaf for all open\textbackslash{}n\$U\$ in some open covering of \$X\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe will study locally constant sheaves through the lens of another sheaf\textbackslash{}nconstruction.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: construction\textbackslash{}n**Construction 69**. Given a morphism of topological spaces\textbackslash{}n\$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$, we define the presheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_Y\$ of sets on\textbackslash{}n\$X\$, called the **presheaf of sections** of \$p\$ as follows:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- for any open subset \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$, let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_Y(U)\$ be the set of\textbackslash{}n  sections of \$p\$ over \$U\$, and\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- for any two open subsets \$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$, the restriction map\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\_\{UV\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_Y\}\$ is defined by restricting the sections to\textbackslash{}n  \$V\$,\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#fibres\_are\_stalks .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 10**. A first interesting fact is that for sheaves of sections\textbackslash{}nof covering maps, fibres and stalks at a point \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$ are the same.\textbackslash{}nIndeed let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_\{Y,x\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$ be the map\textbackslash{}nthat sends the representative \$[s]\_x\$ to its image \$s(x)\$. This map is\textbackslash{}nwell-defined since equivalent sections agree over an open neighbourhood\textbackslash{}nof \$x\$. When \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi([s]\_x) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi([t]\_x)\$ in \$p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$, since \$p\$ is a\textbackslash{}nlocal homeomorphism, there exist an open neighbourhood \$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$ of\textbackslash{}n\$x\$ such that \$s(V)=t(V)\$, and since they are sections, \$s=t\$ near \$x\$,\textbackslash{}nso \$[s]\_x=[t]\_x\$. For any \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in p\^{}\{-1\}(x)\$, we have that\textbackslash{}n\$p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_V:V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow U\$ is a homeomorphism, with \$s:=(p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_V)\^{}\{-1\}\$\textbackslash{}na section such that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi([s]\_x) = s(x) = y\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#sheaf\_of\_sections\_if\_of\_cover .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 70**. *The presheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_Y\$ of sections of \$p\$ is\textbackslash{}nindeed a sheaf. Moreover, if \$p:Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is a covering, then\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_Y\$ is a locally constant sheaf. \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_Y\$ is a\textbackslash{}nconstant sheaf if and only if \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is a trivial cover.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Since sections are continuous maps over an open \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$,\textbackslash{}nthe glueing property of sheaves is immediately verified. Suppose now\textbackslash{}nthat \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is a covering. For any \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$ take a connected\textbackslash{}nopen neighbourhood \$V\$ of \$x\$ such that the cover \$p\$ over \$V\$ is\textbackslash{}ntrivial. So over \$V\$ the cover is isomorphic to \$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times S\$, for \$S\$ the\textbackslash{}nfibre at \$x\$. Let \$s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_Y(V)\$ be a local section of \$p\$ over\textbackslash{}n\$V\$. Its image is a connected open subset of \$Y\$, and is isomorphically\textbackslash{}nsent to \$V\$ by \$p\$. So \$im(s)\$ must be one of the connected components\textbackslash{}nof \$p\^{}\{-1\}(V) = V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times S\$. And since the images of two different\textbackslash{}nsections are isomorphic to two different connected components of\textbackslash{}n\$p\^{}\{-1\}(V)\$, sections of \$p\$ over \$V\$ correspond bijectively to points\textbackslash{}nof the fibre \$S\$. Thus the restriction \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_V\$ is the\textbackslash{}nconstant sheaf with value \$S\$. And we get that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_Y\$ is a\textbackslash{}nconstant sheaf iff the connected open set \$V\$ is the whole of \$X\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe can now define a functor from the category of covering spaces of \$X\$\textbackslash{}nto the category of locally constant sheaves on \$X\$, which sends an\textbackslash{}nobject \$Y\$ to \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_Y\$ and a morphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi :Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ to a\textbackslash{}nmorphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_Z\$. Which is a\textbackslash{}nmorphism of sheaves, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\$ sends a section \$s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_Y(U)\$\textbackslash{}nto a section \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_Z(U)\$ and this is compatible\textbackslash{}nwith the restriction maps.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nIn order to define a functor in the reverse direction, we introduce the\textbackslash{}nnotion of *étale spaces*.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#etale\_space .definition\}\textbackslash{}n**Definition 71**. Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ be a presheaf on a topological\textbackslash{}nspace \$X\$. The **étale space** of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ is the disjoint union of\textbackslash{}nits stalks over \$X\$, denoted\textbackslash{}n\$X\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigsqcup\_\{x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_x\$ where points are\textbackslash{}nrepresented by a pair \$(U,s)\$ and are denoted \$s\_x\$. And for any open\textbackslash{}nset \$U \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$, a section \$s \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U)\$ defines a map\textbackslash{}n\$i\_s : U \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\}\$ sending each \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in U\$ to the germ\textbackslash{}n\$s\_x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_x\$. We can now endow the étale space with an **étale\textbackslash{}ntopology**, which is the coarsest topology for which all sets of the\textbackslash{}nform \$i\_s(U)\$ are open for all \$U\$ and \$s\$ (note this is not the same\textbackslash{}ntopology as the étale topology we encounter in Chapter\textbackslash{}n[2.1](\#nex\_topology)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"nex\_topology\textbackslash{}"\}).\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nNotice that when \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ is a locally constant sheaf, the étale\textbackslash{}nspace is actually a covering space and we consider the following **étale\textbackslash{}ncovering map** \$p\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\}:X\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ sending a\textbackslash{}ngerm to the point over which it is defined (\$s\_x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto x\$). Indeed, for\textbackslash{}n\$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$ open, \$p\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\}\$ is continuous since\textbackslash{}n\$p\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\}\^{}\{-1\}(U) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigcup\_\{s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U)\} i\_s(U)\$ is open\textbackslash{}n(from the étale topology). Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{U\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ be an open affine\textbackslash{}ncovering of connected subsets of \$X\$ such that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_U\$ is\textbackslash{}nthe constant sheaf with values in \$S\$. Then for all \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in U\$, the fibre\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_x=S\$, and from Remark\textbackslash{}n[10](\#fibres\_are\_stalks)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"fibres\_are\_stalks\textbackslash{}"\}, \$p\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\}\^{}\{-1\}(x)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong S\$, so\textbackslash{}n\$p\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\}\^{}\{-1\}(U)\$ is homeomorphic to \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times S\$. Observe that\textbackslash{}n\$p\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\}\$ is always a local homeomorphism but only a covering\textbackslash{}nwhen \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ is locally constant.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#Sheaves\_X\_equiv\_etale\_X .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 11**. Sheaf theory is quite vast. The knowledgeable reader\textbackslash{}nmight recognise the connection above with the theory of *bundles* and\textbackslash{}n*overcategories*. A standard reference is [@sheaves\_geometry\_logic],\textbackslash{}nwhere in chapter II, the authors define the category of étale spaces\textbackslash{}nover \$X\$ as the full subcategory of the category\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Bund\}\}\}(X) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Top\}\}\}/X\$\textbackslash{}nconsisting of étale bundles. And here étale bundles are essentially the\textbackslash{}nsame thing as étale projections. We refer to Corollary \$6.3\$ of that\textbackslash{}nchapter which establishes an equivalence between the category of étale\textbackslash{}nspaces over \$X\$ and the category of sheaves over \$X\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFinally, a morphism of sheaves\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\$ induces maps between\textbackslash{}nstalks \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_x:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_x \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\_x\$ for all \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$\textbackslash{}nand hence a map of étale spaces\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi: X\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\}\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#morphism\_of\_etal\_space .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 72**. *Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ be a locally constant sheaf on \$X\$,the\textbackslash{}nabove map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi : X\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\}\$ is a\textbackslash{}nmorphism of coverings of \$X\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* It is straightforward to see that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\$ is compatible with the\textbackslash{}nprojections \$p:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ and \$q:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$. And we show that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\$ is continuous for the étale topology: pick an open subset\textbackslash{}n\$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$, a section \$t\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(U)\$ and a point \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in U\$. We\textbackslash{}nhave \$i\_t(U) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\_x = t\_x\$ a point in \$X\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\}\$. Now\textbackslash{}neach preimage \$s\_x \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Phi\^{}\{-1\}(i\_t(U))\$ lies in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_x\$ (this\textbackslash{}nshould be clear from our above construction). And each of these\textbackslash{}n\$s\_x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Phi\^{}\{-1\}(i\_t(U))\$ comes from a section \$s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(V)\$ with\textbackslash{}n\$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset U\$ that can be chosen so small such that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi(s) = t\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_V\$. So \$s\_x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in i\_s(V)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\}\$ with\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Phi(i\_s(V)) = i\_t(V)\$ (because we chose \$V\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi(s) = t\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_V\$). So every point in the preimage has an open\textbackslash{}nneighbourhood, the preimage is open, we have a continuous morphism of\textbackslash{}nétale spaces. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe now have the reverse functor and are ready to prove the main theorem\textbackslash{}nof this section.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#LCS\_equiv\_Cov .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 73**. *The categories of covering spaces of \$X\$ and the\textbackslash{}ncategory of locally constant sheaves on \$X\$ are equivalent. Moreover,\textbackslash{}ntrivial coverings correspond to constant sheaves.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Let\textbackslash{}n\$F: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{LCS\}\}\}(X) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Cov\}\}\}(X)\$\textbackslash{}nand\textbackslash{}n\$G:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Cov\}\}\}(X)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{LCS\}\}\}(X)\$\textbackslash{}nbe functors as above. Hence we can consider the functor\textbackslash{}n\$F\_x:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{LCS\}\}\}\_R(X) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Mod\}\}\}\_\{R[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)]\}\$\textbackslash{}nsending \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ to its stalk \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_x\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nIn the reverse direction, let \$M\$ be an \$R[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)]\$-module and give\textbackslash{}nit the usual discrete topology.
