\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_x\}\$\textbackslash{}nsending a section \$s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U)\$ to the corresponding section in\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_x\}\$ is an isomorphism.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nWe have thus showed, for any \$M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Mod\}\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1\}\$\textbackslash{}nand \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{LCS\}\}\}\_R\$, that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\_M\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}beta\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\}\$ are isomorphism and moreover these isomorphisms\textbackslash{}nare functorial in \$M\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ respectively since the following\textbackslash{}ndiagrams commute, \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{tikzcd\}\textbackslash{}n        M \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[r,\textbackslash{}"f\textbackslash{}"] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d, \textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\_M\textbackslash{}"']\textbackslash{}n        \& N \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d,\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\_\{N\}\textbackslash{}"] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n        \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_\{M,x\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[r,\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_\{f\_x\}\textbackslash{}"']\textbackslash{}n        \&  \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_\{N,x\}\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{tikzcd\}\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}hspace\{1cm\}\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{tikzcd\}\textbackslash{}n        \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[r,\textbackslash{}"g\textbackslash{}"] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d, \textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}beta\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\}\textbackslash{}"']\textbackslash{}n        \& \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d,\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}beta\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\}\textbackslash{}"] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n        \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_x\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[r,\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_\{g\_\{x\}\}\textbackslash{}"']\textbackslash{}n        \&  \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\_x\}.\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{tikzcd\}\$\$ ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFinally, we can apply the identification of representation of groups\textbackslash{}nwith group-ring modules described below to the above theorem and obtain\textbackslash{}nthe next corollary.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 76**. *Let \$k\$ be a field. The category of \$k[G]\$-modules and\textbackslash{}nthe category of representations of \$G\$ are isomorphic.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Given a \$G\$-representation over \$k\$, \$(V,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho)\$, we can define\textbackslash{}na \$k[G]\$-module structure on \$V\$ by \$u\_g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot v := \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho(g)(v)\$ for all\textbackslash{}n\$v\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in V\$ and \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\$ (so \$V\$ becomes a free vector space over \$G\$).\textbackslash{}nPrecisely,\textbackslash{}n\$u\_g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot(u\_h\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot v) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho(g)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho(h)(v) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho(gh)(v) = u\_\{gh\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot v = (u\_gu\_h)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot v\$\textbackslash{}nand \$u\_e\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot v= \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho(e)(v)=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{id\}\}\_V(v) = v\$. Given a\textbackslash{}nmorphism \$f:V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow W\$ of \$G\$-representation over \$k\$, (it is\textbackslash{}n\$G\$-equivariant), we obtain a morphism of \$k[G]\$-modules as follow. From\textbackslash{}nabove, any element of \$V\$ can be written as a sum element over the\textbackslash{}ngenerating group.\textbackslash{}n\$\$f \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Bigl( (\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sum\_\{g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\} a\_gu\_g)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot v \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Bigr) = f \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Bigl( \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sum\_\{g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\} a\_g(u\_g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot v) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Bigr) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}stackrel\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{linearity\}\}\{=\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sum\_\{g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\} a\_g f(u\_g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot v) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}stackrel\{G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{-equiv\}\}\{=\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sum\_\{g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\} a\_g u\_gf(v).\$\$\textbackslash{}nThis makes a functor\textbackslash{}n\$F :\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Rep\}\}\}\_k(G) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Mod\}\}\}\_\{k[G]\}\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nIn the reverse direction, consider a \$k[G]\$-module \$M\$, we can define a\textbackslash{}nmorphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho: G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{End\}\}(M)\$ given by\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho(g)(m) = u\_g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot m\$. This makes \$(M,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho)\$ into a representation\textbackslash{}nof \$G\$ over \$k\$. Consider a morphism \$f':M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow N\$ of\textbackslash{}n\$k[G]\$-modules, similarly as above, we can see it is also a morphism of\textbackslash{}n\$G\$-representations over \$k\$. This makes a functor\textbackslash{}n\$G:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Mod\}\}\}\_\{k[G]\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Rep\}\}\}\_k(G)\$.\textbackslash{}nFinally, since our constructions are mutual inverses, we have that\textbackslash{}n\$F\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ G (M) = M\$ and \$G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ F(V)=V\$ for all\textbackslash{}n\$M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Mod\}\}\}\_\{k[G]\}\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Rep\}\}\}\_k(G)\$. Yielding an isomorphism of\textbackslash{}ncategories.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#corollary\_Rpi\_mod .corollary\}\textbackslash{}n**Corollary 77**. *Let \$k\$ be a field. The category of locally constant\textbackslash{}nsheave of \$k\$-modules \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{LCS\}\}\}\_k\$ is equivalent to\textbackslash{}nthe category of representations of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$ over \$k\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThis equivalence is quite strong as it is also an equivalence that\textbackslash{}nstands for the category of complex local systems.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 78**. A **complex local system** on \$X\$ is a locally\textbackslash{}nconstant sheaf of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces. If \$X\$ is\textbackslash{}nconnected, all stalks must have the same dimension, which is called the\textbackslash{}ndimension of the local system.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nHence the category of local systems \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{LS\}\}\}\_X\$ on \$X\$\textbackslash{}nis equivalent to the category of locally constant sheaf\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{LCS\}\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\}(X)\$. The following corollary,\textbackslash{}nis known as the *monodromy representation of local systems*.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#local\_systems\_representations .corollary\}\textbackslash{}n**Corollary 79**. *Let \$X\$ be a connected an locally simply-connected\textbackslash{}ntopological space with \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$. The category of complex local systems\textbackslash{}non \$X\$ is equivalent to the category of finite-dimensional\textbackslash{}nrepresentations of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,s)\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Follows from Theorem\textbackslash{}n[75](\#equi\_R\_mod\_loc\_cst\_sh)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"equi\_R\_mod\_loc\_cst\_sh\textbackslash{}"\} and Corollary\textbackslash{}n[77](\#corollary\_Rpi\_mod)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"corollary\_Rpi\_mod\textbackslash{}"\}. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nLocal systems are a powerful tool from algebraic topology. They also\textbackslash{}narise naturally in differential geometry when one tries computes\textbackslash{}nsolutions of linear differential equations as the following example\textbackslash{}nshows.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: example\textbackslash{}n**Example 80**. Let \$D\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ be a connected open disc.\textbackslash{}nConsider over \$D\$ homogeneous \$n\$-th order linear differential equation\textbackslash{}n\$\$y\^{}\{(n)\} +f\_1y\^{}\{(n-1)\} +\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:...+ f\_\{n-1\}y'+f\_ny = 0\$\$ where the \$f\_i\$ are\textbackslash{}nholomorphic functions on \$D\$. Consider the local holomorphic solutions\textbackslash{}nof the differential equation over each open subset \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset D\$. As\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$-linear combinations of local solutions of the differential\textbackslash{}nequation over \$U\$ are again local solutions, they form a\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$-vector space \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{S\}(U)\$. And due to a classical\textbackslash{}ntheorem from linear differential equations (Theorem \$11.2\$ in\textbackslash{}n[@Forster]), each point of \$D\$ has an open neighbourhood \$U\$ where the\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$-vector space \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{S\}(U)\$ has a finite basis\textbackslash{}n\$x\_1,...,x\_n\$. This actually makes the sets of local solutions of the\textbackslash{}ndifferential equation a sheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{S\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\^{}n\$, a\textbackslash{}nsheaf of complex vector spaces. And since the restriction of the above\textbackslash{}nbasis \$x\_i\$ to smaller open sets still form a basis for the solutions,\textbackslash{}nwe can conclude that the sheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{S\}\$ is locally constant, hence\textbackslash{}na local system of dimension \$n\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 12**. But local systems have a deeper connection to\textbackslash{}ndifferential geometry. Notably, the *Riemann-Hilbert correspondence*\textbackslash{}nsays that the category of holomorphic flat connections on a complex\textbackslash{}nmanifold \$X\$ is equivalent to the category of complex local systems on\textbackslash{}n\$X\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nAnd with the above equivalence, this correspondence partial answers the\textbackslash{}n\$21\$st Hilbert problem which asks about the existence of a linear\textbackslash{}ndifferential equation having a prescribed monodromy group.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\# Covers and Fundamental Groups for Schemes\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn the last chapter, we discussed how the theory of covering spaces\textbackslash{}nprovided a nice geometric interpretation of the fundamental group of\textbackslash{}ntopological spaces. In this chapter, we explain in what manner(s) the\textbackslash{}nZariski topology is too coarse. Then we go through a study of *étale\textbackslash{}nmorphisms* in order to define étale coverings, which will allow us to\textbackslash{}ndefine the *étale fundamental group* similarly as in the previous\textbackslash{}nchapter, denoted by \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1\^{}e\$. Finally, we compare our new fundamental\textbackslash{}ngroup with its topological counterpart by *analytifying* non-singular\textbackslash{}nprojective schemes over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$. We also present a few structural\textbackslash{}nproperties of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1\^{}e(X)\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# The Étale Topology \{\#nex\_topology\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAs one knows, we usually endow an algebraically variety over an\textbackslash{}nalgebraic closed field or a scheme with the Zariski topology. But this\textbackslash{}ntopology is not well-suited for the methods of algebraic topology. In\textbackslash{}nthe 1940's, André Weil conjectured that the number of solutions to a set\textbackslash{}nof polynomials over a finite field might be explained by a cohomology\textbackslash{}ntheory for which the Lefshetz formula for fixed points would hold\textbackslash{}n(roughly), giving motivation to the study of cohomology of algebraic\textbackslash{}nspaces (see Appendix [6.4](\#Sheaf\_cohomology)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Sheaf\_cohomology\textbackslash{}"\}). But the cohomology groups computed using\textbackslash{}nthe Zariski topology (the Z-cohomology) are all zero for an important\textbackslash{}nclass of spaces (this follows from *Grothendieck's vanishing theorem*).\textbackslash{}nThis later led to the definition of the *étale topology* of a scheme by\textbackslash{}nGrothendieck, which in turn gave birth to the theory of *étale\textbackslash{}ncohomology*. It is thus quite awkward to motivate the need for the étale\textbackslash{}ntopology without mentioning strong ideas from cohomology (which fall\textbackslash{}noutside the scope of this thesis). Nonetheless, we will see that for our\textbackslash{}npurposes, the Zariski topology is also ill-suited.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 81** (Grothendieck's vanishing theorem). *If \$X\$ is an\textbackslash{}nirreducible topological space, then \$H\^{}r(X,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}) = 0\$ for all\textbackslash{}nconstant sheaves and all \$r>0\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@milneEtCoH], Theorem \$1.1\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAnd the \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}check\{C\}ech\$ \$cohomology\$ \$groups\$ are also zero.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nThe Zariski topology on an irreducible scheme \$X\$ is quite coarse; it\textbackslash{}nhas very few open sets which are additionally dense, and all its closed\textbackslash{}nsets are finite. From this only, we already understand that some key\textbackslash{}nnotions of algebraic topology fail; it is impossible to ''zoom in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" on a\textbackslash{}npoint, and there is no notion of a small open ball centred at a point\textbackslash{}nthat usual topology is based on.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nEven better, we can show that a very wide range of irreducible varieties\textbackslash{}nand in fact every irreducible schemes are contractible\textbackslash{}n(simply-connected) when endowed with the Zariski topology.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 82**. Let \$X\$ be a topological space. A **cofinite subset**\textbackslash{}nof a set \$X\$ is a subset \$A\$ whose complement is a finite set. The\textbackslash{}n**cofinite topology** is a topology whose open subsets are precisely all\textbackslash{}ncofinite subsets and the empty set.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIt is immediately clear that in dimension \$1\$, the Zariski topology is\textbackslash{}ncofinite.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: lemma\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 83**. *Let \$X\$ be a set of cardinality at least \$2\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}aleph\_0\}\$\textbackslash{}nendowed with the cofinite topology. Then \$X\$ is contractible.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* The assumption is introduced simply to require that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lvert X \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rvert = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lvert [0,1]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rvert\$ (in fact this forces \$X\$ to be\textbackslash{}npath-connected). Now from [@set\_theory] \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}S 10.35\$ , we have the\textbackslash{}nfollowing result :\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lvert X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times [0,1]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rvert = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}max\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lvert X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rvert , \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lvert [0,1]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rvert \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lvert X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rvert\$\textbackslash{}n(since they are both infinite sets). So, we may consider an injection\textbackslash{}n\$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times [0,1] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}hookrightarrow X\$. Such an injection is continuous by\textbackslash{}nthe definition of the cofinite and product topologies. Then for a fixed\textbackslash{}n\$x\_0\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$, we define a homotopy from the constant map to the identity\textbackslash{}nmap : \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{equation*\}\textbackslash{}n    H(x,t)=\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{cases\}\textbackslash{}n        x, \& t=0\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n        f(x,t), \& t\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in (0,1)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n        x\_0, \& t=1\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{cases\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{equation*\}\$\$ continuity of the homotopy follows from the fact that\textbackslash{}nthe inverse image of any point in \$X\$ is closed in the product topology\textbackslash{}n(and since for the cofinite topology, closed set are finite sets, it is\textbackslash{}nenough to check only for points). This proves that \$X\$ is\textbackslash{}ncontractible. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn set theory, the *cardinality of the continuum* is the cardinality of\textbackslash{}nthe set of real numbers \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{R\}\$. It is an infinite cardinal number\textbackslash{}nand it is denoted as \$2\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}aleph\_0\}\$, where \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}aleph\_0\$ represents the\textbackslash{}ncardinality of the set of natural numbers \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{N\}\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 13**. Notice that it is not enough to assume that \$X\$ is\textbackslash{}ninfinite. For example, the set of rational numbers \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Q\}\$ with the\textbackslash{}ncofinite topology is not path-connected, which then implies that it\textbackslash{}ncannot be contractible.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThus, an algebraic curve over an uncountable base field (e.g.\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ or even \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{R\}\$) has trivial fundamental groups. We\textbackslash{}ncan go even further, and claim that every irreducible schemes are\textbackslash{}ncontractible.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nTo show this, we give a preliminary result about irreducible schemes and\textbackslash{}n*generic points*. They are points that are non-necessarily closed and\textbackslash{}nthus in the Zariski topology, their closure is the whole space.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#irreducible\_generic\_point .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 84**. *Let \$X\$ be an irreducible scheme. Then \$X\$ has a unique\textbackslash{}ngeneric point.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* If \$X=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R\$, then the nilradical of \$R\$\textbackslash{}n(\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sqrt\{(0)\}\$) is the generic point. Indeed \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R\$\textbackslash{}nis irreducible if and only if \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sqrt\{(0)\}\$ is a prime ideal : \$X\$ is\textbackslash{}nirreducible if and only if the intersection of two non-empty\textbackslash{}ndistinguished opens \$D(f)\$ and \$D(g)\$ which is \$D(fg)\$ is non-empty. But\textbackslash{}nthis is equivalent to saying that \$f\$ and \$g\$ are not nilpotent then\textbackslash{}n\$fg\$ is not nilpotent, hence that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sqrt\{(0)\}\$ is a prime ideal. And\textbackslash{}nsince the nilradical is the intersection of all prime ideals, it is\textbackslash{}ncontained in every point of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R\$, so\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sqrt\{(0)\}\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R\$. It is unique\textbackslash{}nbecause if another prime ideal \$P\$ were to be a generic point, the\textbackslash{}n\$V(P) = V(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sqrt\{(0)\})\$ and thus \$P = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sqrt\{(0)\}\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nNow in general, if \$X\$ is irreducible and \$U=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R\$\textbackslash{}nis an affine open subset, then any generic point of \$X\$ is a generic\textbackslash{}npoint of \$U\$. Conversely if \$P\$ is a generic point of \$U\$ there cannot\textbackslash{}nbe another affine open subset \$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$ that does not contain \$P\$,\textbackslash{}nsince if it were the case, \$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap U\$ it would be empty, not containing\textbackslash{}nthe generic point of \$U\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIt is now easy to show that\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: lemma\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 85**. *Every irreducible scheme is contractible.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Let \$X\$ be an irreducible scheme and denote by \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta\$ its\textbackslash{}nunique generic point. Then we have the following homotopy\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{equation*\}\textbackslash{}n    H(x,t)=\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{cases\}\textbackslash{}n        x, \& t=0\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n        \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta, \& t \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}neq 0\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{cases\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{equation*\}\$\$ which is again continuous since \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta\$ is a generic\textbackslash{}npoint, every point of \$X\$ is either in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta\$ or in its boundary. And\textbackslash{}nwhich implies that the identity map is homotopic to the constant map.\textbackslash{}nHence \$X\$ is contractible. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWhile the Zariski topology is ideal in many cases, mainly for keeping\textbackslash{}ntrack of algebraic data (such as prime/maximal ideals, dimensionality,\textbackslash{}nlocalisation, nilpotents, homomorphisms, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}...) we have seen that it\textbackslash{}nfails at discerning geometric properties topologically. So, how to\textbackslash{}nproceed from there ?\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nSince there is already a large theory of algebraic geometry built with\textbackslash{}nthe Zariski topology, it is rather clever that we don't discard all of\textbackslash{}nit. To tackle this issue, Grothendieck had the brilliant idea to\textbackslash{}nconsider not only open sets, but at the same time, open immersions.\textbackslash{}nThus, introducing a new kind of topology (that can now even be defined\textbackslash{}non a whole category, see Appendix\textbackslash{}n[5.6](\#Groth\_topo)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"Groth\_topo\textbackslash{}"\}). One\textbackslash{}ncan further define the notion of a sheaf for a category.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nIn our case, recall that in the theory of coverings from algebraic\textbackslash{}ntopology, we are interested in certain morphisms, those which are\textbackslash{}nlocally homeomorphic, so a good guess would be to consider morphisms of\textbackslash{}nschemes that ''look like\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" local isomorphisms. We will see later that\textbackslash{}nthese are naturally étale morphisms. Although the étale topology is\textbackslash{}ndefined through the notion of étale morphisms, we will not define what\textbackslash{}nthey are yet. For now, it is only important to keep in mind that they\textbackslash{}nare the algebraic analogue of local isomorphisms. All of this is\textbackslash{}nexplained in the next section.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#def\_etale\_covering .definition\}\textbackslash{}n**Definition 86**. Let \$X\$ be a scheme. We call an étale covering of \$X\$\textbackslash{}na family of morphisms \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{f\_i:X\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\_\{i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\}\$ of schemes\textbackslash{}nsuch that \$f\_i\$ is étale for all \$i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$ and \$X = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cup\_i f\_i(X\_i)\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nThe **étale topology** is a Grothendieck topology on the category of\textbackslash{}nschemes such that for \$X\$ a scheme, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(X)\$ is an étale\textbackslash{}ncovering of \$X\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe category of schemes allows many different Grothendieck topologies\textbackslash{}nfor different purposes. In this thesis, we will focus on the étale\textbackslash{}ntopology. To establish that it is indeed the correct notion, we can\textbackslash{}ncompare the outcome étale results with results from the analytification\textbackslash{}nof a scheme of finite type over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ (see Section\textbackslash{}n[2.4](\#comparaison\_theorem)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"comparaison\_theorem\textbackslash{}"\} and Appendix\textbackslash{}n[6.5](\#analytification)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"analytification\textbackslash{}"\}), which has the induced complex topology, a\textbackslash{}ntopology standard in the context of algebraic topology and the\textbackslash{}nfundamental groups. The initial comparison theorem is the following, due\textbackslash{}nto Serre and can be found in [@Serre] (Theorem \$1\$, Chapitre \$12\$).\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 87**. *For every coherent sheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ on \$X\$ a\textbackslash{}nprojective scheme and for all \$r \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{N\}\$, the following\textbackslash{}nhomomorphism is a bijection\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varepsilon : H\^{}r(X,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow H\^{}r(X\^{}\{an\},\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\^{}\{an\}).\$\$*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# On Étale Morphisms of Schemes \{\#morphisms\_of\_schemes\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAs motivated previously, to define a fundamental group over schemes, our\textbackslash{}nfirst step will be to introduce *étale morphisms*, the core of the étale\textbackslash{}ntopology. But before doing so, we need to introduce important notions\textbackslash{}nsuch as *finiteness*, *flatness*, *sheaves of differentials* and\textbackslash{}n*smoothness* that are directly related to morphisms of schemes. Such\textbackslash{}nnotions are called relative notions. As Vakil suggests in [@Vakil],\textbackslash{}nthere are a gazillion finiteness conditions on morphisms of schemes. The\textbackslash{}nones we are immediately interested in are (locally of) *finite type*,\textbackslash{}nand (locally of) *finite presentation*.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# Finite morphisms\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn a vacuum, the following finiteness conditions ensure that the\textbackslash{}ndimensions of the fibres of our morphisms do not degenerate (that they\textbackslash{}nstay finite).\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 88**. We say that a morphism of schemes \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$\textbackslash{}nis **locally of finite type** if \$Y\$ has an affine open covering\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{V\_i = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ so that \$f\^{}\{-1\}(V\_i)\$ has itself\textbackslash{}nan affine open covering \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{U\_\{ij\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\_\{ij\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$\textbackslash{}nwith \$A\_\{ij\}\$ finitely generated \$B\_i\$-algebras.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nMoreover, a morphism \$f\$ is said to be of **finite type**, if in\textbackslash{}naddition, each \$f\^{}\{-1\}(V\_i)\$ can be covered by a finite number of\textbackslash{}n\$U\_\{ij\}\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nAnd a morphism \$f\$ is said to be **finite** if each \$f\^{}\{-1\}(V\_i)=U\_i\$ an\textbackslash{}nopen affine subscheme of \$X\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#loc\_finite\_pres\_loc\_finite\_type\_noetherian .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 14**. Usually it is require that smooth or étale morphism are\textbackslash{}nnot only locally of finite type, but locally of finite presentation. A\textbackslash{}nring \$A\$ is said to be a **finitely presented** \$B\$-algebra if\textbackslash{}n\$\$A \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong B[x\_1,...,x\_n]/(r\_1(x\_1,...,x\_n), ..., r\_j(x\_1,...,x\_n)).\$\$ A\textbackslash{}nmorphism \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ is **locally of finite presentation** if for\textbackslash{}neach affine open set \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B\$ of \$Y\$,\textbackslash{}n\$f\^{}\{-1\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B)=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cup\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\_i\$\textbackslash{}nwith \$B\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow A\_i\$ finitely presented.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nNow notice that if we are in the Noetherian setting (so let \$B\$ be\textbackslash{}nNoetherian) then being finitely presented is the same as being of finite\textbackslash{}ntype. And since we are restricting ourselves to the Noetherian case, in\textbackslash{}nthe following we will not consider morphisms locally of finite\textbackslash{}npresentation.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: examples\textbackslash{}n**Examples 89**.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- By definition, finite morphisms are affine.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- And for a scheme \$X\$ and a field \$k\$, if the morphism of schemes\textbackslash{}n  \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:k\$ is finite, then \$X\$ is an\textbackslash{}n  affine scheme.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#base\_change\_locally\_finite .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 90** (Base change). *Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a morphism\textbackslash{}nof schemes, locally of finite type. And consider the following fibre\textbackslash{}nproduct diagram for any morphism \$g:Y'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$with\textbackslash{}n\$X'= X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YY'\$, \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{tikzcd\}\textbackslash{}n        X'  \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[r,\textbackslash{}"f'\textbackslash{}"] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d, \textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\_X\textbackslash{}"'] \& Y' \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d,\textbackslash{}"g\textbackslash{}"] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n        X \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[r,\textbackslash{}"f\textbackslash{}"'] \&  Y.\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{tikzcd\}\$\$ Then the morphism \$f': X'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y'\$ is also\textbackslash{}nlocally of finite type.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{V'\_i = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B'\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ be an affine open\textbackslash{}ncovering of \$Y'\$, which maps into some open affine covering\textbackslash{}n\$V\_i = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B\_i\$ of \$Y\$. Since \$f\$ is locally of\textbackslash{}nfinite type, \$f\^{}\{-1\}(V\_i)\$ has an affine open covering\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{U\_\{ij\}=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\_\{ij\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ such that \$A\_\{ij\}\$ are\textbackslash{}nfinitely generated \$B\_i\$-algebras.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nNow\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_X\^{}\{-1\}(U\_\{ij\})\_\{V'\} = U\_\{ij\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_V V' = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\_\{ij\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B\_i\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B'\_i\$\textbackslash{}nare affine opens and thus \$f\^{}\{-1\}(V\_i)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_VV' \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X'\$ has an open\textbackslash{}naffine covering by the above affine opens which are now finitely\textbackslash{}ngenerated \$B'\_i\$-algebras. Thus \$f'\$ is locally of finite type. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#composition\_locally\_finite\_type .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 91** (Composition). *If \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$g:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ are morphisms of schemes locally of finite type, then\textbackslash{}n\$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f :X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ is again locally of finite type.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Follows by transitivity of finite generation; if \$A\$ is a\textbackslash{}nfinitely generated \$B\$- algebra and \$B\$ is a finitely generated\textbackslash{}n\$C\$-algebra, then \$A\$ is a finitely generated \$C\$-algebra. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: lemma\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 92**. *In the Noetherian setting, schemes of finite type over a\textbackslash{}nfield are of finite dimension.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Let \$X\$ be a scheme of finite type over \$k\$, then \$X\$ can be\textbackslash{}ncovered by affine sets \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: A\_i\$ where the \$A\_i\$\textbackslash{}nare finitely generated \$k\$-algebras. This means that each chain of\textbackslash{}nclosed subscheme with the strict inclusion is finite, therefore the\textbackslash{}nsupremum of the length of chains of strictly increasing irreducible\textbackslash{}nclosed sets of \$X\$ is also finite. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 93**. *Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a morphism of schemes of\textbackslash{}nfinite type. Then for all \$q\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\$, the fibre scheme \$X\_y\$ has finite\textbackslash{}ndimension.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* By base change, the fibre of a morphism of schemes of finite\textbackslash{}ntype is again of finite type over the base change, which is now the\textbackslash{}nresidue field. Hence by the above lemma, its fibres at any point are\textbackslash{}nfinite-dimensional. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#finite\_is\_closed .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 94**. *Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a finite morphism of\textbackslash{}nNoetherian schemes. Then \$f\$ is closed.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Since \$f\$ is finite, locally, consider\textbackslash{}n\$Y = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B\$ and \$X=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\$ with\textbackslash{}n\$A\$ a finitely generated \$B\$-algebra. Pick generators\textbackslash{}n\$a\_1,...,a\_n \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in A\$ and define a surjection\textbackslash{}n\$B[x\_1,...,x\_n] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow A\$, by \$x\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto a\_i\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nSo we can consider the following embedding\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: A \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}hookrightarrow Proj\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B[x\_0,...,x\_n] = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{P\}\_B\^{}n\$.\textbackslash{}nThus we obtain a factorisation\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}hookrightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{P\}\_Y\^{}n \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$, so \$f\$ is projective\textbackslash{}n(locally). Projective morphisms are proper ([@Hartshorne], Theorem\textbackslash{}n\$4.9\$) and properness is local on the base ([@Hartshorne], Corollary\textbackslash{}n\$4.8\$). So \$f\$ is a proper morphisms which is closed since it is\textbackslash{}nuniversally closed. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#closed\_is\_finite .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 95**. *Closed immersions are finite*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a closed immersion. Then locally, it\textbackslash{}nlooks like\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: A/I \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}A\$.\textbackslash{}nSince \$A/I\$ is finitely generated as an \$A\$-module, it follows that \$f\$\textbackslash{}nis finite. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# Flat Morphisms\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn [@Red\_Book], David Mumford begins his section on flat morphisms with\textbackslash{}nthe following quote: *The concept of flatness is a riddle that comes out\textbackslash{}nof algebra, but which technically is the answer to many prayers*.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nAnd indeed, flatness is quite an intuitive notion in algebra while being\textbackslash{}nquite mysterious in the geometric realm. At the level of modules,\textbackslash{}nflatness is a property about the extension of scalar functor. In broad\textbackslash{}nterms, it claims that the tensor product behaves nicely. Now, at the\textbackslash{}nlevel of schemes, it is again a relative notion that encapsulates the\textbackslash{}nconcept of a ''continuous family of schemes\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}". By that we mean that the\textbackslash{}nfibres of a *flat* morphism of schemes does not vary too wildly.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 96**. An \$R\$-module \$M\$ is called **flat** if tensoring\textbackslash{}nwith \$M\$ over \$R\$ as a functor :\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n\$-\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_RM:Mod\_R\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Mod\_\{R'\}\$ is an exact functor. A morphism\textbackslash{}nof rings \$f: B \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow A\$ is said to be **flat** if \$A\$ is flat as a\textbackslash{}n\$B\$-module.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAn additive functor \$F:Mod\_R\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Mod\_\{R'\}\$ is called an *exact\textbackslash{}nfunctor* if it sends (short) exact sequences of \$R\$-modules to (short)\textbackslash{}nexact sequences of \$R'\$-modules. We make the distinction that a functor\textbackslash{}n\$F\$ is *left exact* if it sends a short exact sequence\textbackslash{}n\$0 \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow N \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow N' \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow N'' \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow 0\$ to a\textbackslash{}nsequence that is exact at \$F(N)\$ and \$F(N')\$. Conversely, \$F\$ is *right\textbackslash{}nexact* if it sends the short exact sequence above to a sequence exact at\textbackslash{}n\$F(N')\$ and \$F(N'')\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#restriction\_on\_showing\_exactness .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 15**. Note that the functor\textbackslash{}n\$-\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_RM:Mod\_R \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Mod\_R\$ is always right exact; the\textbackslash{}nextension of scalar functor is a left adjoint of the restriction of\textbackslash{}nscalar functor. Left adjoint functors preserve all colimits, and in\textbackslash{}nparticular they preserve cokernels (much like kernels detect injectivity\textbackslash{}nby trivial kernel, a map is surjective if and only if its cokernel is\textbackslash{}ntrivial). So the extension of scalar functor actually preserves\textbackslash{}nsurjectivity and thus is a right exact functor. Hence, to show the\textbackslash{}nexactness of the extension of scalar functor it is enough to show only\textbackslash{}nleft exactness (that it preserves injections).\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe now show a few important properties of flatness, such as\textbackslash{}ncompatibility with base change and localisation, which are crucial in\textbackslash{}nalgebraic geometry to make sense of pulling back structures and the\textbackslash{}ninterplay between local and global settings.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 97**. *Projective modules are flat.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Consider an injective morphism \$g: N \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow N'\$ of\textbackslash{}n\$R\$-modules and \$P\$ a projective \$R\$-module. We want to show that\textbackslash{}n\$P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_R g:P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_R N'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow I\}\$ be a dual basis of \$P\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nFor any \$i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$, apply \$f\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_R N'\$ Let\textbackslash{}n\$\$0\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow N\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow N'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow N''\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow 0\$\$ be a short\textbackslash{}nexact sequence of \$R\$-modules. And since \$M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_R -\$ is a right exact\textbackslash{}nfunctor, we have \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{equation\}\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}label\{(1)\}\textbackslash{}n        ...\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow L \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_RN\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_RN'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_RN''\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow 0.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{equation\}\$\$ We want to know if \$L=0\$ (remember that it is enough to\textbackslash{}nshow that \$L\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{p\}\}=0\$ for all \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{p\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in R\$). A quasi-coherent sheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ on a scheme \$X\$\textbackslash{}nis said to be **flat at \$p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$** if \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_p\$ is a flat\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,p\}\$-module. It is flat over \$X\$ if it is flat at all\textbackslash{}n\$p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nLet \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a morphism of schemes, and let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$\textbackslash{}nbe an \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$-module. We say that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ is **flat** over\textbackslash{}n\$Y\$ at \$p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$ (or that \$f\$ is flat at \$p\$), if the stalk\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_p\$ is a flat \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{Y,f(p)\}\$-module. We say that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ is **flat** over \$Y\$ is if it is flat at every point\textbackslash{}n\$p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$. Moreover, we say that \$X\$ is **flat** over \$Y\$ if\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$ is.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 16**. Any scheme \$X\$ over a field \$k\$ is flat. If \$k\$ is a\textbackslash{}nfield, then any \$k\$-module is actually a free module, hence a flat\textbackslash{}nmodule. Schematically, we have that \$X\$ is flat at a point \$x\$ if\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,x\}\$ is flat, and since it is a \$k\$-algebra, it is then\textbackslash{}nflat by the preceding argument.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nThis can be understood geometrically as well, flatness means that the\textbackslash{}nfibres of a morphism \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:k\$ ''vary\textbackslash{}ncontinuously\textbackslash{}", and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:k\$ being a single point, it\textbackslash{}nis obviously the case.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nMany flatness results about modules carry over easily to the case of\textbackslash{}nmorphisms of schemes. We give a few below.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#base\_change\_flat\_morphism .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 104** (Base change). *Let \$f: X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a\textbackslash{}nmorphism of schemes and let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ be an \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$-module\textbackslash{}nwhich is flat over \$Y\$. the\textbackslash{}npull-back sheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\_X\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ is flat over \$Y'\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Recall that the pull-back sheaf is defined as\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_X\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_X\^{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_X\^{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YY'\}\$,\textbackslash{}nand that from Appendix [6.2](\#Annexe\_scheme)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Annexe\_scheme\textbackslash{}"\}, we have the following for the structure\textbackslash{}nsheaf of the fibre product :\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YY'\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_X\^{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_\{(f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_X)\^{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_Y\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_\{Y'\}\^{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{Y'\}\$.\textbackslash{}nThus we have\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_X\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_X\^{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_X\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ becomes flat\textbackslash{}nover \$Y'\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#composition\_flat .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 105** (Composition). *Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$g:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ be morphisms such that \$X\$ is flat over \$Y\$ and \$Y\$\textbackslash{}nis flat over \$Z\$. Then \$X\$ is flat over \$Z\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Follows from Proposition\textbackslash{}n[99](\#transitivity\_flatness)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"transitivity\_flatness\textbackslash{}"\} ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#flat\_is\_open .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 106**. *Let \$f:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be flat morphism of schemes\textbackslash{}nlocally of finite type. Then \$f\$ is universally open and in particular\textbackslash{}nit is open.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@EGA], Théorème \$2.4.6\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nHere *universally open* simply means that \$f\$ is open under any base\textbackslash{}nchange, so obviously it implies that \$f\$ is open.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: example\textbackslash{}n**Example 107**. Open embeddings are flat:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nLet \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be an open embedding of schemes. This means that\textbackslash{}n\$X\$ is isomorphic to an open subscheme \$U\$ of \$Y\$ (that \$X\$ and \$U\$ are\textbackslash{}nhomeomorphic and that the induced map\textbackslash{}n\$f\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\#\}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_U \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow f\_*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$ is an\textbackslash{}nisomorphism). From this we have that maps between stalks are\textbackslash{}nisomorphisms as well and so at any point of \$X\$, our map \$f\$ is flat.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe next class of morphism of schemes is a weaker kind of flat\textbackslash{}nmorphisms.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 108**. A morphism \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ is said to be\textbackslash{}n**locally free** if the direct image sheaf \$f\_*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$ is a\textbackslash{}nlocally free as an \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_Y\$-module.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#locally\_free\_are\_flat\_in\_noetherian .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 17**. It is easy and useful to see that locally free morphisms\textbackslash{}nare flat. Indeed if \$f\_*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$ is locally free as an\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_Y\$-module, then locally on \$Y\$, \$f\_*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$ is free,\textbackslash{}nhence flat by Corollary\textbackslash{}n[98](\#free\_modules\_are\_flat)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"free\_modules\_are\_flat\textbackslash{}"\}. Thus \$f\$ is now a flat morphism.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nOn the other hand, the converse is also true in the Noetherian setting.\textbackslash{}nRecall that in this case morphisms of finite type are equivalently of\textbackslash{}nfinite presentations (Remark\textbackslash{}n[14](\#loc\_finite\_pres\_loc\_finite\_type\_noetherian)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"loc\_finite\_pres\_loc\_finite\_type\_noetherian\textbackslash{}"\}), then by\textbackslash{}nCorollary \$24.4.7\$ in [@Vakil], flatness and locally freeness are the\textbackslash{}nsame thing.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 109** (Composition). *The composition of two locally free\textbackslash{}nmorphisms of schemes is again locally free.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ and \$g:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ be locally free\textbackslash{}nmorphisms. Then \$f\_*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$ is locally free as a\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_Y\$-module. And again \$g\_*(f\_*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X)\$ is a locally\textbackslash{}nfree \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_Z\$-module making \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f\$ a locally free morphism. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFinally, we quote the following theorem by Grothendieck (appearing in\textbackslash{}n*Éléments de Géométrie Algébrique IV*), a key result in the quest of\textbackslash{}nunderstanding flatness,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: corollary\textbackslash{}n**Corollary 110**. *Soient \$Y\$ un préschéma localement noethérien,\textbackslash{}n\$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ un morphisme propre, \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\$ un point tel que \$f\$\textbackslash{}nsoit ouvert en tous les points de \$f\^{}\{-1\}(y)\$. Alors la fonction\textbackslash{}n\$z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto dim(f\^{}\{-1\}(z))\$ est constante dans un voisinage de \$y\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@EGA], Corollaire \$14.2.5\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nTranslating everything, and combining it with the fact that flat\textbackslash{}nmorphism of finite type are open (Proposition\textbackslash{}n[106](\#flat\_is\_open)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"flat\_is\_open\textbackslash{}"\}), we\textbackslash{}nget\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 111**. *Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a proper, flat morphism of\textbackslash{}nschemes locally of finite type. Then for \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\$, the map\textbackslash{}n\$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto dim(X\_y)\$ is locally constant.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# The Sheaf of Kähler Differentials\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe motivation behind Kähler differentials is to generalise the\textbackslash{}nintuitive concept of differential forms from differential geometry. One\textbackslash{}nimportant aspect of the sheaf of Kähler differentials is that it is a\textbackslash{}nquasi-coherent sheaf whose fibre at any point is precisely the dual of\textbackslash{}nthe tangent space at that point. It will also be central in the\textbackslash{}ndefinition of smooth and étale morphisms. There are several ways of\textbackslash{}ndefining the module of Kähler differentials, one of them is by means of\textbackslash{}nderivations.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 112**. Suppose \$A\$ is a \$B\$-algebra. We define a\textbackslash{}n**\$B\$-linear derivation** on \$A\$ to be a \$B\$-module homomorphism\textbackslash{}n\$d:A \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow M\$ to an \$A\$-module \$M\$ satisfying the Leibniz rule :\textbackslash{}n\$d(fg) = f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:dg + g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:df\$. We denote the set of such \$B\$-linear\textbackslash{}nderivations by \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Der\}\}\_B(A,M)\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 113**. The **module of Kähler differentials** is defined to\textbackslash{}nbe the \$A\$-module \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{A/B\}\$ for which there is a universal\textbackslash{}nderivation \$d:A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{A/B\}\$. The composition with \$d\$\textbackslash{}nprovides, for every \$A\$-module \$M\$ an \$A\$-module isomorphism\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_A(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{A/B\}, M) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow[]\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Der\}\}\_B(A,M)\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nNow one way to construct \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{A/B\}\$ and \$d\$ is by constructing a\textbackslash{}nfree \$A\$-module as linear combinations of the symbol \$da\$ for each\textbackslash{}n\$a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in A\$ and imposing the following relations :\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- \$da+da' = d(a+a')\$ \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}forall a'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in A\$ (additivity),\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- \$d(aa') = ada' +a'da\$ (Leibniz law) , and\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- \$db = 0\$ \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}forall b\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in B\$ (triviality of pull-back).\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nNotice that \$d:A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{A/B\}\$ is \$B\$-linear. And the\textbackslash{}nuniversal derivation sends \$a\$ to \$da\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFrom the Leibniz law of differentials, we can easily deduce the quotient\textbackslash{}nlaw and the chain rule for differentials.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#example\_kahler .examples\}\textbackslash{}n**Examples 114**.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- If \$A = k[x\_1,...,x\_n]\$ and \$B=k\$, then\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{A/B\} = Adx\_1 \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}oplus ...\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}oplus Adx\_n\$ a free \$A\$-module of\textbackslash{}n  rank \$n\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n  Since for \$p(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha)=0\$ and\textbackslash{}n  \$p'(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}neq 0\$. So by the chain rule we have\textbackslash{}n  \$0 = d(p(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha)) = p'(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha)d\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\$, so \$d\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha=0\$ for all\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in L\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn the last example the converse is also true and it can be shown using\textbackslash{}nseparable algebras. But before we need the following lemma :\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: lemma\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 115**. *If a finitely generated ideal \$I\$ in a commutative ring\textbackslash{}n\$R\$ has \$I\^{}2=  I\$, then \$I = pR\$ for \$p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in R\$ an idempotent.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* The lemma is almost immediate following Nakayama's Lemma\textbackslash{}n[256](\#Nakayama\_lemma)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"Nakayama\_lemma\textbackslash{}"\}.\textbackslash{}nWe apply it to \$M = I\$ and we get that there exist \$i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\$im =m\$ for all \$m\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$. It follows that \$i\^{}2 = i\$ and \$I = iR\$, and\textbackslash{}njust let \$p=i\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 116**. *Let \$A\$ be a commutative \$k\$-algebra. If\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{A/k\} = 0\$ then \$A\$ is a separable \$k\$-algebra.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* We show this later on (Theorem\textbackslash{}n[122](\#second\_def\_Kalher)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"second\_def\_Kalher\textbackslash{}"\}) but, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{A/k\} = 0\$ implies that\textbackslash{}n\$I = I\^{}2\$ for \$I\$ the kernel of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta\$ which is the multiplication map\textbackslash{}nfor our \$k\$-algebra \$A\$. When \$k\$ is a field and \$A\$ is\textbackslash{}nfinite-dimensional, notice that every ideal of \$A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes A\$ is finitely\textbackslash{}ngenerated, so we can apply the above lemma and consider the\textbackslash{}nmultiplication by the idempotent \$p\$ for \$p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes A\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\$I = p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot (A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes A)\$. This gives an \$A\$,\$A\$-bimodule map\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: p: A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow I\$ and we have\textbackslash{}n\$(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:p)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ i = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{id\}\}\_I\$ so by the splitting lemma,\textbackslash{}nthe exact sequence in Lemma\textbackslash{}n[63](\#lemma\_splitting\_exact\_sequence\_separable)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"lemma\_splitting\_exact\_sequence\_separable\textbackslash{}"\} splits making \$A\$\textbackslash{}nseparable. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nSo by combining these results, and remembering that separable\textbackslash{}ncommutative algebras then\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{L,k\}=0\$ if and only if \$L|k\$ is separable.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAs it was the case with flat Recall that the tangent space at a point \$p\$ of an\textbackslash{}nalgebraic variety can be thought of as assigning to a polynomial \$f\$ its\textbackslash{}nlinear term in the Taylor expansion at \$p\$. Consider the following diagonal\textbackslash{}nhomomorphism (induced by diagonal maps of affine schemes)\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta : A \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_B A \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow A\$, given by multiplication. Indeed, if\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sum x\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes y\_i)= \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sum x\_iy\_i=0\$, then\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sum\_i x\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes y\_i = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sum\_i (x\_i \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes y\_i - x\_iy\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes 1) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sum\_i x\_i(1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes y\_i -y\_i \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes 1).\$\$\textbackslash{}nAnd \$I\^{}2\$ is an \$A\$-submodule of \$I\$ generated by all products\textbackslash{}n\$x\_1x\_2\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes y\_1y\_2\$ with \$x\_1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes y\_1,x\_2\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes y\_2\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$ for\textbackslash{}nboth multiplication on the left and on the right. So \$I/I\^{}2\$ is an\textbackslash{}n\$A\$-module.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nLet's check that the map \$d: A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow I/I\^{}2\$,\textbackslash{}n\$a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto 1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes a - a \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes 1\$ is a universal derivation.\textbackslash{}nAdditivity is evident, and if \$b\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in B\$, then \$1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes b-b\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes 1 = 0\$\textbackslash{}nsince remember tensoring is done over \$B\$. It is left to show the\textbackslash{}nLeibniz rule : \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{equation*\}\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{split\}\textbackslash{}n        d(aa') - ada'-a'da \&=  (1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes aa' -aa' \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes 1) - (a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes a'-aa'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes 1) -(a' \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes a - a'a \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes 1) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n        \& = 1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes aa' - a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes a' -a'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes a + a'a \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes 1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n        \& = (1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes a - a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes1)(1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes a'- a'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes 1) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\^{}2\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{split\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{equation*\}\$\$ Since the maps \$a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto 1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes a\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes 1\$ from \$A\$ to \$A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_B A\$ are \$B\$-linear, then so\textbackslash{}nis their difference \$d\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nIt is left to check that the induced map\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{A/B\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow I/I\^{}2\$ sending \$da\$ to\textbackslash{}n\$1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes a-a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes 1\$ is an isomorphism. ad1 = da, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textit\{ and\}\$\$\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sum\_ix\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes y\_i \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sum\_ix\_idy\_i) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sum\_i x\_i(1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes y\_i - y\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes 1) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sum\_ix\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes y\_i\$\$\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\$ is clearly injective, and it is surjective as well since every\textbackslash{}nelement of \$I/I\^{}2\$ is a linear combination of \$1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes a-a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes 1\$ so\textbackslash{}nan image of \$da\$ under \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWith the above construction and analogous description, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{A/B\}\$\textbackslash{}nand the tangent space become intrinsic notions, we use them to define\textbackslash{}nthe sheaf of Kähler differentials on schemes. Let \$f: X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be\textbackslash{}na morphism of schemes (assumed to be separated) and consider the\textbackslash{}ndiagonal morphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta : X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_Y X\$. Remember it is a\textbackslash{}nclosed embedding, so we can consider the ideal sheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{I\}\$ of of\textbackslash{}n\$X\$ in \$Y\$ just as in Lemma [346](\#ideal\_sheaf)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"ideal\_sheaf\textbackslash{}"\}.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 123**. We define the **sheaf of Kähler differentials**\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Y\}\$ of \$X\$ over \$Y\$ as the pull-back\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta\^{}*(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{I\}/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{I\}\^{}2)\$ on \$X\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nNote that it is a quasi-coherent sheaf (see Appendix\textbackslash{}n[6.3](\#annexe\_quasi\_coherent)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"annexe\_quasi\_coherent\textbackslash{}"\}). We can verify that in the affine\textbackslash{}ncase, it is consistent with our previous definition of module of\textbackslash{}nrelative differentials. Let \$U=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$V=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B\$ be an affine open subsets of \$X\$ and \$Y\$\textbackslash{}nrespectively such that \$f(U) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset V\$, then \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_V U\$ is an affine\textbackslash{}nopen subset of \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_Y X\$ isomorphic to\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:(A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_B A)\$. \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(X)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap (U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_V U)\$\textbackslash{}nis the closed subscheme defined by the kernel of the associated diagonal\textbackslash{}nhomomorphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}delta :A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes \_B A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow A\$. That way we see that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{I\}/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{I\}\^{}2\$ is the sheaf of modules associated to the\textbackslash{}n\$A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_BA\$-module \$I/I\^{}2\$. And the restricted sheaf of relative\textbackslash{}ndifferentials \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{U/V\}\$ is the sheaf associated to \$I/I\^{}2\$ as an\textbackslash{}n\$A\$-module, so \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Y\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_\{U/V\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{A/B\}\}\$.\textbackslash{}nIn the language of quasi-coherent sheaves, we have constructed a sheaf\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Y\}\$ on \$X\$ whose fibre\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Y\}(P) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Y\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,P\}\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(P)\$ at\textbackslash{}n\$P\$ is now a finite-dimensional vector space over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(P)\$ that is\textbackslash{}nexactly the dual of the tangent space \$T\_PX\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#open\_embeddings\_zero\_kahler .example\}\textbackslash{}n**Example 124**. Let \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}hookrightarrow X\$ be an open embedding of\textbackslash{}nschemes, then \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{U/X\} = 0\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nIndeed, we can check locally, take an affine open\textbackslash{}n\$V=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$ and suppose that\textbackslash{}n\$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap V = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: B\$. Since \$U\$ is an open subset,\textbackslash{}nthen \$B\$ is a localisation of \$A\$ so \$B=S\^{}\{-1\}A\$ for a multiplicative\textbackslash{}nset \$S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset A\$. And as we saw in Example\textbackslash{}n[114](\#example\_kahler)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"example\_kahler\textbackslash{}"\}\textbackslash{}n\$b)\$, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{A/B\}=0\$ thus on each affine
