for morphisms of schemes.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#exact\_seq\_sheaves\_differential .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 126**. *Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ and \$g:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ be\textbackslash{}nmorphisms of schemes. Then there is an exact sequence of sheaves on \$X\$,\textbackslash{}n\$\$f\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{Y/Z\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Z\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Y\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow 0.\$\$*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Follows from Proposition\textbackslash{}n[120](\#exact\_seq\_differential\_module)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"exact\_seq\_differential\_module\textbackslash{}"\}. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# Regular Schemes and Smooth Morphisms\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nSmoothness is a central and intuitive notion in geometry. In algebraic\textbackslash{}ngeometry, this notion is called *regularity* and it is closely related\textbackslash{}nto the dimension of the tangent space. We begin by defining the tangent\textbackslash{}nspace of a scheme at a point and convince ourselves that it is\textbackslash{}nreasonably defined.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 127**. The **Zariski cotangent space** of a local ring\textbackslash{}n\$(A,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\})\$ is the vector space \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}/\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\^{}2\}\}\$\textbackslash{}nover the residue field \$A/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\$ and its dual is the **Zariski\textbackslash{}ntangent space**. Now if \$X\$ is a scheme, the **Zariski cotangent space**\textbackslash{}n\$T\_pX\^{}*\$ of \$X\$ at \$p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$ is the cotangent space of the local ring\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,p\}\$ (and similarly for the **Zariski tangent space**\textbackslash{}n\$T\_pX\$). Elements of the cotangent space are called differentials (yes,\textbackslash{}nas defined previously) and elements of the tangent space are called\textbackslash{}ntangent vectors.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nOne way to see that this is the right definition is the following:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: construction\textbackslash{}n**Construction 128**. Since we have defined tangent spaces on varieties,\textbackslash{}nlet \$X\$ be a variety and \$p=0\$ be the origin in \$X\$ corresponding to the\textbackslash{}nmaximal ideal \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}trianglelefteq A(X)\$. Consider the\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-linear map\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(TpX,k) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{   \} ;\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{ \}f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto df\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_\{T\_pX\}.\$\$\textbackslash{}nBy definition of the tangent space, this map is well-defined and\textbackslash{}nsurjective since linear maps on \$T\_pX\$ must be combinations of the\textbackslash{}ncoordinate functions \$dx\_1,...,dx\_n\$ We now show that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}ker\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\^{}2\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nNotice that \$W := \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{dg \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I(X)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ is a linear subspace of\textbackslash{}n\$k[x\_1,...,x\_n]\$ of dimension \$t\$, and its zero locus \$T\_pX\$ has\textbackslash{}ndimension \$n-t\$. So the space of linear forms vanishing on \$T\_pX\$, (i.e.\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{ dg \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid dg\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_\{T\_pX\} = 0\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$) has again dimension \$t\$ and also\textbackslash{}ncontains \$W\$. Thus \$W = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{ dg \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid dg\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_\{T\_pX\} = 0\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nNow if \$f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}ker\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\$, we know that \$df \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in W\$, so there exists a\textbackslash{}npolynomial \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I(X)\$ such that \$df=dg\$, where \$dg\$ is a linear\textbackslash{}ncombination of the linear forms defining \$W\$. So \$f-g\$ contains no\textbackslash{}nconstant term (we are at the origin) and no linear term. This means\textbackslash{}nexactly that \$f-g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\^{}2\$. Notice here that we have first\textbackslash{}nunderstood \$f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}ker\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\$ as the restriction of a formal\textbackslash{}npolynomial, defining a variety. We managed to say a lot of things about\textbackslash{}n\$f\$ as a formal polynomial and ended up with two polynomials \$f\$ and \$g\$\textbackslash{}nthat are equal when restricted to \$X\$, hence we could write that\textbackslash{}n\$f = f-g\$ with \$f\$ on the left hand side being the restriction of \$f\$ to\textbackslash{}n\$X\$. While this is confusing, we rather explain it this way than to\textbackslash{}nintroduce new notation.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nAnd since \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\^{}2\$ is generated by products \$fg\$ for\textbackslash{}n\$f,g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\$, we have\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi(fg) =f(p)dg\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_\{T\_pX\} + g(p)df\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_\{T\_pX\} = 0\$ since\textbackslash{}n\$f(p)=g(p) = 0\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nBy the isomorphism theorem, we can conclude that indeed\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\^{}2 \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong T\_pX\^{}*\$ (the dual of \$T\_pX\$).\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe are now able to state the definition of regularity for local rings,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 129**. We say that a local ring \$(R,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\})\$ is\textbackslash{}n**regular** if the dimension of the local ring is equal to the dimension\textbackslash{}nof the Zariski cotangent space, i.e.\textbackslash{}n\$dim\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R = dim\_\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}big/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\^{}2\$, with \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa\$\textbackslash{}nthe residue field \$R/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\$. A scheme \$X\$ is called **regular**\textbackslash{}nat a point \$p\$ if the local ring \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,p\}\$ is regular.\textbackslash{}nOtherwise, \$X\$ is said to be singular at \$p\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nRecall that the sheaf of Kähler differentials encodes the data of\textbackslash{}ntangent spaces of a scheme over a base scheme. Then it would make sense\textbackslash{}nto characterise regularity of a scheme through its sheaf of Kähler\textbackslash{}ndifferentials.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#regularity\_kahler .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 130**. *Let \$X\$ be an irreducible scheme of finite type\textbackslash{}nover \$k\$ an algebraically closed scheme. Then \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/k\}\$ is a\textbackslash{}nlocally free sheaf of rank \$n\$ if and only if \$X\$ is a regular scheme\textbackslash{}nover \$k\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Hartshorne] Theorem \$8.15\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe following result gives us a necessary condition for regularity.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 131** (Auslander--Buchsbaum). *Any regular local ring is a\textbackslash{}nunique factorisation domain (UFD).*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Auslander\_Buchsbaum]. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAnd since, by definition, any UFD is an integral domain, regular local\textbackslash{}nrings are integral domains. Then any point where \$2\$ irreducible\textbackslash{}ncomponents of a variety meet must be a singular point.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#normal\_regular .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 18**. From commutative algebra (Proposition \$4.20\$ in\textbackslash{}n[@Eisenbud]), we have that UFD's are normal rings. So for a scheme \$X\$,\textbackslash{}nregularity at \$P\$ implies normality, i.e. we say that a scheme \$X\$ is\textbackslash{}nnormal at \$P\$ if the local ring \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,P\}\$ is normal: an\textbackslash{}nintegrally closed integral domain.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nBut for schemes of degree \$1\$, so curves, the other implication is also\textbackslash{}ntrue. Indeed, normal local rings are actually also discrete valuation\textbackslash{}nrings (DVR) and in dimension \$1\$, regularity for a local ring is\textbackslash{}nequivalent to being a DVR (again, see \$11.1\$, \$11.2\$ [@Eisenbud]). This\textbackslash{}nmeans that for curves, regularity and smoothness are the same.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nOur next concern is that regularity does not refer to a base scheme. For\textbackslash{}nthis reason, we introduce the notion of *smooth morphisms* of schemes\textbackslash{}nand say that a scheme \$X\$ is smooth over \$k\$ if\textbackslash{}n\$X \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:k\$ is a smooth morphism. One\textbackslash{}nmisconception is that smooth morphisms in algebraic geometry are the\textbackslash{}ncounterpart of smooth morphisms from differential geometry. This is not\textbackslash{}nthe case, the correct picture is the one below, \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{equation\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}label\{relation\_morphism\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{split\}\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{Submersions\} \& \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}longleftrightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{Smooth morphisms\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{Local Isomorphism\} \& \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}longleftrightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}'Etale morphisms\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{Immersions\} \& \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}longleftrightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{Unramified morphisms\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{split\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{equation\}\$\$ As a quick reminder, in differential geometry, a\textbackslash{}nsubmersion is a smooth map of manifolds \$f:M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow N\$ whose\textbackslash{}ndifferential \$Df\_p: T\_pM\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow T\_\{f(p)\}N\$ is surjective at any\textbackslash{}npoint \$p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in M\$. An immersion is similar but requires that the\textbackslash{}ndifferential is injective at any points. And a smooth map is called a\textbackslash{}nlocal isomorphism if it is an immersion and a submersion at the same\textbackslash{}ntime.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 132**. A morphism of schemes \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ is **smooth\textbackslash{}nof relative dimension \$n\$** if it is flat, locally of finite type and\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Y\}\$ is locally free of rank \$n\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nHere, of relative dimension \$n\$ only means that all non-empty fibres\textbackslash{}nhave the same dimension \$n\$. Flatness ensures that the fibres of the\textbackslash{}nmorphism are of the same dimension, and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Y\}\$ is locally free\textbackslash{}nof rank \$n\$ specifies what the dimensions of those fibres are; this last\textbackslash{}ncondition is not surprising considering Proposition\textbackslash{}n[130](\#regularity\_kahler)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"regularity\_kahler\textbackslash{}"\}. Again, smooth morphisms of schemes are\textbackslash{}nalso compatible with base change and composition.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#base\_change\_smooth .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 133** (Base change). *Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a smooth\textbackslash{}nmorphisms of schemes of relative dimension \$n\$ and consider the\textbackslash{}nfollowing fibre product diagram for any morphism \$g:Y'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$\textbackslash{}nwith \$X'=X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_Y Y'\$, Then the morphism \$f': X'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y'\$ is also\textbackslash{}nsmooth of relative dimension \$n\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* By Proposition\textbackslash{}n[104](\#base\_change\_flat\_morphism)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"base\_change\_flat\_morphism\textbackslash{}"\},\textbackslash{}n[90](\#base\_change\_locally\_finite)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"base\_change\_locally\_finite\textbackslash{}"\} and\textbackslash{}n[125](\#base\_change\_Kahler\_sheaf)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"base\_change\_Kahler\_sheaf\textbackslash{}"\} \$f'\$ is smooth again. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#composition\_smooth .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 134** (Composition). *If \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ is smooth of\textbackslash{}nrelative dimension \$n\$, and \$g:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ is smooth of relative\textbackslash{}ndimension \$m\$, then \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f :X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ is smooth of relative\textbackslash{}ndimension \$n+m\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Hartshorne], Proposition \$10.1.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: (c)\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 19**. A nice way to see that smooth morphisms are indeed linked\textbackslash{}nto submersions is by reasoning as follows, let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a\textbackslash{}nsmooth morphism of regular schemes of relative dimension\textbackslash{}n\$n=dim\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:X-dim\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:Y\$ over \$k\$ an algebraically closed field. By Proposition\textbackslash{}n[126](\#exact\_seq\_sheaves\_differential)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"exact\_seq\_sheaves\_differential\textbackslash{}"\}, we get the exact sequence\textbackslash{}nof sheaves :\textbackslash{}n\$\$f\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{Y/k\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/k\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Y\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow 0.\$\$\textbackslash{}nTensoring with the residue field \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(P)\$ for \$P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$, we obtain a\textbackslash{}nsequence of vector spaces over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(P)\$,\textbackslash{}n\$\$f\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{Y/k\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(P) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/k\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(P) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Y\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(P) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow 0.\$\$\textbackslash{}nRecall that since \$X\$ and \$Y\$ are regular schemes over \$k\$ and that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Y\}\$ is locally free of rank \$n\$, the now vector spaces above,\textbackslash{}nhave dimensions \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dim\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:Y\$, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dim\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:X\$ and \$n\$ respectively. By\textbackslash{}nright-exactness, we have that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dim (\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{im\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dim X - n = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dim Y\$, and by the\textbackslash{}nrank-nullity theorem, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dim \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}ker \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi = 0\$ so the map on the left is\textbackslash{}ninjective. Finally, dualising it, we obtain (as seen in Construction\textbackslash{}n[121](\#construction\_tangent\_space\_differential)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"construction\_tangent\_space\_differential\textbackslash{}"\}), that the\textbackslash{}ndifferential map \$Df\_P: T\_PX\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow T\_PY\$ at any point \$P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$,\textbackslash{}ncoming from\textbackslash{}n\$f\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{Y/k\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(P)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/k\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(P)\$\textbackslash{}nis actually surjective.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# Étale Morphisms\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFinally, we arrive at the main definitions of this section.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 135**. A morphism of schemes \$f: X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ is said to\textbackslash{}nbe **étale** if it is flat, locally of finite type and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Y\}=0\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nNotice the resemblance to the definition of smoothness for morphisms of\textbackslash{}nschemes. The only difference being that the sheaf of relative\textbackslash{}ndifferential need not only to be locally free, but it has to be the zero\textbackslash{}nsheaf. This can be interpreted as a ''hidden\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" condition for étaleness,\textbackslash{}nrequiring that the morphism must be at the same time smooth and\textbackslash{}nunramified (see relation picture\textbackslash{}n([\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}[relation\_morphism\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}]](\#relation\_morphism)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"relation\_morphism\textbackslash{}"\}))\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 136**. Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a morphism of schemes\textbackslash{}nlocally of finite type, and \$P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$. \$f\$ is said to be **unramified**\textbackslash{}nat \$P\$ if the residue field of \$X\$ at \$P\$ is a separable field extension\textbackslash{}nof the residue field of \$Y\$ at \$f(P)\$. And\textbackslash{}n\$f\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\#\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\_\{f(P)\})\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,P\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\_P\$ for\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\_P\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\_\{f(P)\}\$ are local rings of the local\textbackslash{}nrings \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,P\}\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{Y,f(P)\}\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe mention the following characterisation of unramified morphism through\textbackslash{}nfibres.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#unramified\_carac .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 137**. *Let \$f: X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ \$P\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@milneEtCoH] Proosition \$3.5\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThus, from Example\textbackslash{}n[124](\#open\_embeddings\_zero\_kahler)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"open\_embeddings\_zero\_kahler\textbackslash{}"\}, we have that open embeddings\textbackslash{}nare unramified (in fact, any immersion is unramified) and with the\textbackslash{}nprevious proposition, we can reformulate our definition for étale\textbackslash{}nmorphisms of schemes.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#etale=flat+unramified .definition\}\textbackslash{}n**Definition 139**. A morphism of schemes \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ is said to\textbackslash{}nbe étale if it is equivalently flat and unramified.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFrom this definition, it is clear that étale morphisms must behave like\textbackslash{}nlocal isomorphisms, being at the same times submersions and immersions.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: examples\textbackslash{}n**Examples 140**. From previous examples, open embeddings are étale.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#base\_change\_etale .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 141** (Base change). *Let \$f: X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be an étale\textbackslash{}nmorphism of schemes and consider \$f' : X' \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y'\$ the base\textbackslash{}nchange of \$f\$. Then \$f'\$ is étale again.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Since smooth morphisms are stable under base change\textbackslash{}n([133](\#base\_change\_smooth)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"base\_change\_smooth\textbackslash{}"\}), we need to show that unramified\textbackslash{}nmorphisms are stable under base change. But they clearly are since by\textbackslash{}nProposition [125](\#base\_change\_Kahler\_sheaf)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"base\_change\_Kahler\_sheaf\textbackslash{}"\} and by the fact that the pull-back\textbackslash{}nof a zero sheaf is again a zero sheaf. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#composition\_etale .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 142** (Composition). *Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$g:Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ be two étale morphisms of schemes. Then\textbackslash{}n\$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$ is also étale.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* By Propositions\textbackslash{}n[91](\#composition\_locally\_finite\_type)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"composition\_locally\_finite\_type\textbackslash{}"\},\textbackslash{}n[105](\#composition\_flat)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"composition\_flat\textbackslash{}"\} and since \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Y\}\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$f\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{Y/Z\}\$ are zero sheave, by Proposition\textbackslash{}n[126](\#exact\_seq\_sheaves\_differential)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"exact\_seq\_sheaves\_differential\textbackslash{}"\}, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Z\}= 0\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#clopen\_immersion .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 143**. *Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a finite étale\textbackslash{}nmorphism,. Then the diagonal morphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta : X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YX\$\textbackslash{}ncoming from \$f\$ is an open and closed immersion (in particular \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta\$\textbackslash{}nis an isomorphism of \$X\$ onto its image).*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Since \$f\$ is finite, it is separated and hence the diagonal\textbackslash{}nmorphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta : X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YX\$ is a closed immersion, it is\textbackslash{}nleft to show that it is an open map. Consider \$U\$ an open subscheme of\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YX\$ such that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow U\$ is a still a closed\textbackslash{}nimmersion. Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{I\}\$ be the sheaf of ideals on \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YX\$,\textbackslash{}nthen restricted to \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(X)\$, the quotient\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{I\}/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{I\}\^{}2\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/Y\}\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nSince we are in the Noetherian setting, \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YX\$ is Noetherian,\textbackslash{}nmaking the ideal sheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{I\}\$ a coherent sheaf, so we can apply\textbackslash{}nNakayama's lemma [256](\#Nakayama\_lemma)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Nakayama\_lemma\textbackslash{}"\}. Thus obtaining that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{I\}=0\$ on an\textbackslash{}nopen subset \$U\$ of \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YX\$, restricting the closed immersion\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(X) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}hookrightarrow X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YX\$ to an isomorphism\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(X) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong U\$. So \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(X)\$ is both open and closed in\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YX\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nNotice in this case, \$X\$ is isomorphic to a union of connected component\textbackslash{}nof \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YX\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: example\textbackslash{}n**Example 144**. A morphism of affine schemes\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: A\$ is\textbackslash{}nfinite étale if and only if \$B\$ is a finite projective \$A\$-module and\textbackslash{}nfor every point \$P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\$, \$B\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(P)\$\textbackslash{}nis a finite separable algebra over the residue field.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#example\_etale\_over\_field .example\}\textbackslash{}n**Example 145**. Let \$k\$ be a field. A scheme\textbackslash{}n\$X=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\$ over \$k\$ is finite étale if and only if\textbackslash{}n\$A\$ is a finite étale \$k\$-algebra. Since \$X\$ is an affine scheme over\textbackslash{}n\$k\$ it is automatically finitely flat, so it is étale if and only if\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{X/k\} = 0\$ which is equivalent to asking that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{A/k\}=0\$.\textbackslash{}nBy Theorem [117](\#separable\_zero\_kahler)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"separable\_zero\_kahler\textbackslash{}"\} this is similar to proving that \$A\$\textbackslash{}nis a finite étale \$k\$-algebra. Moreover, by the following equation:\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: A = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Big( \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod\_\{i=1\}\^{}r L\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Big) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}coprod\_\{i=1\}\^{}r \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:L\_i\$\$\textbackslash{}nif \$X\$ is connected, \$A\$ is actually a single separable field extension\textbackslash{}nof \$k\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Finite Étale Covers and Algebraic Fundamental Groups of Schemes\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nRemember that we are forgoing a Noetherian investigation; all our rings\textbackslash{}nand schemes are to be Noetherian. In that case, we may replace flat by\textbackslash{}nlocally free and we can restrict to working with morphisms of finite\textbackslash{}ntype. Every scheme is defined over a base scheme \$S\$. And since étale\textbackslash{}nmorphisms are insensitive to base change, we can consider the *geometric\textbackslash{}nfibres* instead of the classical fibres. One reason to consider such\textbackslash{}ngeometric fibres is the following construction.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: construction\textbackslash{}n**Construction 146**. Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ be a finite étale morphism\textbackslash{}nof schemes. A **geometric point** \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\$ on \$S\$ is a morphism of\textbackslash{}nschemes \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$,\textbackslash{}nsuch that the image of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\$ is a point \$s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in S\$ and where\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\$ is an algebraically closed field extension of the residue\textbackslash{}nfield \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(s)\$. The **geometric fibre** \$X\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}\$ of \$f\$\textbackslash{}nover \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\$ is defined as the fibre product\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\$. It is often more useful to\textbackslash{}nwork with geometric fibres since it results in working with schemes\textbackslash{}ndefined over algebraically closed fields. Using Theorem\textbackslash{}n[60](\#etale\_algebras)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"etale\_algebras\textbackslash{}"\},\textbackslash{}nwe can actually conclude that the geometric fibre \$X\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}\$ has\textbackslash{}nfinitely many points. Indeed if \$S = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$X=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B\$ locally with \$B\$ a finite \$A\$-algebra,\textbackslash{}nthen \$X\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:(B\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda)\$\textbackslash{}nwith \$B\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\$ a finite (\$n\$-)dimensional \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\$-algebra,\textbackslash{}ninvoking Theorem [60](\#etale\_algebras)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"etale\_algebras\textbackslash{}"\} we obtain that\textbackslash{}n\$B\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times ...\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\$ (\$n\$ times).\textbackslash{}nTherefore\textbackslash{}n\$X\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sqcup \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:...\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sqcup \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\$,\textbackslash{}na scheme consisting of \$n\$ points.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nSo, in light of Proposition\textbackslash{}n[137](\#unramified\_carac)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"unramified\_carac\textbackslash{}"\} and Corollary\textbackslash{}n[139](\#etale=flat+unramified)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"etale=flat+unramified\textbackslash{}"\}, we have an analogue definition.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 147**. A finite morphisms of schemes \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ is\textbackslash{}nsaid to be **finite étale** if it is locally free (flat) and if each\textbackslash{}nfibre \$X\_s\$ of \$f\$ is the spectrum of a finite étale \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(s)\$-algebra\textbackslash{}n(unramified).\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nNotice from Propositions [94](\#finite\_is\_closed)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"finite\_is\_closed\textbackslash{}"\} and\textbackslash{}n[106](\#flat\_is\_open)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"flat\_is\_open\textbackslash{}"\},\textbackslash{}nthat the image of a finite étale morphisms is both open and closed.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 20**. Resuming our discussion over geometric fibres, we get\textbackslash{}nfrom Theorem [60](\#etale\_algebras)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"etale\_algebras\textbackslash{}"\} that the fibres \$X\_s\$ are spectra of a\textbackslash{}nfinite étale \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(s)\$-algebra if and only if its geometric fibres are\textbackslash{}nof the form\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times ...\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda)\$, or in\textbackslash{}nother words that they are finite disjoint union of points defined over\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\$ (when \$f\$ is a finite étale morphism). This is the main reason\textbackslash{}nbehind our preference for the geometric fibres.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn the following, we provide a theory of Galois ''à la Grothendieck\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nfor finite étale covers analogous to the theory developed for the\textbackslash{}nclassification of field extensions and of covering spaces in the first\textbackslash{}nchapter.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# Finite Étale Coverings \{\#finite\_etale\_coverings\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 148**. A morphism \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ of schemes is a\textbackslash{}n**finite étale cover** if \$f\$ is a surjective finite étale morphism. And\textbackslash{}n\$f\$ is called a **trivial finite étale cover** if \$X\$ as a scheme over\textbackslash{}n\$S\$ is isomorphic to a disjoint union of copies of \$S\$, and the map \$f\$\textbackslash{}nrestricts to identity on each component.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: example\textbackslash{}n**Example 149**. The simplest case would be to check how finite étale\textbackslash{}ncoverings would look like over \$S=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:k\$ for \$k\$ an\textbackslash{}nalgebraically closed field. Let us consider \$X\$ any finite étale\textbackslash{}ncovering over \$S\$. Since \$f\$ is finite and étale, we know that \$X\$ is\textbackslash{}nthe spectrum of a finite étale \$k\$-algebra \$A\$. And by Theorem\textbackslash{}n[60](\#etale\_algebras)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"etale\_algebras\textbackslash{}"\},\textbackslash{}nwe have that \$A \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_k\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong k\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}oplus\^{}n\}\$ because\textbackslash{}n\$k\$ is algebraically closed. So\textbackslash{}n\$X = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:k\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sqcup \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:...\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sqcup\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:k\$\textbackslash{}n(\$n\$ times), meaning that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:k\$ only has trivial\textbackslash{}nfinite étale covers which makes sense since \$S\$ is just a point.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn order to make more sense of trivial coverings, we show that finite\textbackslash{}nétale coverings are locally trivial, we want the situation to be\textbackslash{}nanalogous to that of topological coverings. Notice that the restriction\textbackslash{}nof a cover \$Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ above an open subset \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$ is none\textbackslash{}nbut the fibre product \$Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_XU\$, the proposition below then proves\textbackslash{}nour claim.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#etale\_cover\_locally\_trivial .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 150**. *Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ be an affine surjective\textbackslash{}nmorphism of schemes with \$S\$ connected. Then \$f\$ is a finite étale cover\textbackslash{}nif and only if, there is a finite, locally free and surjective morphism\textbackslash{}n\$g:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ such that \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SY\$ is a trivial cover of \$Y\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Suppose that \$g\$ is finite, locally free and surjective and\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SY\$ is a trivial cover of \$Y\$. As \$g\$ is locally free, each\textbackslash{}npoint in \$S\$ is contained in an affine open subset\textbackslash{}n\$U=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\$ over which \$g\$ restricts to a morphism\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:C\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\$ with \$C\$\textbackslash{}nan \$A\$-algebra that is finitely generated and free as an \$A\$-module. If\textbackslash{}n\$f\$ restricts to\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\$ over\textbackslash{}n\$U\$, then we have the following base change\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}(B\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_AC) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B\$\textbackslash{}nwhere \$B\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_AC\$ is a finitely generated free \$C\$-module, hence also\textbackslash{}na finitely generated free \$A\$-module. On the other hand,\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}(B\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_AC)\$ is isomorphic to a finite direct\textbackslash{}nsum of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B\$ since it is a trivial cover, and this\textbackslash{}nis only possible if \$B\$ is finitely generated free \$A\$-module. This\textbackslash{}nshows that \$f\$ must be finite and locally free. Let\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a\textbackslash{}ngeometric point of \$Y\$. By composition with \$g\$ it yields a geometric\textbackslash{}npoint of \$S\$. The geometric fibres\textbackslash{}n\$X\_\{(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ g)\} := X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_S \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\$\textbackslash{}nand\textbackslash{}n\$(X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SY)\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}:= X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SY\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\$\textbackslash{}nare isomorphic and the latter is a finite direct sum of copies of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\$ since \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SY\$ is a finite étale\textbackslash{}ncovering of \$Y\$. And since \$g\$ is surjective, we have that all the\textbackslash{}nfibres of \$f\$ are indeed finite étale \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(s)\$-algebras (invoking\textbackslash{}nTheorem [60](\#etale\_algebras)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"etale\_algebras\textbackslash{}"\}). Thus \$f\$ is a finite étale cover.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nIn the other direction, suppose that \$f\$ is a finite étale cover. \$S\$\textbackslash{}nbeing a connected scheme, then all fibres of \$f\$ have the same\textbackslash{}ncardinality say \$n\$. We now proceed by induction on \$n\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nIf \$n=1\$, then since \$f\$ is finite étale, it is also an isomorphism. So\textbackslash{}nit is possible to find a finite locally free surjective morphism\textbackslash{}n\$g:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ such that \$S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SY\$ is a trivial cover of \$Y\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nFor \$n>1\$, we consider the base change \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SX\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ (notice\textbackslash{}nthat \$(X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SX)\_x \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong X\_s\$ for \$x\$ a point lying above \$s\$, so\textbackslash{}n\$|(X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SX)\_x|=n\$ for all \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$ as well), by Proposition\textbackslash{}n[143](\#clopen\_immersion)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"clopen\_immersion\textbackslash{}"\}, the diagonal map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta\$ induces a\textbackslash{}nsection of the base change map. In fact, \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SX\$ is the disjoint\textbackslash{}nunion of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(X)\$ with some open and closed subscheme \$X'\$ of \$X\$,\textbackslash{}nwith \$X'\$ being the complement of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(X)\$. Now consider the\textbackslash{}ninclusion map \$X'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SX\$ and the projection map\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SX\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$, these maps are both finite étale since\textbackslash{}nrespectively, open embeddings are étale and finite étale morphisms are\textbackslash{}npreserved under base change. Then, by Proposition\textbackslash{}n[142](\#composition\_etale)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"composition\_etale\textbackslash{}"\}, the composition \$X'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is\textbackslash{}nalso finite étale. By construction, we have that the fibres of this\textbackslash{}nmorphism has cardinality \$n-1\$. Indeed, since\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SX = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(X) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sqcup X'\$, we also have that\textbackslash{}n\$(X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SX)\_x = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(X)\_x \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sqcup X'\_x\$ and because\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(X)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong X\$, \$|\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(X)\_x|=1\$, hence \$|X'\_x|=n-1\$. So the\textbackslash{}ninduction hypothesis yields a finite, locally free and surjective\textbackslash{}nmorphism \$g':Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ such that \$X'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_XY\$ is isomorphic to\textbackslash{}nthe disjoint union of \$n-1\$ copies of \$Y\$. But then\textbackslash{}n\$(X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SX)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SY \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SY\$ is the disjoint union of \$n\$\textbackslash{}ncopies of \$Y\$. Lastly, notice that the composition \$g=f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ g'\$ is also\textbackslash{}nfinite, locally free and surjective since \$g'\$ and \$f\$ are. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 151**. We can actually build a category whose objects\textbackslash{}nconsists of finite étale covering \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ over a base scheme\textbackslash{}n\$S\$ and whose morphisms are morphisms of schemes that are compatible\textbackslash{}nover \$S\$. It is a full subcategory of the category of relative schemes\textbackslash{}nover \$S\$ and we denote it \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{F\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}acute\{e\}t\}\}\}\_S\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#reduced\_carry\_above .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 152**. *Let \$S\$ be a connected scheme and\textbackslash{}n\$p:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ is a morphisms in\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{F\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}acute\{e\}t\}\}\}\_S\$. If \$S\$ is a reduced scheme, then\textbackslash{}n\$X\$ is a reduced scheme as well.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* We may assume that \$X= \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:  B\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$S= \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\$. Let \$P\$ be a point of \$S\$ (a prime\textbackslash{}nideal). By assumption, the localisation \$A\_P\$ has no nilpotents and we\textbackslash{}nwill prove that the same holds for \$C\_P = B\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_A A\_P\$. This is\textbackslash{}nsufficient since the local ring of points of \$X\$ lying above \$P\$ are\textbackslash{}nlocalisations of \$C\_P\$ and \$p\$ is surjective.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nLet \$P\_1,..P\_r\$ be the set of minimal prime ideals in \$A\_P\$. Their\textbackslash{}nintersection is the nilradical (see [@Eisenbud] Corollary \$2.12\$), so\textbackslash{}nthe ideal of nilpotents in \$A\_P\$, then the natural map\textbackslash{}n\$A\_P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod(A\_P/P\_i)\$ is injective.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nNow, since \$p\$ is a finite étale cover, it is also locally free, so\textbackslash{}n\$C\_P\$ is a free \$A\_P\$-module. So tensoring the above map with \$C\_P\$, we\textbackslash{}nobtain an injective map \$C\_P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod (C\_P/P\_iC\_P)\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nEach \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:C\_P/P\_iC\_P\$ is finite étale over\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\_P/P\_i\$ (by base change). So by considering\textbackslash{}nthis map, we can reduce to the case where \$A\_P\$ is an integral domain.\textbackslash{}nDenoting by \$K\_P\$ its fraction field, we get that the following map\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: C\_P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_\{A\_P\}K\_P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}K\_P\$\textbackslash{}nis finite étale cover by base change. And the natural map\textbackslash{}n\$K\_P \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow C\_P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_\{A\_P\}K\_P\$ induced by the inclusion\textbackslash{}n\$A\_P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow K\_P\$ is injective since \$p\$ is locally free. So\textbackslash{}n\$C\_P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_\{A\_P\}K\_P\$ is a finite product of fields (by étaleness) which\textbackslash{}nis clearly reduced (reduced rings are stable under finite product),\textbackslash{}nhence \$C\_P\$ ha no nilpotents. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFrom now on, the reader might notice the resemblance of certain of the\textbackslash{}nfollowing results with lemmas and propositions from Section\textbackslash{}n[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}[covering\_spaces\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}]](\#covering\_spaces)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"covering\_spaces\textbackslash{}"\} and the theory of field extensions.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#etale\_between\_composition .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 153**. *Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ and \$g:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be\textbackslash{}nmorphisms of schemes. If \$f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ g\$ and \$f\$ are finite étale, then so is\textbackslash{}n\$g\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* By Proposition [143](\#clopen\_immersion)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"clopen\_immersion\textbackslash{}"\}, the diagonal map\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_S X\$ is finite as it is a closed immersion and\textbackslash{}nsince \$X\$ is isomorphic to a union of connected components in\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SX\$ it is also étale. Considering the fibre product of \$Z\$ over\textbackslash{}n\$X\$ with \$Y\$ via \$g\$, we get a morphism\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\_g : Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YX\$ (the \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}"graph\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" of \$g\$) which is\textbackslash{}nagain finite and étale. The projection \$p\_2:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YX \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is\textbackslash{}nagain finite étale (being the base change of \$f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ g:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$).\textbackslash{}nSo the composition \$p\_2\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\_g = g\$ is finite étale. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#sections\_etale\_cover .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 154**. *Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ be a morphism in\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{F\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}acute\{e\}t\}\}\}\_S\$, and \$s: S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be a\textbackslash{}nsection of \$f\$. Then \$s\$ induces an isomorphism of \$S\$ with an open and\textbackslash{}nclosed subscheme of \$X\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* By Lemma [153](\#etale\_between\_composition)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"etale\_between\_composition\textbackslash{}"\}, \$s\$ is a finite étale morphism.\textbackslash{}nNow since \$s\$ is finite, it is closed\textbackslash{}n([94](\#finite\_is\_closed)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"finite\_is\_closed\textbackslash{}"\}), so its image is closed as well. Since\textbackslash{}n\$s\$ is flat and locally of finite type, the image of \$s\$ is open as well\textbackslash{}n([106](\#flat\_is\_open)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"flat\_is\_open\textbackslash{}"\})\textbackslash{}nAnd since sections are injective morphisms, the proof is done. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn particular, if \$S\$ is connected, then the section \$s\$ maps \$S\$\textbackslash{}nisomorphically onto a whole connected component of \$X\$ (this is similar\textbackslash{}nto what happened in Chapter \$1\$ for coverings of connected topological\textbackslash{}nspaces). The next result is of utmost importance as it is analogous to\textbackslash{}nProposition [15](\#property\_morphism\_covers)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"property\_morphism\_covers\textbackslash{}"\}. And if you recall, it as used\textbackslash{}nprofusely throughout the first chapter.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#proporty\_mono\_etale\_cover .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 155**. *Let \$g:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ be a morphism of schemes\textbackslash{}nwith \$S\$ a connected scheme and \$h\_1,h\_2: Z \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ are two\textbackslash{}nmorphisms of schemes over \$S\$, with \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ an étale morphism\textbackslash{}nwith \$h\_1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{z\} = h\_2\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{z\}\$ for some geometric\textbackslash{}npoint \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{z\}: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$.\textbackslash{}nThen \$h\_1 = h\_2\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Consider the fibre product \$Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SX\$, since étaleness is\textbackslash{}npreserved under base change, we may assume that \$Z=S\$. Now, morphisms\textbackslash{}n\$h\_1\$ and \$h\_2\$ become sections of \$f\$, so it is enough to check that if\textbackslash{}ntwo sections of a finite étale cover of a connected scheme \$S\$ coincide\textbackslash{}nat a geometric point, then they are equal. This follows from Proposition\textbackslash{}n[154](\#sections\_etale\_cover)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"sections\_etale\_cover\textbackslash{}"\} since each section is an isomorphism\textbackslash{}nof (now) \$S\$ onto a connected component of \$X\$, thus it is determined by\textbackslash{}nthe image of a geometric point. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFor a morphism of schemes \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$, we define the group of\textbackslash{}nscheme automorphisms of \$X\$ preserving \$f\$ to be\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(X|S)\$. Notice that there is a natural left action\textbackslash{}nof \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(X|S)\$ on the geometric fibre\textbackslash{}n\$X\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\} = X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{};\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\$ (coming\textbackslash{}nfrom the base change of its action on \$X\$).\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#no\_fixed\_points .corollary\}\textbackslash{}n**Corollary 156**. *Let\textbackslash{}n\$f: X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{F\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}acute\{e\}t\}\}\}\_S\$. Then the\textbackslash{}nnontrivial elements of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(X|S)\$ act without fixed\textbackslash{}npoints on each geometric fibre. Hence \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(X|S)\$ is\textbackslash{}nfinite.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Just as in the proof of Corollary\textbackslash{}n[19](\#corollary\_property\_morphism\_covers)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"corollary\_property\_morphism\_covers\textbackslash{}"\}, the first statement is\textbackslash{}nimmediate from Proposition\textbackslash{}n[155](\#proporty\_mono\_etale\_cover)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"proporty\_mono\_etale\_cover\textbackslash{}"\} by taking \$Z=X\$, \$h\_1 = id\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$h\_2 = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(X|S)\$. So it follows that the\textbackslash{}naction of an elements of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(X|S)\$ on the underlying\textbackslash{}nset of geometric fibres is faithful. And since geometric fibres of\textbackslash{}nfinite étale morphisms are finite sets, and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(X|S)\$\textbackslash{}nacts faithfully on such fibres, then \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(X|S)\$ is a\textbackslash{}nsubgroup of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Sym\}\}(X\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\})\$ a finite group. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAgain, one important construction is that of making new finite étale\textbackslash{}ncovers from existing ones. This is done by considering quotients of\textbackslash{}ngroup actions as follow, and then checking that they are indeed schemes.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: construction\textbackslash{}n**Construction 157**. Let \$f: X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ be an *affine* surjective\textbackslash{}nmorphism of schemes, and \$G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}leq \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(X|S)\$ a finite\textbackslash{}nsubgroup. We define the ringed space \$X/G\$ for which the underlying\textbackslash{}ntopology is the quotient topology of \$X\$ by the action of \$G\$. And the\textbackslash{}nmorphism of ringed spaces \$p :X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X/G\$ for which the underlying\textbackslash{}ncontinuous map is the natural projection. And we define the structure\textbackslash{}nsheaf of \$X/G\$ to be the subsheaf \$(p\_*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X)\^{}G\$ of\textbackslash{}n\$G\$-invariant elements in \$p\_*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 158**. *The ringed space \$X/G\$ above is indeed a scheme,\textbackslash{}nthe morphism \$p\$ is affine and surjective, and \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$\textbackslash{}nfactors as \$f = g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ p\$ for \$g:X/G \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ an affine morphism.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Using the affine assumption on \$f\$, we may assume that\textbackslash{}n\$S=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\$ and \$X=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:B\$ and \$f\$\textbackslash{}ncomes from a ring homomorphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lambda: A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow B\$. Since embeddings and trivial coverings are\textbackslash{}nfinite étale, by composition (Proposition\textbackslash{}n[142](\#composition\_etale)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"composition\_etale\textbackslash{}"\}), \$f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ p :Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ is a finite\textbackslash{}nétale covering.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nLet \$p\_\{ij\} : X\^{}n \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_SX\_j\$ for \$1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}leq i <j\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}leq n\$ be\textbackslash{}nthe projection onto the product of the \$i\$-th and \$j\$-th factors. Let\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(X)\$ be the diagonal of \$X\$ in \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_S X\$ of image\textbackslash{}n\$p\_\{ij\}(X)\$. By Proposition\textbackslash{}n[143](\#clopen\_immersion)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"clopen\_immersion\textbackslash{}"\}, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(X)\$ is open and closed and\textbackslash{}ntherefore so is its inverse image by a projection \$p\_\{ij\}\$. Denote\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta\^{}\{-1\} := \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigcup\_\{i,j\} p\_\{ij\}\^{}\{-1\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(X))\$. As \$Y\$ is\textbackslash{}nconnected, if \$Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta\^{}\{-1\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}neq \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}emptyset\$, then\textbackslash{}n\$Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta\^{}\{-1\}\$, but this cannot occur since\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}notin \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta\^{}\{-1\}\$. Whence \$Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta\^{}\{-1\}\$ is empty\textbackslash{}nand each point in the geometric fibre \$Y\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}\$ is represented\textbackslash{}nby an \$n\$-tuple with distinct elements.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nWe now show that \$Y\$ is Galois over \$S\$. Every permutation \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma\$ of\textbackslash{}nthe \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\_i\$ induces an automorphism \$f\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma\}\$ of \$X\^{}n\$ over\textbackslash{}n\$S\$ permuting the components. If\textbackslash{}n\$f\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}\$, since\textbackslash{}n\$f\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma\}(Y)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}neq \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}emptyset\$ and \$Y\$ is connected, then\textbackslash{}n\$f\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma\}(Y) = Y\$ and \$f\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|S)\$. Thus\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y|S)\$ act transitively on one geometric fibre,\textbackslash{}nmaking \$Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ Galois in\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{F\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}acute\{e\}t\}\}\}\_S\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nFinally, let \$q:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be a morphism in\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{F\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}acute\{e\}t\}\}\}\_S\$ with \$Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ a Galois\textbackslash{}nobject and let us choose a preimage \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{z\}\$ of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\_1\$.\textbackslash{}nThen by Theorem\textbackslash{}n[161](\#Galois\_correpondance\_etale\_cov)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Galois\_correpondance\_etale\_cov\textbackslash{}"\}, \$q\$ is in particular a\textbackslash{}nsurjective morphism of covers. Composing \$q\$ with distinct elements of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Z|S)\$, we get \$n\$ maps\textbackslash{}n\$q\_1, ..., q\_n : Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\$q\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{z\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\_i\$ for every\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in F\$. From these \$q\_1,...,q\_n\$, we get a morphisms of\textbackslash{}nschemes \$Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\^{}n\$ over \$S\$ that factors through \$P\$ since it\textbackslash{}nmaps \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{y\}\$ to \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\$, and \$Z\$ is connected. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# Étale Group Schemes \{\#etale\_group\_scheme\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAnother useful point of view is to consider schemes with the extra\textbackslash{}nstructure of a group. This yields a nice parallel between finite étale\textbackslash{}ncovers as group schemes and the notion of *principal homogeneous\textbackslash{}nspaces*, that we will explain below.
