The construction being duals, one sees that\textbackslash{}n\$(G, m, e,i)\$ is an affine group scheme over \$k\$ if and only if\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}(G)\$ with \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta\$, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}epsilon\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Sigma\$ becomes a\textbackslash{}ncommutative Hopf algebra.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe have defined group schemes over \$S\$ as group objects from the\textbackslash{}ncategory of schemes over \$S\$. But sometimes this definition is not\textbackslash{}npractical, for example, to define a group scheme one would have to give\textbackslash{}na scheme \$G\$, then one needs to define the morphisms \$m,i\$ and \$e\$ and\textbackslash{}nfinally that they respect the commutative diagrams. There is an\textbackslash{}nincentive to describe a group scheme as a scheme whose points form a\textbackslash{}ngroup, it can be done as follows:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: construction\textbackslash{}n**Construction 166**. Suppose we have a scheme \$X\$ over \$S\$. The notion\textbackslash{}nof points of \$X\$ is not as transparent as in the case of sets or\textbackslash{}ntopological spaces. If \$T\$ is a scheme over \$S\$, then we define a\textbackslash{}n\$T\$-valued point of \$X\$, as a morphism \$x : T\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ over \$S\$ and\textbackslash{}ndenote the set of such points by \$X(T)\$. In the particular case where\textbackslash{}n\$S = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: k\$ and \$T : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:K\$\textbackslash{}nwhere \$K|k\$ is a field extension, we refer to such points of \$X\$ as\textbackslash{}n\$K\$-rational points.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 167**. A functor\textbackslash{}n\$F:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Grp\}\}\}\$ is said to be a\textbackslash{}n**representable group-valued functor** if and only if the functor\textbackslash{}n\$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ F :\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Set\}\}\}\$ is\textbackslash{}nrepresentable where\textbackslash{}n\$U:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Grp\}\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Set\}\}\}\$ is\textbackslash{}nthe forgetful functor. Now the category of representable group-valued\textbackslash{}nfunctors and natural transformations between them is denoted as\textbackslash{}n\$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Grp\}\}\}]\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe following result is quite powerful. It says that we can understand\textbackslash{}ngroup schemes as functors and it concludes our above construction by\textbackslash{}nendowing spaces of the form \$X(T)\$ with a group structure for \$X\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$T\$ schemes over \$S\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#group\_scheme\_are\_representable\_functors .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 168**. *There is an equivalence between the category of\textbackslash{}ngroup schemes over \$S\$ and the category\textbackslash{}n\$[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\_S, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Grp\}\}\}]\$ of\textbackslash{}nrepresentable group-valued functors from\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\_S\$ to \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Grp\}\}\}\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Consider the category \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\_S\$ of\textbackslash{}nschemes over \$S\$ and write\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Fun\}\}\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\_S, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Set\}\}\})\$\textbackslash{}nthe category of representable functors. Now for any scheme\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\_S\$, we define the representable\textbackslash{}nfunctor\textbackslash{}n\$h\_X = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\_S\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\_,X)\$\textbackslash{}nin \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$. Sending \$X\$ to \$h\_X\$ gives a covariant functor\textbackslash{}n\$h:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\_S \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ that is\textbackslash{}nmoreover fully faithful (it is actually a Yoneda embedding, see\textbackslash{}nProposition [273](\#yoneda\_embeddings)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"yoneda\_embeddings\textbackslash{}"\}).\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nSo by the Yoneda lemma, any \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\_S\$ is\textbackslash{}nuniquely determined by a representable functor \$F\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ of the\textbackslash{}nform by being its unique representative up to isomorphism.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nWe can now define group objects in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\_S\$\textbackslash{}nvia the above embedding \$h\$. Let\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\_S\$, to give a group law on an\textbackslash{}nobject \$X\$ means that for each scheme \$T\$ over \$S\$, we have to specify a\textbackslash{}ngroup law on the set\textbackslash{}n\$h\_X(T) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\_S\}(T,X) = X(T)\$\textbackslash{}nsuch that for every morphism \$f:T\_1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow T\_2\$, the induced map\textbackslash{}n\$h\_X(f) : X(T\_2) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X(T\_1)\$ is a homomorphism of groups. Note\textbackslash{}nthat a category allows group objects if it has a terminal object and\textbackslash{}nfinite product, which is the case for \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\_S\$\textbackslash{}n(a terminal object is the scheme \$S\$ and fibre products of schemes over\textbackslash{}n\$S\$ are finite products).\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nSo we can now define a functor\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{h\}\_G = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\_S\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\_,G): \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Grp\}\}\}\$\textbackslash{}nsending any scheme \$T\$ over \$S\$ to the group \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{h\}\_G(T) = G(T)\$,\textbackslash{}nby the above discussion this is a representable group-valued functor.\textbackslash{}nAnd it gives rise to the functor \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{h\}\$ from the category of\textbackslash{}ngroup schemes over \$S\$ to the category of representable group-valued\textbackslash{}nfunctors by sending \$G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto h\_G\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nWe now establish the equivalence :\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nGiven a group scheme \$(G,m,e,i)\$ over \$S\$, its group axioms ensure that\textbackslash{}nfor every scheme \$T\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\_S\$, the set \$G(T)\$\textbackslash{}ninherits a group structure as above, making the functor \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{h\}\_G\$\textbackslash{}na representable group-valued functor. Conversely, given a representable\textbackslash{}ngroup-valued functor \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{h\}\_G\$, the group structure on\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{h\}\_G(T)\$ defines natural transformations\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{m\}\_G :\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{h\}\_G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{h\}\_G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{h\}\_G\$,\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{e\}\_G :\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{h\}\_S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{h\}\_G\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{i\}\_G :\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{h\}\_G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{h\}\_G\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nAnd the Yoneda lemma tells us that these natural transformations\textbackslash{}ncorrespond uniquely to \$S\$-morphisms \$m\_G:G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_S G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow G\$,\textbackslash{}n\$e\_G:S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow G\$ and \$i\_G:G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow G\$. Moreover, because the\textbackslash{}nembedding is fully faithful, the above natural transformations induced\textbackslash{}nby group axioms over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{h\}\_G(T)\$ for any schemes \$T\$ over \$S\$\textbackslash{}ntranslate directly into the commutative diagrams required for \$G\$ to be\textbackslash{}na group scheme. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#affine\_group\_schemes\_as\_functors .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 23**. Since the category of affine schemes is anti-equivalent\textbackslash{}nto that of commutative \$k\$-algebras via the \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\$\textbackslash{}nfunctor, from the above proposition, an affine group schemes \$G\$ over\textbackslash{}n\$k\$ is equivalent to a group-valued representable functor from the\textbackslash{}ncategory of \$k\$-algebras to the category of groups, represented by some\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-algebra \$A\$ called the coordinate ring of \$G\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nRecall from algebraic geometry that there is an anti-equivalence between\textbackslash{}nthe category of affine schemes over \$k\$ and the category of commutative\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-algebras. We can then restrict the above equivalence by an\textbackslash{}nequivalence between affine group schemes over \$k\$ and representable\textbackslash{}ngroup-valued functors on \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Alg\}\}\}\_k\$. We continue by\textbackslash{}nstudying a few examples of group schemes.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: example\textbackslash{}n**Example 169**. Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\$ be a finite group of order \$n\$. We define\textbackslash{}nthe **constant group scheme** over \$S\$, denoted \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\_S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$,\textbackslash{}nto be the disjoint union of \$n\$ copies of \$S\$ indexed by \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\$,\textbackslash{}nequipped with the projective map given by the identity on each element,\textbackslash{}ni.e., \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\_S = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigsqcup\_\{g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\} S\_g\$\$ Then,\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\_S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\_S = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigsqcup\_\{g,h\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\} S\_\{(g,h)\}, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{ with \}S\_\{(g,h)\} = S\_g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times S\_h\$\$\textbackslash{}nThe group operation on \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\_S\$ is induced by \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma\$ and defined by\textbackslash{}nthe multiplication map \$m\$ sending \$S\_\{(g,h)\}\$ to \$S\_\{gh\}\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn light of Theorem\textbackslash{}n[58](\#equivalence\_catgory\_etale\_algebra)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"equivalence\_catgory\_etale\_algebra\textbackslash{}"\}, we can ask ourselves if\textbackslash{}nan equivalence of this type exists for finite étale group schemes over a\textbackslash{}nfield \$k\$. The next lemma is necessary to answer this question. It is\textbackslash{}nactually a result from Galois descent theory, and is due to *Andreas\textbackslash{}nSpeiser* (it can be seen as a reinterpretation of Hilbert's Theorem\textbackslash{}n\$90\$). For more on Galois descent, see [@galois\_descent\_Szamuely]\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: 2.3\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#descent\_argument .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 170**. *Let \$L|k\$ be a Galois extension with Galois group\textbackslash{}n\$G=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(L|k)\$. Given a relative Galois representation\textbackslash{}n\$V\$ \$\$V \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong L \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes V\^{}G\$\$*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@galois\_descent\_Szamuely], Lemma \$2.3.8\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 171**. *The category of finite étale group schemes over\textbackslash{}n\$k\$ is equivalent to the category of finite groups carrying a continuous\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$-action.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Assume the base field \$S = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:k\$ for \$k\$ a\textbackslash{}nfield. Then by Theorem [60](\#etale\_algebras)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"etale\_algebras\textbackslash{}"\}, a finite étale group scheme\textbackslash{}n\$G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ is of the form \$G = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: A\$ with a\textbackslash{}n\$A\$ finite étale \$k\$-algebra.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nAnd by Theorem\textbackslash{}n[58](\#equivalence\_catgory\_etale\_algebra)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"equivalence\_catgory\_etale\_algebra\textbackslash{}"\}, it corresponds to a\textbackslash{}nfinite set equipped with a continuous\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$-action.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nThat finite set being the fibre \$G\_\{k\_s\}\$ of \$G\$ over the geometric\textbackslash{}npoint \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: k\_s \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow G\$, it carries a group\textbackslash{}nstructure coming from that of \$G\$, meaning it is compatible with the\textbackslash{}nGalois action.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nConversely, the Galois-equivariant group operations on a finite\textbackslash{}ncontinuous \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$-set, yield a group scheme\textbackslash{}nstructure on the corresponding finite étale scheme over \$k\$. Over \$k\_s\$,\textbackslash{}nthe corresponding constant group of such a\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$-set \$X\$ has a coordinate algebra\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod\_\{x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\} k\_s\$. Naturally, it is isomorphic to the vector space\textbackslash{}n\$V = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow k\_s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ where an element \$a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod k\_s\$ is of the\textbackslash{}nform \$(a\_\{x\_1\},...,a\_\{x\_n\})\$ and is defined by a function \$f(x) = a\_x\$.\textbackslash{}nThe absolute Galois group has an action over this vector space, for any\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$, we have\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot (a\_x)\_\{x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\} = (\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma(a\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma\^{}\{-1\}x\}))\_\{x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\}\$.\textbackslash{}nNotice that this equips \$V\$ with a semi-linear\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$-action. Now we can apply our above lemma for\textbackslash{}nthe descent argument. Consider the subalgebra \$A = V\^{}G\$ consisting of\textbackslash{}nall \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$-equivariant functions in \$V\$. Since all\textbackslash{}nthe requirements of the lemma are verified, we have\textbackslash{}n\$A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_k k\_s \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod k\_s\$. From Theorem\textbackslash{}n[60](\#etale\_algebras)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"etale\_algebras\textbackslash{}"\},\textbackslash{}nthis means that \$A\$ is a finite étale algebra, and so its spectrum gives\textbackslash{}na finite étale group scheme over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: k\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nTo conclude that the resulting finite étale scheme admits a group\textbackslash{}nstructure making it a group scheme, we are going to check that its\textbackslash{}ncoordinate ring \$A\$ is a Hopf \$k\$-algebra.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nWe define a map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta:A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_k A\$ as follow, for an\textbackslash{}nelement \$f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in A\$, we set \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(f)\$ a function on \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times X\$ to be\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(f)(x,y) = f(x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y)\$. Since the group operation on \$X\$ is\textbackslash{}ncompatible with the action of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$, for\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k)\$, we hve\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma (\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(f)(x,y)) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma (f(x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y)) = f(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma (x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot y)) = f(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma(x)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma(y)) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta(f)(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma(x),\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sigma(y))\$\$\textbackslash{}nso it is a well-defined map of \$k\$-algebras, induced by the group law on\textbackslash{}n\$X\$. Similarly, we can define maps \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}epsilon\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Sigma\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nThus by Remark [22](\#Hopf\_algebra\_group\_scheme)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Hopf\_algebra\_group\_scheme\textbackslash{}"\}, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\$ is a\textbackslash{}nfinite étale group scheme over \$k\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#constant\_group\_scheme\_etale .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 24**. The previous proposition actually tells us more. Consider\textbackslash{}n\$G\$ a finite étale group scheme over \$k\$, and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Gamma = G(k\_s)\$ the\textbackslash{}ngroup of \$k\_s\$-valued points of \$G\$. Given a scheme \$S\$ and a geometric point\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$, we define\textbackslash{}nthe **étale fundamental group** \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1\^{}e(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\})\$ as the\textbackslash{}nautomorphism group of the fibre functor\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}\$ on the category of finite étale\textbackslash{}ncovers of \$S\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 25**. This obviously implies that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1\^{}e(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\})\$\textbackslash{}nacts naturally on \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}(X)\$ for any \$X\$\textbackslash{}nbeing a finite étale cover of \$S\$, so\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}\$ takes its values in the category\textbackslash{}nof \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\})\$-sets. However this is not a monodromy\textbackslash{}naction as it was the case for topological coverings.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn order to understand the étale fundamental group of a connected scheme\textbackslash{}n\$S\$ at a geometric point \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\$, we need to understand the\textbackslash{}nautomorphisms of the fibre functor. Suppose \$R\$ is a finite\textbackslash{}nset with a continuous \$G\$-action. As above, we may assume that the\textbackslash{}naction of \$G\$ on \$R\$ is transitive by decomposing \$R\$ into finitely many\textbackslash{}norbits and considering them separately since the fibre product of\textbackslash{}nschemes preserves disjoint unions. The action being continuous, we know\textbackslash{}nthat the stabiliser \$U\_r\$ of the point \$r\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in R\$ is an open subgroup of\textbackslash{}n\$G\$ (Lemma [43](\#continuous\_open\_stabiliser)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"continuous\_open\_stabiliser\textbackslash{}"\}) and by Corollary\textbackslash{}n[47](\#open\_subgroup\_profinite)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"open\_subgroup\_profinite\textbackslash{}"\} it is also finite and closed. By\textbackslash{}nTheorem [264](\#Cameron\_1\_3)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Cameron\_1\_3\textbackslash{}"\}, just as in the Reformulation of Galois Theory\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}ref\{Grot\_reformulation\_Galois\}\$, we have that \$R \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong G / U\_r\$ as a\textbackslash{}n\$G\$-set. The stabiliser \$U\_r\$ being open, it also contains subgroups \$V\$\textbackslash{}nwhich are basis of open neighbourhoods of \$1\$ in \$G\$ arising as the\textbackslash{}nkernel of the projection\textbackslash{}n\$G \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow[]\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{pr\}\}\_k\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y\_k|S)\^{}\{op\}\$,\textbackslash{}nmoreover these subgroups are normal in \$G\$ (see Remark\textbackslash{}n[5](\#prof\_are\_top)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"prof\_are\_top\textbackslash{}"\}).\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nConsider \$Y\_k\$ a Galois cover of \$S\$ as above, as we have seen in\textbackslash{}nprevious proofs, the action of \$G\$ on the fibre\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}(Y\_k)\$ factors through\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y\_k|S)\^{}\{op\}\$ and of course since \$Y\_k\$ is Galois,\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y\_k|S)\$ acts transitively on\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}(Y\_k)\$. Thus\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}(Y\_k)\$ is a transitive \$G\$-set. So\textbackslash{}nonce again, from Theorem [264](\#Cameron\_1\_3)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Cameron\_1\_3\textbackslash{}"\}, we have\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}(Y\_k) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong G/H\$ for \$H\$ the\textbackslash{}nstabiliser of a point in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}(Y\_k)\$.\textbackslash{}nBut the stabiliser of a point of the fibre is precisely the subgroup \$V\$\textbackslash{}nabove. Indeed, an element \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G\$ acts trivially on a point of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}(Y\_k)\$ if and only if the image in\textbackslash{}nthe quotient group \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y\_k|S)\^{}\{op\}\$ is trivial. That\textbackslash{}ncondition is precisely \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}ker(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{pr\}\}\_k)= V\$, so\textbackslash{}n\$V = H\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nNow denote by \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{U\}\$ the image of \$U\_r\$ by the group\textbackslash{}nhomomorphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{pr\}\}\_k\$, which is a finite subgroup of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y\_k|S)\^{}\{op\}\$ since \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{pr\}\}\_k\$ is\textbackslash{}ncontinuous as well, and notice that by the first isomorphism theorem, we\textbackslash{}nalso have that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{U\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong U\_r /V\$. As in Proposition\textbackslash{}n[159](\#quotient\_finite\_etale\_cover)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"quotient\_finite\_etale\_cover\textbackslash{}"\}, we construct the finite étale\textbackslash{}ncover \$X\$ as the quotient of \$Y\_k\$ by the action of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{U\}\$, then\textbackslash{}nwe have\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}(X) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}(Y\_K/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{U\}) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}(Y\_k)/ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{U\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong (\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1\^{}e(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\})/ V) / (U\_r/V) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1\^{}e(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}) / U\_r\$\$\textbackslash{}nconcluding our proof. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThere is an interesting way of seeing sets equipped with a certain\textbackslash{}naction that we describe now.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 26**. Recall that a permutation representation of a group \$G\$\textbackslash{}non a finite set \$X\$ is a homomorphism\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho:G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Sym\}\}(X)\$. There is an equivalence of\textbackslash{}ncategories between finite sets equipped with a continuous action of a\textbackslash{}ngroup \$G\$ and finite continuous permutation representations of \$G\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nIndeed, in our case, for \$S\$ a connected scheme and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\$ a\textbackslash{}ngeometric point of \$S\$, given a continuous action of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\})\$ onto a finite set \$X\$, we define a\textbackslash{}nhomomorphism\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Sym\}\}(X)\$ by\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho(g)(x):= g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot x\$. Then \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho:\$ is a group homomorphism, and it is\textbackslash{}na continuous map when \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Sym\}\}(X)\$ is equipped with the\textbackslash{}ndiscrete topology. It is thus a finite continuous permutation\textbackslash{}nrepresentation.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nOn the other hand, given a finite continuous permutation representation\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Sym\}\}(X)\$,\textbackslash{}nsimilarly as above we clearly have that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\})\$ acts\textbackslash{}ncontinuously on \$X\$ via the operation defined by\textbackslash{}n\$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot x := \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho(g)(x)\$, making it a continuous finite\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\})\$-set.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nBoth constructions being literally the same data viewed differently,\textbackslash{}ncomposing them gives back exactly what we started with, and the same is\textbackslash{}ntrue for morphisms of the two categories. Therefore, we have an\textbackslash{}nequivalence of categories described below.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#corollary\_representation .corollary\}\textbackslash{}n**Corollary 185**. *For \$S\$ a connected scheme with a geometric point\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\$, we have an equivalence of categories between finite\textbackslash{}nétale covers of \$S\$ and finite continuous permutations representation of\textbackslash{}nits étale fundamental group*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nOur goal was to reconcile the étale fundamental group with its\textbackslash{}ntopological counterpart. These results align perfectly with the\textbackslash{}nclassical properties of topological fundamental groups, confirming that\textbackslash{}nour definition of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1\^{}e\$ is the appropriate algebraic analogue. We\textbackslash{}ncan already compute a few examples.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#fundamental\_group\_over\_field .example\}\textbackslash{}n**Example 186**. Let \$S=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:k\$ for \$k\$ a field and\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ a geometric\textbackslash{}npoint with \$k\_s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subseteq \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\$. From Example\textbackslash{}n[145](\#example\_etale\_over\_field)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"example\_etale\_over\_field\textbackslash{}"\}, connected finite étale covers are\textbackslash{}nspectrums of separable field extensions \$L\_i\$ of \$k\$. The fibre functor\textbackslash{}nsends \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:L\_i\$ to the underlying set of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:(L\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_k\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda)\$. The image of the fibre\textbackslash{}nfunctor is thus a finite set indexed by the \$k\$-algebra homomorphisms\textbackslash{}n\$L\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\$. Finally, since the image of each such\textbackslash{}nhomomorphism lies in the separable closure \$k\_s\$ of \$k\$ in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\$, we\textbackslash{}nhave that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}(X) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(L,k\_s)\$\textbackslash{}nfor all \$X = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:L\$, so by classical Galois theory,\textbackslash{}nthe étale fundamental group is the absolute Galois group\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1\^{}\{e\}(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k\_s|k)\$. In\textbackslash{}nparticular, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\})\$ is trivial for \$k\$ separably\textbackslash{}nclosed.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 27**. Using the above example, we can justify our initial\textbackslash{}nassumption: that the fibre functor is not representable. We may think\textbackslash{}nthat if \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}\$ over\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: k\$ were representable then it would be by\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: k\_s\$, although, \$k\_s\$ is not a finite étale\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-algebra. So by Definition\textbackslash{}n[270](\#(pro)\_representable)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"(pro)\_representable\textbackslash{}"\} even over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:k\$\textbackslash{}nthe fibre functor cannot be representable.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: example\textbackslash{}n**Example 187**.
