trivial.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Comparison Theorems \{\#comparaison\_theorem\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn this section, our goal is to convince the reader that our definition\textbackslash{}nof étale fundamental groups does make sense. We do this by comparing\textbackslash{}nétale fundamental group of schemes over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ with the\textbackslash{}ntopological fundamental group of complex analytic spaces.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nA first issue is that the theorems used to compare such objects are very\textbackslash{}nelaborate. In this thesis, we present no proof of these renowned\textbackslash{}ntheorems, but instead try to motivate and guide their usage. It is\textbackslash{}nimportant to know that in the following we will frequently mention\textbackslash{}nconcepts or ideas arising from Riemann surfaces and complex analytic\textbackslash{}nspaces which in themself are already very rich theories and certainly\textbackslash{}ndeserve another presentation like this one. An interesting comment we\textbackslash{}ncan already make about (complex) analytic spaces is that they are\textbackslash{}ntopological spaces, which can usually be embedded with very nice\textbackslash{}ntopologies, this is important because it means that our previous\textbackslash{}ndiscussion on topological covers is totally applicable here and it will\textbackslash{}nnot result in an irrelevant study as it was the case for schemes.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nBefore delving into deeper explanations, recall that we have presented\textbackslash{}nin Section [6.5](\#analytification)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"analytification\textbackslash{}"\} the *analytification functor*, sending\textbackslash{}nobjects from the category of algebraic spaces (such as affine varieties,\textbackslash{}nprojective curves or schemes) to objects of the category of analytic\textbackslash{}nspaces (such as manifolds, Riemann surfaces or complex manifolds).\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nOne of the first comparison theorems available is the following result\textbackslash{}nby Chow from \$1949\$ [@Chow].\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 188** (Chow). *Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}chi\$ be a compact analytic subspace of\textbackslash{}nthe complex manifold \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{P\}\^{}n\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\}\$. Then there is a\textbackslash{}nsubscheme \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{P\}\^{}n\$ with \$X\^{}\{an\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}chi\$. Furthermore,\textbackslash{}nholomorphic maps between compact analytic subspaces of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{P\}\^{}n\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\}\$ induce regular rational morphisms between\textbackslash{}nsubschemes.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Chow] Theorem \$V\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThis theorem is often considered as the first bridge between complex\textbackslash{}nanalytical geometry and algebraic geometry. The next collection of\textbackslash{}nresults we mention are found in the more than influential paper written\textbackslash{}nin French by J.P Serre in \$1955\$ called *Géométrie Analytique et\textbackslash{}nGéométrie Algébirque* or GAGA for short [@Serre]. Which as the name\textbackslash{}nsuggests contains results deepening the connection between analytical\textbackslash{}nspaces and algebraic ones. In particular, Serre showed that there is an\textbackslash{}nequivalence between the category of coherent sheaves on \$X\$ and the\textbackslash{}ncategory of coherent analytic sheaves on \$X\^{}\{an\}\$ for a \$X\$ a projective\textbackslash{}nvariety over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$. From his results, he was able to prove Chow's\textbackslash{}ntheorem as a consequence of this, GAGA can now provide the backbone for\textbackslash{}ncomparing covers of schemes and covers of analytical spaces. A few of\textbackslash{}nhis results are listed in Appendix\textbackslash{}n[6.5](\#analytification)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"analytification\textbackslash{}"\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFor simplicity, from now on we will focus our study on a subcategory of\textbackslash{}ncomplex analytic spaces, namely that of compact Riemann surfaces.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# Overview of Riemann Surfaces\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 189**. A **Riemann surfaces** \$X\$ is a \$1\$-dimensional\textbackslash{}ncomplex manifold. That is, \$X\$ is a Hausdorff topological space with an\textbackslash{}nopen covering \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{U\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$, together with maps\textbackslash{}n\$f\_i:U\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ called *complex charts* mapping \$U\_i\$\textbackslash{}nhomeomorphically onto an open subset \$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ such that for\textbackslash{}neach pair \$i,j\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$, the map\textbackslash{}n\$f\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f\_j\^{}\{-1\} : f\_j(U\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap U\_j) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ is\textbackslash{}nholomorphic. This is called a *complex atlas* on \$X\$ and two complex\textbackslash{}natlases \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{U\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{ U'\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ on \$X\$ are\textbackslash{}nequivalent if their union is also a complex atlas.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFrom this definition, we can already see that Riemann surfaces inherits\textbackslash{}nthe topological property of locally compactness from \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 190**. A **holomorphic (or analytic) map** \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\$\textbackslash{}nbetween two Riemann surfaces \$X\$ and \$Y\$ is a continuous map such for\textbackslash{}neach pair of open subsets \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$, \$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset Y\$ satisfying\textbackslash{}n\$f(U)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset V\$ and complex charts \$f:U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$,\textbackslash{}n\$g:V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$, the functions\textbackslash{}n\$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ f\^{}\{-1\}: g(V)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ are holomorphic.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFor more on this topic, we refer to the book *Riemann Surfaces*\textbackslash{}n[@Donaldson] of S.Donaldson and we suppose below that basic results of\textbackslash{}nRiemann surfaces and complex analysis are known. We will also assume\textbackslash{}nthat holomorphic maps between Riemann surfaces are non-constant and that\textbackslash{}nthe Riemann surfaces we consider are connected.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 28**. Since compact Riemann surfaces are obviously topological\textbackslash{}nspaces, one can apply our theory of topological covering spaces to them.\textbackslash{}nBut notice that we obtain much more information on these covers when\textbackslash{}nthey carry the additional structure of a complex manifold. In\textbackslash{}nparticular, we can consider a whole new kind of covers for compact\textbackslash{}nRiemann surfaces.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe following results are well-known facts about holomorphic maps\textbackslash{}nbetween Riemann surfaces.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#holo\_are\_locally\_ramified .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 191**. *Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ be a holomorphic map\textbackslash{}nof Riemann surfaces. For each point \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\$, there is a unique integer\textbackslash{}n\$k=k\_y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}ge 1\$ such that we can find complex charts around \$y\$ in \$Y\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi(y)\$ in \$X\$ in which \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\$ is represented by the complex map\textbackslash{}n\$z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto z\^{}k\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See Proposition \$3\$ of Chapter \$4\$ in [@Donaldson]. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAs a natural consequence, one sees that holomorphic maps between Riemann\textbackslash{}nsurfaces are open, indeed the maps \$z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto z\^{}k\$ is open.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 192**. The above integer \$k\_y\$ is called the **ramification\textbackslash{}nindex** of the map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\$ at \$y\$. And the points \$y\$ with \$k\_y> 1\$\textbackslash{}nare called **branch points**, we call the set of branch points of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\$ **ramification locus** and denoted it by \$B\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\}\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 193**. *Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi: Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a holomorphic map\textbackslash{}nof Riemann surfaces. Then the set of branch points \$B\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\}\$ is\textbackslash{}nfinite.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See Proposition \$4\$ of Chapter \$4\$ from [@Donaldson]. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe now restrict our attention to proper maps, recall that a map\textbackslash{}n\$f : S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow T\$ between topological spaces \$S,T\$ is said to be\textbackslash{}n**proper** if for any compact set \$K\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset T\$, the preimage \$f\^{}\{-1\}(K)\$\textbackslash{}nis also compact. Note that any map between compact topological sets is\textbackslash{}nproper, and for \$f:S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow T\$ a proper map of topological spaces,\textbackslash{}nits fibre at any point \$t\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in T\$ is finite (Proposition \$4\$ Chapter \$4\$\textbackslash{}n[@Donaldson]).\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#proper\_map\_closed .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 194**. *A proper map \$f:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ to a compactly generated\textbackslash{}nHausdorff space is a closed map (a space \$X\$ is called *compactly\textbackslash{}ngenerated* if any subset \$A\$ of \$X\$ is closed when \$A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap K\$ is closed\textbackslash{}nin \$K\$ for each compact \$K\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$).*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Let \$C\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset Y\$ be closed, and let \$K\$ be a compact subspace\textbackslash{}nof \$X\$. Then \$f\^{}\{-1\}(K)\$ is compact and so is \$f\^{}\{-1\}(K) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap C\$ that we\textbackslash{}ndenote as \$B\$. Then \$f(B) = K\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap f(C)\$ which is compact, indeed\textbackslash{}n\$f(C\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap f\^{}\{-1\}(K)) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subseteq K \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap f(C)\$ and suppose\textbackslash{}n\$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in f(C)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap K\$, there exists \$c\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in C\$ with \$y= f(c)\$ and for\textbackslash{}n\$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in K\$, we have that \$c\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in f\^{}\{-1\}(K)\$. And as \$X\$ is Hausdorff, \$f(B)\$\textbackslash{}nis closed. Finally by compact generation, \$f(C)\$ is closed in \$Y\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nNotice that locally compact spaces (in particular Riemann surfaces) are\textbackslash{}ncompactly generated, thus we can conclude that the finite set\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi(B\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\})\$ of critical values is also closed. We can now\textbackslash{}nstate the main topological property of proper holomorphic maps.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 195**. *Let \$X\$ be a Riemann surface (connected), and\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ a proper holomorphic map. The map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\$ is\textbackslash{}nsurjective with finite fibres, and its restriction to\textbackslash{}n\$Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}backslash\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\^{}\{-1\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi(B\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\}))\$ is a finite\textbackslash{}ntopological cover.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Finiteness of fibres follows from the above discussion. And\textbackslash{}nsurjectivity follows from the fact that the image \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi(Y)\$ is open\textbackslash{}nand closed (proper maps are open and closed by Lemma\textbackslash{}n[194](\#proper\_map\_closed)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"proper\_map\_closed\textbackslash{}"\}) and that \$X\$ is connected. For the last\textbackslash{}nstatement, note that by Proposition\textbackslash{}n[191](\#holo\_are\_locally\_ramified)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"holo\_are\_locally\_ramified\textbackslash{}"\}, each of the finitely many\textbackslash{}npreimages of \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}backslash\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi(B\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\})\$ has an open\textbackslash{}nneighbourhood mapping homeomorphically onto some open neighbourhood of\textbackslash{}n\$x\$ ; the intersection of these is a distinguished open neighbourhood of\textbackslash{}n\$x\$ as in the definition of cover. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 196**. We call a proper surjective map of locally compact\textbackslash{}nHausdorff spaces that restricts to a cover outside a discrete closed\textbackslash{}nsubset a **finite branched cover**.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe say that a finite branch cover is of degree \$d\$ or has \$d\$ many\textbackslash{}nsheets if the covering obtained by restriction is \$d\$-sheeted. And since\textbackslash{}nwe have assumed Riemann surfaces to be connected, by Remark\textbackslash{}n[2](\#connected\_constant\_sheets)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"connected\_constant\_sheets\textbackslash{}"\}, the degree of finite branch\textbackslash{}ncovers is also constant. In that regard, for \$X\$ a Riemann surface,\textbackslash{}nstudying covering spaces above \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}backslash B\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\}\$ is done\textbackslash{}nsimilarly as in Chapter \$1\$. We thus already know how to compute\textbackslash{}nuniversal covers, automorphism groups of covers and fundamental groups\textbackslash{}nof Riemann surfaces.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nHowever, it is interesting to discuss that in the case of compact\textbackslash{}nRiemann surfaces, fundamental groups are much more restricted. An\textbackslash{}ninteresting way to understand this is by looking at the classification\textbackslash{}nof compact Riemann surfaces,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 197**. *Every compact Riemann surface is homeomorphic to a\textbackslash{}ntorus with \$g\$ holes*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cite\{Donaldson\}\$ Theorem \$3\$ in Chapter \$6\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n:::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 29**. The takeaway here is that one can construct a torus by\textbackslash{}nidentifying opposite sides of a square, with the same orientation. This\textbackslash{}ngeneralises for tori with \$g\$ holes in the following way :\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nTake a regular \$4g\$-gon and label its sides clockwise by\textbackslash{}n\$b,a,b,a,d,c,d,c, ...\$, considering the first two letters of each\textbackslash{}nquadruplet with clockwise orientation and the last two having\textbackslash{}ncounter-clockwise orientation. By identifying each pair of same letters,\textbackslash{}nrespecting the orientation, one obtains a sphere with \$g\$ handles, and\textbackslash{}nthe sides of each quadruplet get mapped to closed paths all going\textbackslash{}nthrough a common point \$x\$. The following picture from [@Hatcher] page\textbackslash{}n\$5\$ is much more intuitive:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: center\textbackslash{}n![image](g-torus)\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n::::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe above representation of tori with \$g\$ holes, together with the\textbackslash{}nclassification of compact Riemann surfaces with \$g\$ holes allows us to\textbackslash{}ncompute the fundamental group of a Riemann surface of genus \$g\$. We\textbackslash{}nconveniently take the base point \$x\$ to be where paths coming from the\textbackslash{}nfirst quadruplet \$a,b,a,b\$ meet. Then\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 198**. *The fundamental group of a compact Riemann surface \$X\$\textbackslash{}nof genus \$g\$ has a finite presentation of the form\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}langle a,b,c,d,...\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid [a,b][c,d]... = 1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rangle\$, where\textbackslash{}nthe brackets \$[a,b]\$ denote the commutators \$aba\^{}\{-1\}b\^{}\{-1\}\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* The proof is an application of Van Kampen's theorem to cell\textbackslash{}ncomplexes, see [@Hatcher] Chapter \$1.2\$ ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# Main Results\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nNext, we touch upon the main tool for this section, namely, non-singular\textbackslash{}nprojective curves over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ and compact Riemann surfaces are\textbackslash{}nequivalent. One direction is easier than the other.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: construction\textbackslash{}n**Construction 199**. Let \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{CP\}\^{}n\$ be a smooth\textbackslash{}nprojective curve over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ given by \$r\$ homogeneous polynomials\textbackslash{}n(with \$r\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}geq n-1\$). Consider \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{U\_i \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ an affine covering of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{CP\}\^{}n\$, then passing to affine charts, the homogeneous\textbackslash{}npolynomials become holomorphic (polynomial) functions\textbackslash{}n\$f\_1,...,f\_r :\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\^{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$. Recall that since \$X\$\textbackslash{}nis a smooth projective variety of dimension \$1\$ (so of codimension\textbackslash{}n\$n-1\$), then its Jacobian at any (smooth) point \$p\$ of \$X\$ has full rank\textbackslash{}n\$n-1\$. So there exists a neighbourhood \$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\^{}n\$ of\textbackslash{}n\$p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$ and \$n-1\$ holomorphic functions\textbackslash{}n\$f\_1,...,f\_\{n-1\}:V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ such that the ideal of\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap V\$ is generated by those \$n-1\$ functions. Let us define a map\textbackslash{}n\$F=(f\_1,...,f\_\{n-1\}) : V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\^{}\{n-1\}\$. Since\textbackslash{}n\$F:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\^{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\^{}\{n-1\}\$ is holomorphic and its\textbackslash{}ndifferential at \$p\$ has rank \$n-1\$, by the holomorphic implicit function\textbackslash{}nfunction theorem, near \$p\$, the zero locus \$F\^{}\{-1\}(0)\$ is a complex\textbackslash{}nsubmanifold of dimension \$1\$. Thus near every point \$p\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$, the set\textbackslash{}n\$X\$ is biholomorphic to an open subset of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$, giving us local\textbackslash{}nholomorphic charts on \$X\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nAnd what is left to check is that these local charts define a global\textbackslash{}ncomplex structure. Suppose we have two different systems of equations\textbackslash{}n\$F=(f\_1,...,f\_\{n-1\})\$ and \$G=(g\_1,...,g\_\{n-1\})\$ as above. By the\textbackslash{}nimplicit function theorem they each give a local parametrisation of \$X\$,\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi : U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: ,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:t\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto (t,a\_2(t),...,a\_n(t))\$\textbackslash{}nand\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi : V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: ,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto(s,b\_2(s),...,b\_n(s))\$.\textbackslash{}nIt is now easy to check that the transition map\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi\^{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi : U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow V\$ is holomorphic, because\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi\^{}\{-1\}\$ is a biholomorphism onto its image (by the implicit function\textbackslash{}ntheorem) so its inverse is also holomorphic. And on overlaps\textbackslash{}n\$U\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap U\_j\$, the transition maps are restrictions of the standard\textbackslash{}nprojective coordinate changes \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\^{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\^{}n\$. So\textbackslash{}n\$X\$ naturally has the structure of a Riemann surface. Moreover, since\textbackslash{}n\$X\$ is embedded in a compact space \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{CP\}\^{}n\$ with the usual\textbackslash{}ntopology, \$X\$ is actually a compact Riemann surface. And we can identify\textbackslash{}nthe compact Riemann surface structure of a smooth projective curve \$X\$\textbackslash{}nover \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ by denoting it \$X\^{}\{an\}\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe other direction is significantly deeper. A proof may require the\textbackslash{}nintroduction of notion of divisors and a thorough study of meromorphic\textbackslash{}nfunctions, as well as the Riemann-Roch theorem (Theorem \$VI, 1.3\$ in\textbackslash{}n[@Hartshorne]) and Chow's theorem.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nA similar reasoning allows us to see smooth projective schemes over\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ to be compact complex manifolds.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nReturning to branched coverings, we now study when finite branched\textbackslash{}ncoverings are étale. It is important to note that we are now not only\textbackslash{}nconsidering finite branched coverings between Riemann surface, but as\textbackslash{}nmorphism of complex analytical spaces, so we also consider the\textbackslash{}nassociated structure sheaf. And the structure sheaf of a Riemann surface\textbackslash{}n\$X\$ is the sheaf of holomorphic functions, so for all \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$ open,\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X(U)=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{f:U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid f \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{ holomorphic\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$.\textbackslash{}nFrom complex analysis, one knows that holomorphic functions are locally\textbackslash{}ngiven by convergent power series, so at any point \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in U\$, the stalk at\textbackslash{}n\$x\$, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,x\}\$ consists in germs of functions, where each germ\textbackslash{}ncorresponds to a convergent power series, at each point \$x\$,\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,x\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$. From Proposition\textbackslash{}n[191](\#holo\_are\_locally\_ramified)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"holo\_are\_locally\_ramified\textbackslash{}"\}, around any point \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$ there\textbackslash{}nexist local coordinates such that a covering \$f:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is of\textbackslash{}nthe form \$z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto z\^{}k\$, this is now also true for the induced map\textbackslash{}nbetween the structure sheaves. In that regard, on every stalk, we can\textbackslash{}nconsider \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ as a module over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{w\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ via\textbackslash{}n\$w = z\^{}k\$ (we get \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{w\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}/(z\^{}k-w)\$), more\textbackslash{}nprecisely,\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{w\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}oplus z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{w\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}oplus\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:...\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}oplus \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:z\^{}\{k-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{w\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$\textbackslash{}nis a free and finite \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{w\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$-module of rank \$k\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nSo what we have just shown is that finite branch coverings are indeed\textbackslash{}nfinite flat morphisms.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nFinally, we show that a finite branch covering is unramified if and only\textbackslash{}nif it has no branch points. Let us consider the sheaf of Kähler\textbackslash{}ndifferentials of the Riemann surface \$X\$ over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ locally. As\textbackslash{}nwe have seen above, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,x\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ so locally\textbackslash{}nwe have\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\} /\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot dz\$, the\textbackslash{}nfree module of rank \$1\$. Indeed, any derivations satisfies the chain\textbackslash{}nrule, \$d(f(z)) = f(z)dz\$ and since \$X\$ is a smooth \$1\$-dimensional\textbackslash{}ncomplex manifold, \$dz\$ is just a local basis. With the same being true\textbackslash{}nfor \$Y\$, we can now write \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_X = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot dz\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_Y = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot dw\$. From Proposition\textbackslash{}n[126](\#exact\_seq\_sheaves\_differential)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"exact\_seq\_sheaves\_differential\textbackslash{}"\}, for \$f:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$, the\textbackslash{}nexact sequence gives us the following isomorphism :\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{Y/X\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_Y / (\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{im\}\}f\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_X\$).\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nSo we now compute the pull-back of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_X\$ locally. There is a\textbackslash{}nnatural map \$f\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_Y\$ coming from the universal\textbackslash{}nproperty of differentials, which concretely gives\textbackslash{}n\$dw \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto d(f\^{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\#(w))\$. Recall that since locally \$f(z) = z\^{}k\$, then\textbackslash{}n\$f\^{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\#(w) = z\^{}k\$, so \$dw\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto d(z\^{}k) = kz\^{}\{k-1\}dz\$ (by the chain rule).\textbackslash{}nTherefore, \$f\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_X \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_Y\$ is generated by \$kz\^{}\{k-1\}dz\$.\textbackslash{}nSo, as above, we can write\textbackslash{}n\$f\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_Y = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot (kz\^{}\{k-1\}dz)\$. And we now compute\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{Y/X\}\$ in each cases : \$k=1\$, or \$k>1\$ ,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nCase \$k=1\$ : we have\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{Y/X\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}frac\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot dz\}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot (kz\^{}\{k-1\}dz)\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}frac\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\}\{(kz\^{}\{k-1\})\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot dz\$\textbackslash{}nand,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nsince \$k\$ is invertible in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$,\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{Y/X\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}frac\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\}\{(z\^{}\{k-1\})\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot dz \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}frac\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\}\{(1)\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot dz \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong 0\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nCase \$k>1\$ : we have\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\_\{Y/X\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}frac\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\}\{(z\^{}\{k-1\})\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot dz\$ is\textbackslash{}nsupported at \$z=0\$, indeed, if we look at a point \$x\$ with \$z=0\$, on the\textbackslash{}nlocal ring \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,x\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$, \$z\^{}\{k-1\}\$ is not a\textbackslash{}nunit, so the quotient \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}/(z\^{}\{k-1\})\$ is non-zero and in\textbackslash{}nfact it is finite-dimensional over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ with basis\textbackslash{}n\$1,z,...,z\^{}\{k-2\}\$. So it is ramified.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 30**. We have established that (non-constant) finite branched\textbackslash{}ncoverings with zero ramification locus (so finite topological covering\textbackslash{}nspaces) are the same as finite étale coverings over compact Riemann\textbackslash{}nsurfaces. And from our previous discussion, we know that there is an\textbackslash{}nequivalence (through the analytification functor) between compact\textbackslash{}nRiemann surfaces and non-singular projective curves over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$.\textbackslash{}nLet \$X\$ be a projective curve over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$, the analytification\textbackslash{}nfunctor thus, induces an equivalence of the category of finite étale\textbackslash{}ncovers of \$X\$ with that of finite topological coverings of \$X\^{}\{an\}\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nSince we know that for a projective curve \$X\$ over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ (also a\textbackslash{}nscheme), the étale fundamental group is the automorphism group of the\textbackslash{}nfibre functor \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\}\$ at any geometric\textbackslash{}npoint \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\$ of \$X\$, we now show that this fibre functor is\textbackslash{}nactually identical to the topological fibre functor defined in Section\textbackslash{}n[1.3](\#universal\_cover\_section)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"universal\_cover\_section\textbackslash{}"\}, restricted to the finite case,\textbackslash{}nwhich we now denote \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\^{}\{top\}\_x\$. First, notice that\textbackslash{}nover \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$, for \$Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{F\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}acute\{e\}t\}\}\}\_X\$ the\textbackslash{}nunderlying set\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\}(Y) = Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$\textbackslash{}nconsists of points \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\$ whose image in \$X\$ must be \$x\$, together\textbackslash{}nwith a map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(x)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ (which is always the\textbackslash{}nidentity). So we get that\textbackslash{}n\$|\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\}(Y)| = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid f(y)=x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ for\textbackslash{}n\$f\$ the associated finite étale morphism (as a morphism of sets).\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nNow, by ''analytifying\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" the setup, we get a finite topological covering\textbackslash{}n\$f\^{}\{an\}:Y\^{}\{an\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\^{}\{an\}\$. Recall that points of \$X\^{}\{an\}\$ are\textbackslash{}nclosed points of \$X\$ and since \$Y\$ is finite étale over \$X\$, as we have\textbackslash{}nseen, the algebraic fibre of \$Y\$ is a disjoint union of copies of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$, so closed points. Hence\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\^{}\{top\}\_\{(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{im\}\}x)\}(Y\^{}\{an\}) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid f(y)=x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$.\textbackslash{}nAnd we have that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\}(Y) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\^{}\{top\}\_\{(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{im\}\}x)\}(Y\^{}\{an\})\$\textbackslash{}nas sets. Taking a morphism of covers \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi:Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\$, we get a\textbackslash{}nmorphism of sets\textbackslash{}n\$Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$\textbackslash{}nwhich sends \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi(y)\$. On the topological side, we get a\textbackslash{}nmorphism of sets\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\^{}\{top\}\_\{(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{im\}\}x)\}(Y\^{}\{an\})\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\^{}\{top\}\_\{(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{im\}\}x)\} (Z\^{}\{an\})\$\textbackslash{}nwhich also sends \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi(y)\$. And the above identification of\textbackslash{}nsets commutes with such morphisms of covers, yielding a natural\textbackslash{}nisomorphism of the fibre functors. Now, what would be the automorphism\textbackslash{}ngroup of the topological fibre functor ? By fully faithfulness of the\textbackslash{}nYoneda embedding, and since the topological fibre functor is represented\textbackslash{}nby the universal cover, we get that the automorphisms of the topological\textbackslash{}nfibre functor are precisely elements of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\^{}\{an\}\}|X\^{}\{an\})\$. As usual, this forms\textbackslash{}na group under composition and from the reformulation Theorem\textbackslash{}n[67](\#covering\_reformulation\_2)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"covering\_reformulation\_2\textbackslash{}"\}, we actually have that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{X\^{}\{an\}\}|X\^{}\{an\}) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X\^{}\{an\},x')\}\$\textbackslash{}nfor \$x'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\^{}\{an\}\$ the corresponding point of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\$. And by\textbackslash{}nchain of isomorphisms, we get that\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(X,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X\^{}\{an\},x')\}.\$\$\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nBefore ending this section, it is worthwhile pointing out that the\textbackslash{}nequivalence of categories between compact Riemann surfaces and\textbackslash{}nprojective curves over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ is deeper. Indeed, we have the\textbackslash{}nfollowing three-way equivalence of categories:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Smooth projective algebraic curves over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ and non-constant\textbackslash{}n  algebraic maps,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Compact connected Riemann surfaces and non-constant holomorphic maps,\textbackslash{}n  and\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Finite field extensions of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ of transcendence degree \$1\$\textbackslash{}n  and morphisms of extensions of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nwith the first two categories being anti-equivalent to the third one.\textbackslash{}nThis situation is explained in detail in Chapter \$4\$ of [@Szamuely].\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nWe end this section by mentioning that Grothendieck, in [@SGA] (Théorèm\textbackslash{}n\$XII.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:5.1\$) proved a generalisation of Riemann's existence theorem:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 200**. *Let \$X\$ be a scheme over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ locally of\textbackslash{}nfinite type and \$X\^{}\{an\}\$ the analytical space associated to \$X\$. The\textbackslash{}nanalytification functor which to any finite étale cover \$Y\$ associates\textbackslash{}n\$Y\^{}\{an\}\$ is an equivalence of categories between finite étale covers of\textbackslash{}n\$X\$ and finite topological covers of \$X\^{}\{an\}\$*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@SGA], Théorèm \$XII.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:5.1\$ ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWhich has the following corollary (\$XII.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:5.2\$ in [@SGA]) who\textbackslash{}ngeneralises our whole discussion to schemes of higher dimensions:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: corollary\textbackslash{}n**Corollary 201**. *Let \$X\$ be a connected scheme over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$\textbackslash{}nlocally of finite type, \$x'\$ a point in \$X\^{}\{an\}\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\$ its\textbackslash{}ncorresponding point in \$X\$. We have the following canonical isomorphism\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(X,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X\^{}\{an\},x')\}\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#etale\_fund\_grp\_fin\_gen .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 31**.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- One might guess that such a result is quite powerful. An immediate\textbackslash{}n  application is that every smooth projective scheme over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$\textbackslash{}n  has a topologically finitely generated étale fundamental group.\textbackslash{}n  Indeed, when \$X\^{}\{an\}\$ is a compact complex manifold, its fundamental\textbackslash{}n  group is finitely presented (so also finitely generated) and by Remark\textbackslash{}n  [6](\#finite\_generated\_prof\_grp)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}n  reference=\textbackslash{}"finite\_generated\_prof\_grp\textbackslash{}"\}, its profinite completion must\textbackslash{}n  be topologically finitely generated.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- It is also worthwhile mentioning that a similar result holds for the\textbackslash{}n  cohomology groups of coherent sheaves and analytic coherent sheaves.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Properties of Étale Fundamental Groups\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn this section, we discuss a few interesting properties of the étale\textbackslash{}nfundamental group. Namely, we prove its insensitivity to the change of\textbackslash{}ngeometric base points for connected schemes; this should not be\textbackslash{}nsurprising as it was already the case for the topological fundamental\textbackslash{}ngroup. Then, as the étale fundamental group is an object emanating from\textbackslash{}nalgebraic geometry, we will study how it behaves under functorial base\textbackslash{}nchange. And finally, we finish this section by providing useful tools\textbackslash{}nfor computing étale fundamental groups, relying on powerful exact\textbackslash{}nsequences.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nLet us first show the following lemma.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#fiber\_isomorphism .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 202**. *Let \$S\$ be a connected scheme. Give, two geometric\textbackslash{}npoints \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$s':\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Lambda'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$, there exists an\textbackslash{}nisomorphism of fibre functors\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow[]\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sim\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}'\}\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* By proposition\textbackslash{}n[182](\#fib\_pro\_representable)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"fib\_pro\_representable\textbackslash{}"\}, both fibre functors are\textbackslash{}npro-representable. Thus, by\textbackslash{}nconstruction we have,\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}(f\_\{ij\})(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{y\}\_j) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{y\}\_i\$\textbackslash{}nand let us set\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{y\}\_i':= \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}(g\_\{ij\})(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_j(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{y\}\_j))\$.\textbackslash{}nSince \$Y\_i\$ is Galois, from Remark\textbackslash{}n[21](\#remark\_Galois)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}" reference=\textbackslash{}"remark\_Galois\textbackslash{}"\}\textbackslash{}n\$b)\$, there exist a unique \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}(Y\_i|S)\$\textbackslash{}nmapping \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{y\}\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{y\}\_i'\$. As a consequence of this, every automorphism of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}\$ is induced by an automorphism of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}'\}\$ via composition with the functor\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Bc\}\}\_\{S,S'\}\$, and thus we obtain a map\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_* : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(S',\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}')\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}).\$\$\textbackslash{}nThe map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_*\$ is actually a continuous homomorphism of profinite\textbackslash{}ngroups. We study when this morphism is injective or\textbackslash{}nsurjective and we will fit such morphisms into an exact sequence.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#image\_base\_change\_induce .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 205**. **\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *The map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_*\$ is trivial if and only if for every connected finite\textbackslash{}n  étale cover \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$, the base change\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Bc\}\}\_\{S,S'\}(X)\$ is a trivial cover.*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *The map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_*\$ is surjective if and only if for every connected\textbackslash{}n  finite étale cover \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$, the base change\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Bc\}\}\_\{S,S'\}\$ is connected as well.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Suppose the map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_*\$ is trivial. We have, for any finite étale\textbackslash{}n  connected cover \$X\$ of \$S\$ a corresponding finite\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\})\$-set,\textbackslash{}n  \$F:= \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Fib\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\}(X)\$. The finite set\textbackslash{}n  corresponding to the base change \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Bc\}\}\_\{S,S\}(X)\$ which\textbackslash{}n  is now a finite étale cover of \$S'\$ is again \$F\$ (by the above\textbackslash{}n  construction) and has a \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(S',\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}')\$-action, given by\textbackslash{}n  pull-back via \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_*\$. Since \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_*\$ is trivial, for every \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in F\$,\textbackslash{}n  \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot x =x\$ for all \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(S',\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}')\$, so the action\textbackslash{}n  of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(S',\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}')\$ on \$F\$ is trivial. And from the main\textbackslash{}n  Theorem\textbackslash{}n  [184](\#main\_theorem\_etale\_fundamental\_group)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}n  reference=\textbackslash{}"main\_theorem\_etale\_fundamental\_group\textbackslash{}"\}, a finite étale\textbackslash{}n  cover is trivial if and only if it corresponds to a finite set with\textbackslash{}n  trivial action of the fundamental group.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n  For the other direction, assume \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{im\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_*\$ is\textbackslash{}n  non-trivial, and choose an open subgroup\textbackslash{}n  \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\})\$, not containing the whole of\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{im\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\_*\$. From Theorem\textbackslash{}n  [161](\#Galois\_correpondance\_etale\_cov)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}n  reference=\textbackslash{}"Galois\_correpondance\_etale\_cov\textbackslash{}"\}, we can obtain every\textbackslash{}n  finite étale cover via correspondence with a coset space\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}) / U\$. The natural map\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(X\_L,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\_L)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(X,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\})\$ is an\textbackslash{}nisomorphism for every geometric point \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\$ of \$X\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* If \$Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is a connected finite étale cover, then \$Y\$\textbackslash{}nis reduced by Proposition\textbackslash{}n[152](\#reduced\_carry\_above)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"reduced\_carry\_above\textbackslash{}"\} since \$X\$ is also reduced (Proposition\textbackslash{}n[314](\#integral\_iff\_irr\_red)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"integral\_iff\_irr\_red\textbackslash{}"\}). And by Lemma\textbackslash{}n[59](\#finite\_dimensional\_direct\_sum\_reduced)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"finite\_dimensional\_direct\_sum\_reduced\textbackslash{}"\}, \$Y\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta\}\$ is the\textbackslash{}nspectrum of a direct sum of field extensions of \$K(X)\$, the function\textbackslash{}nfield of \$X\$. The generic fibre also being connected, it must be a\textbackslash{}nsingle finite field extension of the function field of \$X\$. Now \$Y\$ is\textbackslash{}nalso irreducible, it has \$1\$ minimal prime ideal (as does \$Y\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta\}\$),\textbackslash{}nthen \$Y\$ is an integral scheme as well. And since \$k\$ is algebraically\textbackslash{}nclosed in \$L\$, the tensor product \$K(Y)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_k L\$ is a field, where\textbackslash{}n\$K(Y)\$ is the function field of \$Y\$. This shows that the base change\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}(K(Y)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_kL)\$, the part of \$Y\_L\$ lying over\textbackslash{}nits generic point \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta\$, is connected, and in turn, that \$Y\_L\$ is\textbackslash{}nconnected. With Proposition\textbackslash{}n[205](\#image\_base\_change\_induce)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"image\_base\_change\_induce\textbackslash{}"\} \$b)\$, we have that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(X\_L,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\_L) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(X,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\})\$ is\textbackslash{}nsurjective.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nFor injectivity, this is where the previous corollary intervenes. For every geometric base point \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}\$ the étale\textbackslash{}nfundamental group \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(X,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\})\$ is topologically finitely\textbackslash{}ngenerated.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# Some Examples\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe have already computed the étale fundamental groups of\textbackslash{}n\$X = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: k\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$X = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{F\}\_p\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe next examples illustrate the projective case. 0.\$\$\textbackslash{}nAnd by with the injection\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}hookrightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$, we can We can conclude that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{P\}\^{}1\_\{k\}, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(k\_s|k)\$.\textbackslash{}nWhich is trivial when \$k\$ is separably closed.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nUsing the above example we can compute the étale fundamental group of\textbackslash{}nthe following punctured projective lines over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Q\}\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: examples\textbackslash{}n**Examples 216**.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Suppose we consider the projective line over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Q\}\$ minus two\textbackslash{}n  points, say \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{0,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}infty\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$. As in the previous example, using a\textbackslash{}n  combination of Theorem\textbackslash{}n  [210](\#first\_homotopy\_exact\_sequence)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}n  reference=\textbackslash{}"first\_homotopy\_exact\_sequence\textbackslash{}"\} and Proposition\textbackslash{}n  [213](\#invariant\_under\_field\_extension)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}n  reference=\textbackslash{}"invariant\_under\_field\_extension\textbackslash{}"\}, provided the embedding\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Q\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}hookrightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$, we can compute its\textbackslash{}n  étale fundamental group. We can conclude that the following sequence\textbackslash{}n  is exact\textbackslash{}n  \$\$0\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Z\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{P\}\^{}1\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Q\}\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}backslash\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{0,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}infty\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Q\}\}|\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Q\})\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow 0.\$\$\textbackslash{}n  Indeed, notice that the Riemann sphere minus two points is\textbackslash{}n  homotopically equivalent to the circle which we showed has fundamental\textbackslash{}n  group \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Z\}\$ at any point.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- We can proceed similarly to compute the étale fundamental group of the\textbackslash{}n  projective line over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Q\}\$ minus three points (say\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{0,1,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}infty\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$). In this case, notice that the complex projective\textbackslash{}n  line minus three points is actually homotopically equivalent to a\textbackslash{}n  figure eight: the wedge sum of two circle \$S\^{}1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vee S\^{}1\$. Now to\textbackslash{}n  compute the fundamental group of a wedge sum of say two WC complexes\textbackslash{}n  (which is the case for \$S\^{}1\$) one can use Van Kampen' theorem\textbackslash{}n  [@Hatcher], (Theorem \$1.20\$). It says that the fundamental group of\textbackslash{}n  the wedge is the free product of the fundamental groups of the two\textbackslash{}n  spaces. Thus \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(S\^{}1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vee S\^{}1) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Z\}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Z\}\$, which is\textbackslash{}n  the free group on two generators \$F\_2\$. This gives us the following\textbackslash{}n  exact sequence,\textbackslash{}n  \$\$0\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widehat\{F\_2\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{P\}\^{}1\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Q\}\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}backslash\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{0,1,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}infty\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\}) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Gal\}\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Q\}\}|\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Q\})\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow 0.\$\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nGrothendieck suggested that the most interesting group in mathematics is\textbackslash{}narguably\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\^{}e\_1(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{P\}\^{}1\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Q\}\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}backslash\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{0,1,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}infty\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\},\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{x\})\$.\textbackslash{}nLater on, he advised P. Deligne to study this group, which he did\textbackslash{}nextensively, leading to a \$200\$-pages monograph [@droit\_p\_minus\_3\_pts].\textbackslash{}nIn his paper, Deligne introduced a Tannakian framework for the category\textbackslash{}nof *mixed motives*. Without delving further into motivic theory, we can\textbackslash{}nsummarize Deligne's objective in defining a ''*motivic*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" version of the\textbackslash{}nfundamental group through the following question:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nThere are many ways through which one can understand a (algebraic)\textbackslash{}nspace, this can be done through theories such as *Betti* cohomology, *de\textbackslash{}nRham* cohomology, *\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}ell\$-adic* cohomology and *crystalline* cohomology.\textbackslash{}nThe problem is that these theories may feel like different ''shadows\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nof the same object. Now Grothendieck hoped for a universal theory,\textbackslash{}nsitting above them all, which he called the theory of motives. And\textbackslash{}nDeligne's approach consisted of finding a way to unify this perspective\textbackslash{}nby applying it to objects richer than cohomology groups: non-abelian\textbackslash{}nfundamental groups.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nIn [@droit\_p\_minus\_3\_pts], he successfully defined what it meant for a\textbackslash{}nnon-abelian group to be motivic by working with a Tannakian realisation\textbackslash{}nof the étale fundamental group of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{P\}\^{}1\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{Q\}\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}backslash \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{0,1,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}infty\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ as a non-trivial\textbackslash{}nexample. This the motivation behind the next chapter.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\# Tannakian Fundamental Groups\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn the last chapter, we established an equivalence of categories between\textbackslash{}nthe category of finite étale covers over a connected scheme and that of\textbackslash{}nfinite continuous representations of its étale fundamental group. In\textbackslash{}nthis chapter, we study a linearisation of this concept by replacing\textbackslash{}nfinite étale covers by linear algebraic data. We begin by studying\textbackslash{}nrepresentations of affine group schemes and their relation with\textbackslash{}ncomodules over Hopf algebras. Then introduce monoidal categories and\textbackslash{}ndevelop the categorical language required for *Tannaka duality*. And\textbackslash{}nfinish with a specialisation of this reconstruction for neutral\textbackslash{}nTannakian categories, and define their Tannakian fundamental group.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Representation of Group Schemes and Comodules\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nBefore defining comodules, one has to make sense of the kind of object\textbackslash{}nwe define comodules over. It is quite natural that we want comodules to\textbackslash{}nbe the dual notion of modules. And since we will study modules over\textbackslash{}nalgebras, we introduce below the notion of a coalgebra. This will allow\textbackslash{}nus to have a clean definition for coations of comodules.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 217**. A coalgebra is a \$k\$-vector space \$C\$ endowed with a\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-linear comultiplication : \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta:C\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow C\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_k C\$ and a\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-linear counit : \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}epsilon : C\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow k\$ satisfying the The next result tells us that under a\textbackslash{}nfiniteness condition, dualising a coalgebra, we get an algebra as well.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#dualize\_algebra\_coalgebra .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 218**. *The contravariant dualisation functor\textbackslash{}n\$A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto A\^{}*\$ induces an anti-equivalence between the category of\textbackslash{}nfinite-dimensional \$k\$-coalgebras and that of finite-dimensional\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-algebras.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Given a \$k\$-coalgebra \$A\$, the \$k\$-linear dual\textbackslash{}n\$A\^{}* = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(A,k)\$ of the underlying\textbackslash{}nfinite-dimensional \$k\$-vector space carries additional structure. The\textbackslash{}ncomultiplication \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta\$ induces a \$k\$-bilinear map\textbackslash{}n\$m:A\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_kA*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow A\^{}*\$ mapping a pair \$(f,g)\$ of maps in\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(A,k)\$ to the \$k\$-linear map\textbackslash{}n\$(f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes g)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta : A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow k\$. The counit \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}epsilon\$ has a\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-linear dual \$e :k\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow A\^{}*\$ determined by the image of\textbackslash{}n\$1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in k\$ in \$A\^{}*\$. By the coassociativity and counity axioms, the maps\textbackslash{}n\$m\$ and \$e\$ define a multiplication and a unit satisfying associativity\textbackslash{}nand unity, making \$A\^{}*\$ a \$k\$-algebra.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nConversely, given a finite-dimensional \$k\$-algebra \$B\$, the\textbackslash{}nmultiplication map \$m\$ induces a map \$B\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow (B\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes B)\^{}*\$ on\textbackslash{}nthe \$k\$-linear duals. Here enters our crucial assumption that algebras\textbackslash{}nmust be finite-dimensional. Indeed, the natural map\textbackslash{}n\$B\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes B\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow (B\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes B)\^{}*\$ sending \$(f,g)\$ to the\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-linear map \$a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes b\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto f(a)g(b))\$ is an isomorphism if \$B\$ is\textbackslash{}nfinite-dimensional over \$k\$, in that case it is an injective map between\textbackslash{}nvector spaces of the same dimension. And by reversing the above\textbackslash{}nprocedure, we can endow \$B\^{}*\$ with a structure of \$k\$-coalgebra. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#dual\_algebara\_no\_coalgebra .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 33**. The above equivalence restricts to the finite-dimensional\textbackslash{}ncase, because whereas it is true that arbitrary \$k\$-coalgebras dualise\textbackslash{}ninto algebras, the converse is false for infinite-dimensional\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-algebras. For example, the \$k\$-algebra \$A = k[x]\$ does not dualise\textbackslash{}ninto a coalgebra. Denote \$A\^{}* = (k[x])\^{}*\$, then the natural map\textbackslash{}n\$A\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes A\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow (A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes A)\^{}*\$ is not surjective anymore.\textbackslash{}nIndeed, elements of \$A\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes A\^{}*\$ are finite sum tensors (they have\textbackslash{}nfinite rank) while elements of \$(A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes A)\^{}*\$ are infinite sequences\textbackslash{}nof evaluation on the basis.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 219**. A **bialgebra** \$H\$ is a vector space that is at the\textbackslash{}nsame time an algebra with multiplication \$m\$ and unit \$u\$ and a\textbackslash{}ncoalgebra with comultiplication \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta\$ and counit \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}epsilon\$, such\textbackslash{}nthat \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}epsilon\$ are algebra morphisms (or equivalently that\textbackslash{}n\$m\$ and \$u\$ are coalgebra morphisms).\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nA **Hopf algebra** is a bialgebra that possesses an additional map\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Sigma: H\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow H\$, which makes the following
