remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 34**. Similarly to Proposition\textbackslash{}n[218](\#dualize\_algebra\_coalgebra)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"dualize\_algebra\_coalgebra\textbackslash{}"\}, there is an equivalence between\textbackslash{}n(left) finite-dimensional \$C\$-comodules and (right) finite-dimensional\textbackslash{}n\$C\^{}*\$-modules. For \$A\$ a finite-dimensional \$k\$-algebra, we even have\textbackslash{}nthe following equivalence of categories:\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Mod\}\}\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{f.d.\}\}\_A \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}simeq \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{CoMod\}\}\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{f.d.\}\}\_\{A\^{}*\}\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe now state the fundamental theorem of comodules,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#fundamental\_theorem\_comodule .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 221**. *Let \$C\$ be a \$k\$-coalgebra and \$M\$ a right\textbackslash{}n\$C\$-comodule. The any element \$m\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in M\$ is contained in a \$C\$-subcomodule\textbackslash{}nthat is finite-dimensional over \$k\$. Consequently, any\textbackslash{}nfinite-dimensional subspace \$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset M\$ is contained in a\textbackslash{}n\$C\$-subcomodule of \$M\$ that is finite-dimensional over \$k\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Milne\_alg\_group], Proposition \$4.7\$, where the statement\textbackslash{}ncan be generalised to \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}(G)\$ an arbitrary \$k\$-coalgebra ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#representation\_of\_group\_as\_functor .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 35**. Recall that in the last chapter, we identified group\textbackslash{}nschemes with group-valued representable functors (Proposition\textbackslash{}n[168](\#group\_scheme\_are\_representable\_functors)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"group\_scheme\_are\_representable\_functors\textbackslash{}"\}). And that in\textbackslash{}nparticular, we can see affine group schemes \$G\$ over \$k\$ as\textbackslash{}nrepresentable group-valued functors\textbackslash{}n\$R\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_k(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R,G)\$ from the\textbackslash{}ncategory of \$k\$-algebras to that of groups, that is represented by the\textbackslash{}ncoordinate ring \$A\$ of \$G\$ which is a Hopf algebra (Remark\textbackslash{}n[22](\#Hopf\_algebra\_group\_scheme)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Hopf\_algebra\_group\_scheme\textbackslash{}"\}). In that case, a representation\textbackslash{}n\$(V,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho)\$ of an affine group scheme \$G\$ consists of giving for each\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-algebra \$R\$ a \$G(R)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{End\}\}(V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_kR)\$.\textbackslash{}nFunctorially, this amounts to defining a natural transformation\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho:G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{GL\}\}\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#representations\_iso\_comodules .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 222**. *There is a bijection between right comodules over\textbackslash{}nthe commutative Hopf algebra \$A\$ and left representations of the\textbackslash{}ncorresponding affine group scheme.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Let \$M\$ be an \$A\$-comodule where \$A\$ is a commutative Hopf\textbackslash{}nalgebra. Given a \$k\$-algebra \$R\$, an element of \$G(R)\$ corresponds to a\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-algebra homomorphism \$g: A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow R\$. The composite map\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_R : M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\}M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_kA\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{id\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes g\} M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_kR\$\textbackslash{}ninduces an \$R\$-linear map \$M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_kR\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_kR\$, so an\textbackslash{}nobject of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{GL\}\}(M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_kR)\$ that depends on \$R\$\textbackslash{}nfunctorially. The maps \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_R\$ are actually actions, as in remark\textbackslash{}n[35](\#representation\_of\_group\_as\_functor)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"representation\_of\_group\_as\_functor\textbackslash{}"\}. The identity\textbackslash{}n\$e\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G(R)\$ is given by the counit\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}epsilon:A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow k \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow R\$ and for \$g,h\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G(R)\$, the\textbackslash{}nproduct \$g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot h\$ in \$G(R)\$ is \$m\_R\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ (g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes h) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Delta\$. By\textbackslash{}nthe counit and coassociativity of the comodule \$M\$, we have\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_R(e) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{id\}\}\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_R(g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot h) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_R(g)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_R(h)\$. So this is a left\textbackslash{}nrepresentation of the affine group scheme \$G\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nOn the other hand, let \$(V,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho)\$ be a left representation of an affine\textbackslash{}ngroup scheme \$G\$, so it has an action \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_A\$, such that for\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{id\}\}\_A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in G(A)\$ the identity element,\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_A(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{id\}\}\_A):V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes A\$ is\textbackslash{}n\$A\$-linear. The composition of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_A(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{id\}\}\_A)\$ with\textbackslash{}n\$v\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto v\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes 1\$ defines a map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nu:V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes A\$, which\textbackslash{}ncan be seen as a coaction on the \$A\$-comodule \$V\$. The two construction\textbackslash{}nbeing inverse to one another, we have a bijection.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWhat we have seen so far is that for an affine group scheme \$G\$, one can\textbackslash{}nconsider its coordinate ring, which is a Hopf algebra. Then studying its\textbackslash{}ncategory of representations is the same as studying comodules over its\textbackslash{}ncoordinate ring. Now we want to know if the reverse computation is\textbackslash{}npossible. By that, we mean if it is possible to recover the affine group\textbackslash{}nscheme \$G\$ from its category of representations (which is equivalent to\textbackslash{}na certain category of comodules). This problem has been extensively\textbackslash{}nstudied and is largely understood through the lens of *Tannaka-Krein\textbackslash{}nduality*. We shall give a somewhat motivation for this. We start with\textbackslash{}nthe theory of *Morita equivalence*, which states that one can determine\textbackslash{}nan algebra \$A\$ from its category of modules\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Mod\}\}\}\_A\$ up to Morita equivalence (see [@Etingof],\textbackslash{}nChapter \$7.8\$). But in the case of finite-dimensional, by considering\textbackslash{}nthe associated forgetful functor\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Mod\}\}\}\_A\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Vect\}\}\}\_k\$,\textbackslash{}nour \$k\$-algebra can be recovered up to *isomorphism* as the endomorphism\textbackslash{}nalgebra of the forgetful functor. If \$A\$ is a finite-dimensional\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-algebra, then the category of finite-dimensional \$A\$-modules is a\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-linear abelian category. The other way around, for \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ a\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-linear abelian category, then one can take\textbackslash{}n\$A=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{End\}\}(P)\^{}\{op\}\$ for \$P\$ a progenerator of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$. That same progenerator in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ represents a\textbackslash{}nforgetful functor\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega :\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Vect\}\}\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{f.d.\}\}\_k\$,\textbackslash{}ngiving us\textbackslash{}n\$A = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{End\}\}(P)\^{}\{op\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{End\}\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega)\$\textbackslash{}n(see [@Etingof], Chapter \$1.8\$). And a similar statement holds for\textbackslash{}narbitrary \$k\$-algebras. What we are interested in is what happens in the\textbackslash{}ncase of comodules (corresponding to representations), we want to dualise\textbackslash{}nthe finite-dimensional statement to obtain a similar reconstruction but\textbackslash{}nfor coalgebras from a category of comodules over a coalgebra. However,\textbackslash{}nas we saw in Remark\textbackslash{}n[33](\#dual\_algebara\_no\_coalgebra)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"dual\_algebara\_no\_coalgebra\textbackslash{}"\} a similar procedure in the\textbackslash{}ninfinite-dimensional case fails in general. Still, it is possible to\textbackslash{}nrecover an arbitrary \$k\$-coalgebra \$C\$ from the category\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{CoMod\}\}\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{f.d.\}\}\_C\$ of finite-dimensional\textbackslash{}nright \$C\$-comodules with the associated forgetful functor\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega :\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{CoMod\}\}\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{f.d.\}\}\_C\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Vect\}\}\}\^{}\{f.d.\}\_k\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nOur first result in that direction comes from an application of the\textbackslash{}nfundamental theorem of comodules. We call the forgetful functor\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega :\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{CoMod\}\}\}\_C\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Vect\}\}\}\_k\$\textbackslash{}na *fibre functor* and we define its restriction\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega\^{}f: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{CoMod\}\}\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{f.d.\}\}\_C\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Vect\}\}\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{f.d.\}\}\_k\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: lemma\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 223**. *Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega\^{}f\$ be fibre functors as above,\textbackslash{}nthen\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega) =\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega\^{}f,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega\^{}f)\$\$*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Let \$M\$ be a \$C\$-comodule and let \$N\$ be a subcomodule of \$M\$\textbackslash{}nvia the inclusion \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}iota :N \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}hookrightarrow M\$. Then, for\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lambda\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{End\}\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega)\$, by naturality, the\textbackslash{}nrestriction of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lambda\_M\$ is given exactly by \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lambda\_N\$, i.e.\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{tikzcd\}[column sep = large]\textbackslash{}n        N \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[r,\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lambda\_N\textbackslash{}"]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d,\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}iota\textbackslash{}"'] \& N\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d,\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}iota\textbackslash{}"]\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n        M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[r,\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lambda\_M\textbackslash{}"'] \& M.\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{tikzcd\}\$\$ From the fundamental theorem of comodules\textbackslash{}n[221](\#fundamental\_theorem\_comodule)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"fundamental\_theorem\_comodule\textbackslash{}"\}, \$M\$ is the sum of all its\textbackslash{}nfinite-dimensional subcomodules. Hence, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lambda\_M\$ is completely\textbackslash{}ndetermined by the natural transformation \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lambda\$ in each of these\textbackslash{}nfinite-dimensional subcomodules. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 36**. In light of Proposition\textbackslash{}n[222](\#representations\_iso\_comodules)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"representations\_iso\_comodules\textbackslash{}"\}, the previous lemma states\textbackslash{}nthat in order to study arbitrary representations of an affine group\textbackslash{}nscheme, it suffices to study the finite-dimensional ones.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe following lemma will help us recover a coalgebra from its category\textbackslash{}nof comodules with the fibre functor \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega\$. We denote\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes V\$, the functor from\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{CoMod\}\}\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{f.d.\}\}\_C\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Vect\}\}\}\_k\$\textbackslash{}nsending \$M\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega(M)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes V\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#useful\_lemma\_underlying\_coalgebra .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 224**. *Let \$A\$ be a \$k\$-coalgebra and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega\^{}f\$ the fibre\textbackslash{}nfunctor as above. We now introduce the\textbackslash{}nlanguage necessary to understand those extra conditions.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Monoidal Categories and Tannaka-Krein Theorem\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nMonoidal categories, also often called *tensor categories*, can be seen\textbackslash{}nas the generalisation of categories carrying a tensor product, such as\textbackslash{}nthe categories of vector spaces, abelian groups, \$R\$-modules, or\textbackslash{}n\$R\$-algebras. We will use the theory developed in the previous section\textbackslash{}nto prove that the category of finite-dimensional representations of an\textbackslash{}naffine group scheme over \$k\$ is equivalent to a monoidal category under\textbackslash{}nnecessary and sufficient conditions. \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Vect\}\}\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{f.d.\}\}\_k\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Neutral Tannakian Categories and Tannakian Fundamental Groups\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe are finally able to introduce *Tannakian categories* and the\textbackslash{}n*Tannakian fundamental group*.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 241**. A **neutral Tannakian category** over a field \$k\$ is\textbackslash{}na rigid, \$k\$-linear, abelian, symmetric monoidal category \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$\textbackslash{}nwhose unit \$1\$ satisfies \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{End\}\}(1) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong k\$, and is\textbackslash{}nmoreover equipped with an exact faithful tensor functor\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega :\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Vect\}\}\}\^{}\{f.d.\}\_k\$.\textbackslash{}nThe functor \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega\$ is called a (neutral) **fibre functor**\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: example\textbackslash{}n**Example 242**. Let \$G\$ be an affine group scheme over \$k\$. The\textbackslash{}ncategory \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Rep\}\}\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{f.d.\}\}(G)\$ of\textbackslash{}nfinite-dimensional representations of \$G\$ with its usual tensor product\textbackslash{}nand the forgetful functor\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Rep\}\}\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{f.d.\}\}(G)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Vect\}\}\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{f.d.\}\}\_k\$\textbackslash{}nas the fibre functor is a neutral Tannkian category.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe converse is a consequence of Tannaka duality\textbackslash{}n[240](\#Tannaka\_duality)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Tannaka\_duality\textbackslash{}"\} and we get the following theorem,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 243**. *Neutral Tannakian categories over \$k\$ are equivalent\textbackslash{}nto categories of finite-dimensional representations of an affine group\textbackslash{}nschemes over \$k\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* This is a direct application of Theorem\textbackslash{}n[240](\#Tannaka\_duality)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Tannaka\_duality\textbackslash{}"\} and Proposition\textbackslash{}n[222](\#representations\_iso\_comodules)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"representations\_iso\_comodules\textbackslash{}"\}. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 244**. Consider \$(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\},\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega)\$ a Tannakian\textbackslash{}ncategory. The associated functor\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Aut\}\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega)\$ is called the **Tannakian\textbackslash{}nfundamental group** of \$(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\},\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega)\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nNotice that with the previous theorem and Proposition\textbackslash{}n[239](\#automorphism\_group\_scheme)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"automorphism\_group\_scheme\textbackslash{}"\}, the Tannakian fundamental group\textbackslash{}nis always isomorphic to some group scheme as a functor.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nOur next goal is to give a result identifying somewhat quotients of\textbackslash{}nTannakian fundamental groups with affine subgroup schemes of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{GL\}\}\_n\$. But first, let us give two constructions:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#construction\_algebraic\_hull .construction\}\textbackslash{}n**Construction 245**. Let \$G\$ be an arbitrary group and \$k\$ a field.\textbackslash{}nThen the category of finite-dimensional representations of such an\textbackslash{}narbitrary group is still a neutral Tannakian with its usual forgetful\textbackslash{}nfunctor. The Tannakian fundamental group of its category of\textbackslash{}nfinite-dimensional representations together with the forgetful functor\textbackslash{}nis usually called the *algebraic hull* . One can also consider the\textbackslash{}nalgebraic hull of a topological group by taking its category of\textbackslash{}nfinite-dimensional continuous representations.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe next construction tells us how to consider quotient of the Tannakian\textbackslash{}nfundamental group,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: construction\textbackslash{}n**Construction 246**. Given a Tannakian category \$(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\},\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}omega)\$\textbackslash{}nand an object \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$, we denote \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}langle X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rangle\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\}\$\textbackslash{}nthe *smallest full Tannakian subcategory of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ containing\textbackslash{}n\$X\$*. Its objects are subquotients of finite direct sums of objects of\textbackslash{}nthe form \$X\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes r\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes (X\^{}*)\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes s\}\$ for some \$r,s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}geq 0\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAnd we have the following result,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#Tannaka\_subcat\_Zariski\_closure .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 247**. *Let \$G\$ be an arbitrary group, \$k\$ a field and\textbackslash{}n\$(V,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho)\$ finite-dimensional representation of \$G\$ over \$k\$. Then the\textbackslash{}nTannakian fundamental group of the full Tannakian subcategory\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}langle V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rangle\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\}\$ of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Rep\}\}\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{f.d.\}\}\_k(G)\$ is canonically\textbackslash{}nisomorphic to the Zariski closure of the image of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\$ in\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{GL\}\}\_n\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nNotice that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{im\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\}\$ is actually an\textbackslash{}naffine group scheme in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{GL\}\}\_n\$. It is a closed\textbackslash{}nsubvariety and since \$G\$ is a group, using the fact\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{G\})\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho(G)\}\$, then\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho(G)\}\$ has a group structure.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nIn order to prove the above proposition, we need a lemma that is\textbackslash{}nequivalent to the following Theorem in [@waterhouse]\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 248** (Waterhouse). *Let \$k\$ be a field and \$G\$ a closed\textbackslash{}nsubgroup scheme of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{GL\}\}\_n\$. Every finite-dimensional\textbackslash{}nrepresentation of \$G\$ can be reconstructed from its original\textbackslash{}nrepresentation on \$k\^{}n\$ by the process of forming tensor products,\textbackslash{}ndirect sums, subrepresentations, quotients and duals.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@waterhouse] Chapter \$3.5\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: corollary\textbackslash{}n**Corollary 249**. *Let \$k\$ be a field and \$G\$ a closed subgroup scheme\textbackslash{}nof \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{GL\}\}\_n\$ over \$k\$. Denote by \$X\$ the \$n\$-dimensional\textbackslash{}nrepresentation of \$G\$ corresponding to its action on \$k\^{}n\$ via the\textbackslash{}ninclusion \$G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{GL\}\}\_n\$. Then the full Tannakian\textbackslash{}nsubcategory\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}langle X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rangle\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Rep\}\}\}\_k(G)\$ is\textbackslash{}nthe whole of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Rep\}\}\}\_k(G)\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Since Tannakian categories are rigid monoidal and abelian, they\textbackslash{}nare closed under taking the tensor product, dual, direct sum and taking\textbackslash{}nquotients and subrepresentations since both last are instance of kernels\textbackslash{}nand cokernels. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof of Proposition\textbackslash{}n[247](\#Tannaka\_subcat\_Zariski\_closure)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Tannaka\_subcat\_Zariski\_closure\textbackslash{}"\}.* Denote \$G\$ the affine\textbackslash{}ngroup scheme over \$k\$ defined by \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{im\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\}\$\textbackslash{}nin \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{GL\}\}\_n\$. The representation\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho:V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{GL\}\}\_n(V)\$ give rise to a\textbackslash{}nrepresentation of the affine group scheme \$G\$ in a natural way by taking\textbackslash{}nthe inclusion \$G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{GL\}\}\_n(V)\$, we denote it by\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{V\}\$. Similarly, any object of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}langle V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rangle\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\}\$\textbackslash{}ngive rise to an object of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Rep\}\}\}\_G\$ and e obtain an\textbackslash{}nequivalence between \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}langle V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rangle\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\}\$ and the full Tannakian\textbackslash{}nsubcategory \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}langle \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{V\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rangle\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\}\$ of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Rep\}\}\}\_G\$. In particular the two categories have\textbackslash{}nisomorphic Tanakian fundamental group. But by the above corollary,\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}langle\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{V\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rangle\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\}\$ is the whole of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Rep\}\}\}\_G\$, proving our proposition.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: example\textbackslash{}n**Example 250**. One interesting example of Tannakian categories, is\textbackslash{}nthat of complex local systems. Consider \$X\$ a connected and locally\textbackslash{}nsimply-connected topological space and fix \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$ a base point. The\textbackslash{}ncategory \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{LS\}\}\}\_X\$ of local systems on \$X\$ is a\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$-linear abelian category (since\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{LCS\}\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\}(X) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}simeq \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Mod\}\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}[\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)]\}\$,\textbackslash{}nand a category of \$R\$-modules is abelian). With the usual tensor product\textbackslash{}nand dual construction from linear algebra, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{LS\}\}\}\_X\$\textbackslash{}nis endowed with a symmetric rigid monoidal structure. Taking the stalk\textbackslash{}nof a local system at \$x\$ yields a fibre functor with values in\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Vect\}\}\}\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{f.d.\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\}\$. This means\textbackslash{}nthat \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{LS\}\}\}\_X\$ with the functor taking stalks of\textbackslash{}nlocal systems at \$x\$ is a neutral Tannakian category.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nRecall that in Corollary\textbackslash{}n[79](\#local\_systems\_representations)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"local\_systems\_representations\textbackslash{}"\} we have established an\textbackslash{}nequivalence of categories between complex local systems on \$X\$ and\textbackslash{}nfinite-dimensional representations of the fundamental group\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$. Notice that this is an equivalence of (neutral) Tannakian\textbackslash{}ncategories, thus the Tannakian fundamental group of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{LS\}\}\}\_X\$ is isomorphic to the algebraic hull of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\$ over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ as in Construction\textbackslash{}n[245](\#construction\_algebraic\_hull)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"construction\_algebraic\_hull\textbackslash{}"\}.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nFinally, using our previous Proposition\textbackslash{}n[247](\#Tannaka\_subcat\_Zariski\_closure)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Tannaka\_subcat\_Zariski\_closure\textbackslash{}"\}, the Tannakian fundamental\textbackslash{}ngroup of each full Tannakian subcategory\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}langle \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{S\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rangle\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\}\$ of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{LS\}\}\}\_X\$\textbackslash{}nis isomorphic to the Zariski closure of the image of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{S\},x\} : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1(X,x)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{GL\}\}\_n(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\})\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# Nori's Fundamental Group Scheme\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe end this chapter with a correspondence between the above Tannakian\textbackslash{}nformalism and the étale fundamental group of schemes from the previous\textbackslash{}nchapter presented by Nori in his PhD thesis [@Nori]. For \$S\$ a proper\textbackslash{}nintegral scheme over a field \$k\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$s:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: k\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ a \$k\$-rational point, Nori\textbackslash{}nshowed that the full subcategory of essentially finite vector bundles\textbackslash{}nover \$S\$ denoted \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{EF\}\}\}\_S\$ of the category of\textbackslash{}nlocally free sheaves on \$S\$ spanned by the essentially finite sheaves\textbackslash{}ntogether with the usual tensor product of sheaves and the functor\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{E\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow s\^{}*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{E\}\$, is a neutral Tannakian category\textbackslash{}nover \$k\$ (see section \$2.3\$, page \$83\$, in [@Nori]).\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 251**. For \$S\$ and \$s\$ as above, we define the **Nori\textbackslash{}nfundamental group scheme** of \$S\$ at the base point \$s\$ to be the\textbackslash{}nTannakian fundamental group of the neutral Tannakian category\textbackslash{}n\$(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{EF\}\}\}\_S, s\^{}*)\$ mentionned above. We denote it by\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1\^{}N(S,s)\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#Nori\_invers\_limit .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 252**. *The fundamental group scheme \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1\^{}N(S,s)\$ is an\textbackslash{}ninverse limit of finite \$k\$-group schemes.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Nori], Conclusion \$I.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:3.\$ ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe majority of [@Nori] focuses on what happens to that fundamental\textbackslash{}ngroup, in the case where \$S\$ is defined over fields of positive\textbackslash{}ncharacteristic. However, what is really surprising is that over a field\textbackslash{}nof characteristic \$0\$, we can compare the Nori fundamental group scheme\textbackslash{}nand the étale fundamental group scheme. Indeed, this is due to the fact\textbackslash{}nthat in characteristic \$0\$, every finite group scheme is étale and\textbackslash{}ncombining this with the above Proposition\textbackslash{}n[252](\#Nori\_invers\_limit)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"Nori\_invers\_limit\textbackslash{}"\}, gives us the following corollary.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: corollary\textbackslash{}n**Corollary 253**. *When \$k\$ is an algebraically closed field of\textbackslash{}ncharacteristic \$0\$. For \$S\$ a proper integral scheme over \$k\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$s:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:k \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ a \$k\$-rational point, there\textbackslash{}nis a canonical isomorphism\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1\^{}N(S,s) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow[]\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sim\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}pi\_1\^{}e(S,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\})\$ for each\textbackslash{}n\$k\$-valued geometric point \$s = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{s\}\$ of \$S\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\# Selected Results from Commutative Algebra and Groups Theory\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nFor this thesis, most results from (non-)commutative algebra that can be\textbackslash{}nfound in [@Lang\_algebra] and [@Eisenbud] are assumed to be known by the\textbackslash{}nreader. However, for the sake of keeping this document self-contained,\textbackslash{}nwe recall a few important and necessary results.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#Lang\_1\_10 .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 254**. *Let \$A\$be a subring of \$B\$, let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{p\}\$ be a\textbackslash{}nprime ideal in \$A\$ and assume that \$B\$ is integral over \$A\$. Then\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{p\}B\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}neq B\$ and there exists a prime ideal \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{q\}\$ in\textbackslash{}n\$B\$ lying above \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{p\}\$*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See Proposition \$1.10\$ in Chapter \$VII, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}S1\$ of\textbackslash{}n[@Lang\_algebra]. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe following lemmas are the famous Nakayama Lemmas. They have many\textbackslash{}ndifferent statements, we give two of them here and the latter can be\textbackslash{}nseen as a consequence of the former.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#Nakayama\_first\_lemma .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 255** (Nakayama). *Let \$I\$ be an ideal in \$R\$, and \$M\$ a\textbackslash{}nfinitely generated module over \$R\$. If \$IM=M\$, then there exists\textbackslash{}n\$r\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in R\$ with \$r\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}equiv 1 \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mod\{I\}\$ such that \$rM=0\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#Nakayama\_lemma .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 256** (Nakayama). *Let \$I\$ be an ideal in \$R\$, and \$M\$ a\textbackslash{}nfinitely generated \$R\$-module. If \$I=IM\$, then there exists an \$i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$\textbackslash{}nsuch that \$im = m\$ for all \$m\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in M\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Krull Dimension and Artinian Rings\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 257**. The **Krull dimension** of a commutative ring \$R\$ is\textbackslash{}nthe supremum of the lengths of all increasing chain of prime ideals in\textbackslash{}n\$R\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 258**. A ring \$R\$ is called **Noetherian** if there is no\textbackslash{}ninfinite increasing sequence of ideals\textbackslash{}n\$I\_1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subsetneq I\_2 \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subsetneq \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dots\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subsetneq I\_n \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subsetneq \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dots\$,\textbackslash{}nwhile it is called **Artinian** if there is no infinite descending\textbackslash{}nsequence of ideals\textbackslash{}n\$I\_1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}supsetneq I\_2 \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}supsetneq \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dots\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}supsetneq I\_n \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}supsetneq \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dots\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#f\_d\_k\_alg\_artinian .example\}\textbackslash{}n**Example 259**.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Let \$k\$ be a field, then finite-dimensional \$k\$-algebras are Artinian.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- The ring of polynomials with finite variables over a field, such as\textbackslash{}n  \$k[x\_1,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dots , x\_n]\$ is Noetherian.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn the following we wish to show that ant Artinian ring has zero Krull\textbackslash{}ndimension.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: lemma\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 260**. *Let \$A\$ be an Artinian ring which is also an integral\textbackslash{}ndomain. Then \$A\$ is a field.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Let \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in A\$ be non-zero. We hae a descending chain\textbackslash{}n\$1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}supseteq (x) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}supseteq (x\^{}2) ...\$, which must stabilise, so\textbackslash{}n\$(x\^{}n) = (x\^{}\{n+1\})\$ for some \$n\$. This implies that \$x\^{}n = yx\^{}\{n+1\}\$ for\textbackslash{}nsome \$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in A\$. Since \$A\$ is an integral domain and \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}neq 0\$, we can\textbackslash{}ncancel \$x\^{}n\$ to get \$xy = 1\$ making \$x\$ a unit. This holds for all\textbackslash{}nnon-zero \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in A\$, hence the ring \$A\$ is a field. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: lemma\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 261**. *In an Artinian ring, every prime ideal is maximal.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* If \$A\$ is Artinian and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{p\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset A\$ is a prime\textbackslash{}nideal, then \$A/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{p\}\$ is still Artinian. Since \$A/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{p\}\$\textbackslash{}nis an integral domain, by the previous lemma it is a field, so\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{p\}\$ is actually a maximal ideal. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 262**. *A ring \$A\$ has Krull dimension zero if and only if\textbackslash{}nevery prime ideal is maximal.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* If \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{p\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset A\$ is a non-maximal prime ideal, then\textbackslash{}nthere is some maximal ideal \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\$ with\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{p\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subsetneq\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\$, giving a chain of length \$1\$, and\textbackslash{}nso \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dim A \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}geq 1\$. Conversely, if \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dim A \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}geq 1\$, then there is some\textbackslash{}nchain of prime ideals\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{p\}\_0 \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}supsetneq \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{p\}\_1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}supsetneq ...\$, whereby\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{p\}\_1\$ is not a maximal prime ideal. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#Artin\_zero\_dim .corollary\}\textbackslash{}n**Corollary 263**. *Artinian rings have zero Krull dimension.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Classification of Transitive \$G\$-Spaces\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe result we mention in this subsection is used extensively in the\textbackslash{}nfirst chapter. It is quite powerful as it gives a classification of\textbackslash{}ntransitive \$G\$-spaces by means of stabiliser.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#Cameron\_1\_3 .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 264**. **\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Omega\$ be a transitive \$G\$-space. non-empty\textbackslash{}ncompact topological spaces is non-empty*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* Consider the subsets \$C\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}beta\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod C\_\{i\}\$\textbackslash{}nconsisting of sequences \$(c\_i)\$ satisfying\textbackslash{}n\$f\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}beta\}(c\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}beta\}) = c\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\}\$ for a fixed pair\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}leq \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}beta\$. These are closed subsets of the product, and their\textbackslash{}nintersection is precisely \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varprojlim C\_i\$. Furthermore, since the\textbackslash{}nindex set is directed, then finite intersections of the\textbackslash{}n\$C\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}beta\}\$ are non-empty. Since \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}prod C\_i\$ is compact by\textbackslash{}nTychonoff's theorem (see [@Intro\_manifolds], Proposition \$IV.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:4.36.\$),\textbackslash{}nit ensures that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varprojlim C\_i\$ is non-empty. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#direct\_limit\_modules .remark\}\textbackslash{}n**Remark 42**. Direct and inverse limits are usually referred to as\textbackslash{}n*filtered colimit/limit* respectively. Often filtered (co)limits\textbackslash{}npreserve a lot of structure, notably, taking the direct limit of\textbackslash{}n\$R\$-module gives again a \$R\$-module. This is checked in the following\textbackslash{}ntheorem.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#direct\_limit\_R\_module .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 280**. *Let \$R\$ be a ring and let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{M\_i, f\_\{ij\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ be a\textbackslash{}ndirected system of \$R\$-modules over some directed set \$(I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}leq)\$. Let\textbackslash{}n\$M=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigoplus\_\{i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\}M\_i\$ and for every \$i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$, let\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\_i:M\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow M\$ be the natural injection map. Define the \$N\$\textbackslash{}nthe \$R\$-submodule of \$M\$ by\textbackslash{}n\$\$N = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}langle \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\_jf\_\{ij\}(x\_i) - \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\_i(x\_i) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}leq j,x\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in M\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rangle.\$\$\textbackslash{}nThen \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varinjlim M\_i = M/N\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Lang\_algebra], Theorem \$III.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:10.1\$ ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAn important construction we can make from filtered limits are\textbackslash{}n*pro-objects*. They allow one to work with systems that behave like a\textbackslash{}nlimit even if a limit does not exist in a category. We enumerate the\textbackslash{}nfollowing interesting pro-objects :\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#profinite\_group .definition\}\textbackslash{}n**Definition 281**. A **profinite group** is defined to be an inverse\textbackslash{}nlimit of a system of finite groups.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#pro\_representable .definition\}\textbackslash{}n**Definition 282**. Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ be a category, and \$F\$ a\textbackslash{}nset-valued functor on \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$. We say that \$F\$ is\textbackslash{}n**pro-representable** if there exists an direct system \$(C\_i , f\_\{ij\})\$\textbackslash{}nof objects and morphisms in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ indexed by the directed set\textbackslash{}n\$(I,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}leq)\$ and a functorial isomorphism\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varinjlim \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}(C\_i, X) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong F(X)\$ for each object\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nA way of generalising the notion of directed system is by considering\textbackslash{}nthe directed system to be a category called *(co)-filtered* in the\textbackslash{}nfollowing way :\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 283**. A category \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{J\}\$ is said to be **filtered**\textbackslash{}nwhen it is non-empty, for every two objects \$J\$ and \$J'\$ in\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{J\}\$, there exists an object \$K\$ and two morphisms\textbackslash{}n\$f:J\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow K\$ and \$f':J'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow K\$ in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{J\}\$, and for\textbackslash{}nevery two morphisms \$u,v:I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow J\$ in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{J\}\$, there exists\textbackslash{}nan object \$K\$ and a morphism \$w:J\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow K\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\$w\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ u = w\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ v\$. Dually, a category \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{J\}\$ is said to be\textbackslash{}n**cofiltered** if the opposite category \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{J\}\^{}\{op\}\$ is filtered.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe category \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{Z\}\$ in Lemma\textbackslash{}n[277](\#lemma\_joost\_direct\_limit)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"lemma\_joost\_direct\_limit\textbackslash{}"\} and Definition\textbackslash{}n[278](\#def\_direct\_inverse\_limit)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"def\_direct\_inverse\_limit\textbackslash{}"\} is first a filtered category and\textbackslash{}nsecondly a cofiltered category and the functor\textbackslash{}n\$F:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{Z\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ is thus often called a filtered\textbackslash{}ndiagram and dually a cofiltered diagram.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#cofinal\_identic\_colim .theorem\}\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 284**. *Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{K\}\$ be a subcatecory of a filtered\textbackslash{}ncategory \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{J\}\$ such that it is a cofinal set. Suppose that the\textbackslash{}nfunctors \$F:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{J\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$F':\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{K\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ have colimits. Then there is a\textbackslash{}ncanonical isomorphism between there colimits.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@McLane\_Sau], Theorem \$IX.3.1\$ ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nA subset \$I \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset J\$ of a poset \$J\$ is said to be *cofinal* if for\textbackslash{}nevery \$j\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in J\$, there exists some \$i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$ such that \$j\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}leq i\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# Products and Coproducts \{\#products-and-coproducts .unnumbered\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nLet \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ be a category, \$X\_1\$ and \$X\_2\$ objects of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$. morphisms\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{pr\}\}\_1:X \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\_1\$
