Similarly we define a **coequaliser** \$(Q,q)\$\textbackslash{}nin \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ as the dual of the equaliser.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nA **kernel** of a morphism \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ is an\textbackslash{}nequaliser of \$f\$ and the zero morphism from \$X\$ to \$Y\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nA **cokernel** of \$f\$ in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ is defined as the coequaliser of\textbackslash{}n\$f\$ and the zero morphism from \$X\$ to \$Y\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\#\# Initial and terminal objects: \{\#initial-and-terminal-objects .unnumbered\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 285**. *Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{Z\} =  \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}emptyset\$ be the empty\textbackslash{}ncategory, and let \$F : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{Z\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ be the unique\textbackslash{}nfunctor. Then*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *the limit of \$F\$ is an object \$T\$ in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ with the property\textbackslash{}n  that for any (other) object \$C\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ there exists a unique\textbackslash{}n  morphism \$C\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow T\$. In particular, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}(T,T)\$\textbackslash{}n  is a singleton. If \$T\$ exists, it is called a (the) **terminal\textbackslash{}n  object** of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$.*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *the colimit of \$F\$ is an object \$I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ with the property\textbackslash{}n  that for any object \$C\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$, there exists a unique morphism\textbackslash{}n  \$I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow C\$. In particular, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}(I,I)\$ is a\textbackslash{}n  singleton. If \$I\$ exists, it is called a (the) **initial object** of\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nRemark that if they exist, the initial and terminal object are unique up\textbackslash{}nto isomorphism.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Adjoint Functors\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 286**. Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$ be categories;\textbackslash{}nlet \$L : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$R : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ be functors. We say that \$(L,R)\$\textbackslash{}nis a pair of **adjoint functors**, or \$L\$ is a **left adjoint** to \$R\$,\textbackslash{}nor \$R\$ is a **right adjoint** to \$L\$ if and only if for any objects\textbackslash{}n\$C \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ and \$D\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$, there is an isomorphism\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}theta\_\{C,D\} : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_D(LC,D)  \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_C (C,RD)\$\$\textbackslash{}nthat is natural in both arguments \$C\$ and \$D\$. If there exists an\textbackslash{}nadjoint pair of functors between the categories \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$, we refer to this situation as an **adjunction** and\textbackslash{}ndenote it by \$(L,R):\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightleftarrows \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: examples\textbackslash{}n**Examples 287**.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi : R \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ be a morphism of rings. Then this induces\textbackslash{}n  a functor \$R\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi\} : M\_S \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow M\_R\$, from (right) \$S\$-modules\textbackslash{}n  to (right) \$R\$-modules, called the **restriction of scalars**, that\textbackslash{}n  defines on a right \$S\$-module \$M\$ a right \$R\$-module structure by the\textbackslash{}n  formula \$m\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot r = m\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}phi(r)\$, \$m\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in M, r\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in R\$. This functor\textbackslash{}n  has a left adjoint, called the **extension of scalars**, given by\textbackslash{}n  \$-\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_R S :M\_R \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow M\_S\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- The **pull-back** and **pushout** functors defined above are\textbackslash{}n  respectively left and right adjoint one to another.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 288**. *Consider the functor\textbackslash{}n\$L:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$R:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$. Then there is a bijective\textbackslash{}ncorrespondence between the natural isomorphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}theta\_\{C,D\}\$ (as above)\textbackslash{}nthat turn \$(L,R)\$ into a pair of adjoint functors, and pair of natural\textbackslash{}ntransformations \$(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varepsilon)\$ defined by\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta\_C: C\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow RLC\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_D:LRD\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow D\$ that\textbackslash{}nsatisfy \$R\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}epsilon\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta R = R\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varepsilon L\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ L\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta=L\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@McLane\_Sau]. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn that case, we call the above natural transformations of the\textbackslash{}nadjunction \$(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varepsilon)\$, respectively *unit* and *counit* .\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 289**. *Let \$(L,R) : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightleftarrows \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$\textbackslash{}nbe an adjoint pair of functors. Then \$R\$ preserves all limits that exist\textbackslash{}nin \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$; \$L\$ preserves all colimits that exist in\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@McLane\_Sau], Theorem \$V.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:5.1\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Abelian Categories\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 290**. A category is **preadditive** if every\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\}\$-sets are abelian groups and the\textbackslash{}ncomposition of morphisms is bilinear.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nA preadditive category is **additive** if every finite set of objects\textbackslash{}nhas a biproduct, so we can form firect sums and direct products (which\textbackslash{}nare isomorphic) and zero object (which are empty biproducts).\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nAn additive category is **preabelian** if every morphism has both a\textbackslash{}nkernel and a cokerel.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nFinally, a preablian category is **abelian** if every monomorphism is a\textbackslash{}nkernel of some morphism and every epimorphism is a cokernel of some\textbackslash{}nmorphism.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nAn additive category **\$k\$-linear** if every of its\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\$-sets are \$k\$-vector space.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 291**. A functor \$F:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$\textbackslash{}nbetween two preadditive categories is called **additive** if\textbackslash{}n\$F(f+g) = F(f)+F(g)\$ for any two object \$A,B\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ and any two\textbackslash{}nmorphisms \$f,g\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\}(A,B)\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nA functor \$F:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$ between two preabelian\textbackslash{}ncategories is called **exact** if for any exact sequence of the form\textbackslash{}n\$0\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow A \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow\{f\} B\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow\{g\}C\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow 0\$ in\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$, there is an exact sequence\textbackslash{}n\$0\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow F(A) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow\{F(f)\} F(B)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow\{F(g)\}F(C)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow 0\$\textbackslash{}nin \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: examples\textbackslash{}n**Examples 292**.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Trivially, the category of abelian groups is an abelian category.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Let \$R\$ be a ring, then the category of \$R\$-modules is an abelian\textbackslash{}n  category.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Let \$G\$ be a group. The category of finite-dimensional representation\textbackslash{}n  of \$G\$ over \$k\$ being equivalent to the category of \$k[G]\$-modules\textbackslash{}n  makes it an abelian category. It is even a \$k\$-linear abelian\textbackslash{}n  category.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#comodules\_abelian .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 293**. *Let \$C\$ be a coalgebra over a field \$k\$. Then the\textbackslash{}ncategory of finite-dimensional \$C\$-comodules is \$k\$-linear and abelian.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@DNR] Corollary \$2.1.19\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Equivalence of Categories\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe have introduced the notion of an isomorphism of categories (a pair of\textbackslash{}nfunctors\textbackslash{}n\$F :\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}, G: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$\textbackslash{}nsuch that \$F\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ G= 1\_D\$ and \$G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ F = 1\_C\$). This definition is\textbackslash{}nhowever very rigid and many natural examples of \textbackslash{}"equivalent theories\textbackslash{}" do\textbackslash{}nnot fall under this definition.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nHence, it would be very reasonable to introduce a new definition where\textbackslash{}nwe replace the above identities by natural isomorphisms\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 294**. Two categories \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$ are\textbackslash{}n**equivalent** if there exist two functors\textbackslash{}n\$F : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$G: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$, and two natural isomorphisms\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}alpha:F\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ G \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sim\} 1\_D\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}beta : G\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ F \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xrightarrow\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sim\} 1\_C\$. In this situation we say that\textbackslash{}nthe functor \$G\$ is a quasi-inverse for \$F\$ (and \$F\$ is a quasi-inverse\textbackslash{}nfor \$G\$). Finally, we say that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$ are\textbackslash{}nanti-equivalent if \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ is equivalent to \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\^{}\{op\}\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe say that an adjunction \$(L,R):\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightleftarrows\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$\textbackslash{}nis an **adjoint equivalence** if both the unit \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta\$ and counit\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varepsilon\$ are natural isomorphisms.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: theorem\textbackslash{}n**Theorem 295**. *The following properties of a functor\textbackslash{}n\$F:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$ are equivalent :*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *\$F\$ is an equivalence of categories,*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *\$F\$ is part of an adjoint equivalence\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightleftarrows\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{D\}\$.*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *\$F\$ is fully faithful and essentially surjective*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@McLane\_Sau], Theorem \$IV.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:4.1.\$ ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Grothendieck Topologies \{\#Groth\_topo\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe finish our review on categories by an interesting way of endowing a\textbackslash{}ncategory with a sort of topology called a Grothendieck topology. These\textbackslash{}nkinds of topologies allow to axiomatise the notion of an open cover for\textbackslash{}na category.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 296**. A **Grothendieck topology** \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\$ on a\textbackslash{}ncategory \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ is a collection of maps\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(X) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{(U\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X)\_\{i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ for all\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ called coverings, such that,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- If \$X'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ is an isomorphism, then\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{X'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(X)\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- If \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{U\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\_\{i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(X)\$ and\textbackslash{}n  \$W\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$, then\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{U\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_XW \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow W\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(X)\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- If \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{U\_i \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\_\{i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(X)\$ and\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{V\_\{ij\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow U\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\_\{j\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in J\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(U\_i)\$ for all\textbackslash{}n  \$i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$, then\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{V\_\{ij\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\_\{(i,j)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times J\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(X)\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe can now define the analogue of topological spaces but for categories,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 297**. A **site** is a pair \$(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\},\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\})\$,\textbackslash{}nsuch that \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$ is a category and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\$ is a\textbackslash{}nGrothendieck topology on \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{C\}\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nNow it becomes possible to define sheaves on a category and so it is\textbackslash{}neven possible to define their sheaf cohomology.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 43**. As it is the case for topological spaces, categories can\textbackslash{}nbe endowed with many different Grothendieck topologies. The category of\textbackslash{}nschemes is of particular interest to us here.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nThe category \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\$ can be endowed with the\textbackslash{}nelementary *Zariski topology*, in that case a Zariski covering is a\textbackslash{}nfamily of morphisms \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{(f\_i:U\_i \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X)\_\{i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ of schemes\textbackslash{}nsuch that each \$f\_i\$ is an open immersion and such that\textbackslash{}n\$X =\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigcup\_\{i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\} f\_i(U\_i)\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nWe gave an introduction to *étale topology* on the category of schemes\textbackslash{}nin Chapter [2.1](\#nex\_topology)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"nex\_topology\textbackslash{}"\}.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nAnd as other classes of Grothendieck topologies we may find flat\textbackslash{}ntopologies. Among them we have the *fppf topology* (as in fidèlement\textbackslash{}nplate de présentation finie) and the *fpqc topology* (as in fidèlement\textbackslash{}nplate et quasi-compacte). In these topologies, the morphisms of affine\textbackslash{}nschemes that are covering morphisms are respectively *faithfully flat,\textbackslash{}nof finite presentation, and is quasi-finite*, and *faithfully flat and\textbackslash{}nquasi-compact*.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\# Review of Algebraic Geometry\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nOften, before introducing schemes, one defines the notion of an\textbackslash{}nalgebraic variety. It can be seen as the set of common solutions of a\textbackslash{}nsystem of polynomial equations over a field (usually algebraically\textbackslash{}nclosed). Here, we take the liberty of referring to the first chapter of\textbackslash{}n[@Hartshorne], and immediately start by introducing the theory of\textbackslash{}nsheaves, then schemes.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Sheaves \{\#review\_sheaves\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 298**. A **presheaf** \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ of sets \$(\$resp. rings,\textbackslash{}nabelian groups, \$R\$-modules, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}...\$)\$ on a topological space \$X\$ consists\textbackslash{}nof the following data:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- for every open set \$U \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$, a set \$(\$resp. ring, abelian group,\textbackslash{}n  \$R\$-module, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}...\$)\$ \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U)\$, and\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- for every inclusion \$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset U\$ of open sets in \$X\$ a morphism of\textbackslash{}n  sets \$(\$resp. rings, abelian groups, \$R\$-modules, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}...\$)\$\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\_\{UV\}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(V)\$ called the\textbackslash{}n  restriction map, such that\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n  - \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}emptyset) = 0\$,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n  - \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\_\{UU\}\$ is the identity map on \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U)\$ for all open\textbackslash{}n    sets \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$, and\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n  - for any inclusion \$W\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset U\$ of opens of \$X\$, we have\textbackslash{}n    \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\_\{UV\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}circ\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\_\{VW\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\_\{UW\}\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThe elements of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U)\$ are called sections of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$\textbackslash{}nover \$U\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe can reformulate the definition of a presheaf in the language of\textbackslash{}ncategory, for any topological space \$X\$, we define a category\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Top\}\}\}(X)\$ whose objects are open subsets of \$X\$\textbackslash{}nand where the morphisms are inclusion maps. So if \$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset U\$ in \$X\$,\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}(U,V)=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}emptyset\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Hom\}\}(V,U)\$\textbackslash{}nhas just one element. Now a presheaf is just a contravariant functor\textbackslash{}nfrom the category \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Top\}\}\}(X)\$ to the category of\textbackslash{}nsets (resp. rings, abelian groups, \$R\$-modules, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}...).\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 299**. Now a presheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ is a called a **sheaf**\textbackslash{}nif it satisfies the following *glueing property* :\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nFor \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$ a non-empty open subset, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{U\_i : i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ a non-empty\textbackslash{}nopen cover of \$U\$ and \$s\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U\_i)\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\$s\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_\{U\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap U\_j\} = s\_j\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_\{U\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap U\_j\}\$ for all \$i,j\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$,\textbackslash{}nthen there is a unique \$s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U)\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\$s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_\{U\_i\} = s\_i\$ for all \$i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 300**. Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ be a presheaf on \$X\$, and let\textbackslash{}n\$U \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$ be an open subset. Then the restriction of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$\textbackslash{}nto \$U\$ is defined to be the presheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_U\$ on \$U\$ with\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_U(V) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(V)\$ for every open subset\textbackslash{}n\$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset U\$, and with the restriction maps taken from \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ .\textbackslash{}nNote that if \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ is a sheaf then so is \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_U\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: examples\textbackslash{}n**Examples 301**.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Let \$X\$ be a complex manifold. Due to the maximum modulus principle\textbackslash{}n  from complex analysis, we know that the only holomorphic functions\textbackslash{}n  \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ are the constant functions. To resolve\textbackslash{}n  this challenge, we work ''locally\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" and define the following sheaf\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$ to keep track of the holomorphic structure on the\textbackslash{}n  underlying topological space of \$X\$ on arbitrary open subsets. For\textbackslash{}n  every open subset \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$, we define \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X(U)\$ to be the\textbackslash{}n  ring (commutative) of holomorphic functions from \$U\$ to \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$\textbackslash{}n  with the restriction being the restriction of domain of functions.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Let \$S\$ be a topological space (or abelian group, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}...), then we can\textbackslash{}n  define a sheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_S\$ on any topological space \$X\$ by setting\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_S(U)\$ to be the set (or abelian group, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}...) of\textbackslash{}n  continuous maps \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ and taking the restriction maps to be\textbackslash{}n  the usual restriction of functions. Accordingly, this construction\textbackslash{}n  defines a sheaf. Moreover, if \$S\$ has the discrete topology, every\textbackslash{}n  continuous map \$f:U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow S\$ is constant on each connected\textbackslash{}n  component of \$U\$, so \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_S(U) = S\$. And in that case, we call\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_S\$ the constant sheaf on \$X\$ with value \$S\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 302**. If \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\$ are presheaves on\textbackslash{}n\$X\$, a **morphism of presheaves**\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\$ consists of a morphism of\textbackslash{}nsets (resp. rings, abelian groups, \$R\$-modules, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}...)\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_U : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(U)\$ for each open set\textbackslash{}n\$U\$, such that for every inclusion \$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset U\$, the following diagram\textbackslash{}ncommutes,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{tikzcd\}\textbackslash{}n        \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[r,\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_U\textbackslash{}"] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d, \textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\}\_\{UV\}\textbackslash{}"']\textbackslash{}n        \& \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(U) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d,\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\^{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\}\_\{UV\}\textbackslash{}"] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n        \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(V) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[r,\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_V\textbackslash{}"']\textbackslash{}n        \&  \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(V)\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{tikzcd\}\$\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThis forms a category of presheaves of sets (resp. rings, abelian\textbackslash{}ngroups, \$R\$-modules, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}...) on a fixed topological space \$X\$, denoted\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{PSh\}\}\}(X)\$. And the category of sheaves of sets\textbackslash{}n(resp. rings, abelian groups, \$R\$-modules, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}...) on \$X\$, denoted\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sh\}\}\}(X)\$ is defined as the full subcategory of\textbackslash{}nthe corresponding presheaf category. This means that a morphism of\textbackslash{}nsheaves is just a morphism of the underlying presheaves.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 303**. Let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ be a presheaf of sets (resp.\textbackslash{}nrings, abelian groups, \$R\$-modules, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}...) on \$X\$ and \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$. The\textbackslash{}n**stalk** \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_x\$ of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ at \$x\$ is defined as the\textbackslash{}ndirect limit of the sets (resp. rings, abelian groups, \$R\$-modules,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}...) \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U)\$ for all open subsets \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$ containing \$x\$,\textbackslash{}nvia the restriction maps \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rho\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 44**. An element of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_x\$ is represented by a pair\textbackslash{}n\$(U,s)\$, where \$U\$ is an open neighbourhood of \$x\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U)\$. And two such elements \$(U,s)\$ and \$(U',s')\$ are\textbackslash{}nequivalent in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_x\$ if and only if there is an open\textbackslash{}nneighbourhood \$W\$ of \$x\$, with \$W\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap U'\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\$s\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_W = s'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_W\$. The elements of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_x\$ are called germs\textbackslash{}nof \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ at \$x\$. Note that a morphism\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\$ of presheaves on \$X\$\textbackslash{}ninduces a morphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\_x:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\_x\$ on\textbackslash{}nthe stalks, for any point \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 304**. Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a continuous map of\textbackslash{}ntopological spaces. For any sheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ on \$X\$, we define the\textbackslash{}n**direct image sheaf** or **push forward sheaf** \$f\_\{*\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ on\textbackslash{}n\$Y\$ by \$(f\_*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\})(V) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(f\^{}\{-1\}(V))\$ for any open set\textbackslash{}n\$V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset Y\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#almost\_pullback\_sheaf .construction\}\textbackslash{}n**Construction 305**. For \$f: X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ a continuous map of\textbackslash{}ntopological spaces, the direct image functor\textbackslash{}n\$f\_* : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sh\}\}\}(X) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sh\}\}\}(Y)\$\textbackslash{}nhas an adjoint functor called the **inverse image functor** \$f\^{}\{-1\}\$.\textbackslash{}nLet \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\$ be a sheaf on \$Y\$, unlike the direct image sheaf, the\textbackslash{}ninverse image sheaf cannot be defined as simply as\textbackslash{}n\$f\^{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(U) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(f(U))\$ for each open set\textbackslash{}n\$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$ as unfortunately \$f(U)\$ is not necessarily open. What we do\textbackslash{}nthen is to define \$f\^{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\$ to be the sheaf associated to the\textbackslash{}npresheaf \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mapsto \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varinjlim\_\{V\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}supset f(U)\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(V)\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nThe process of considering a sheaf associated to a presheaf is called\textbackslash{}nsheafification and is described in [@Hartshorne] Proposition-Definition\textbackslash{}n\$II.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:1.2\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Schemes \{\#Annexe\_scheme\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn classical algebraic geometry, a scheme is a generalisation of a\textbackslash{}nvariety (it allows to consider non-reduced rings and thus it allows for\textbackslash{}nnilpotents). We begin with the affine case.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 306**. Let \$R\$ be a ring. The set of all prime ideals of\textbackslash{}n\$R\$ is called the **spectrum** of \$R\$ or the **affine scheme**\textbackslash{}nassociated to \$R\$, and is denoted by \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 307**. Let \$R\$ be a ring and\textbackslash{}n\$P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R\$ a prime ideal of \$R\$ (a point in the\textbackslash{}ncorresponding affine scheme).\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- We denote \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(P)\$ the quotient field of the integral domain \$R/P\$.\textbackslash{}n  It is called the **residue field** of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R\$ at\textbackslash{}n  \$P\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- For any \$f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in R\$, we define the value of \$f\$ at \$P\$, to be the image\textbackslash{}n  of \$f\$ under the composite ring homomorphism\textbackslash{}n  \$R\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow R/P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(P)\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 308**. An affine scheme \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: R\$ is\textbackslash{}ncalled **integral** if it is non-empty and the ring \$R\$ is an integral\textbackslash{}ndomain.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 309**. An affine scheme \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: R\$ is\textbackslash{}ncalled **reduced** if the ring \$R\$ is also reduced, i.e. it contains no\textbackslash{}nnilpotent elements.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nLet \$R\$ be a ring, similarly as in the case of affine varieties, we\textbackslash{}ndefine the *zero locus* \$V(S)\$ of \$S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset R\$ and the *ideal* \$I(X)\$ of\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: R\$ to be : \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{equation*\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{split\}\textbackslash{}n    V(S) \&:= \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid f(P)=0\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}forall \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R, f(P)=0,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}forall\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\} R\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{split\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{equation*\}\$\$\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe can now endow an affine scheme with a topology.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 310**. We define the **Zariski topology** on an affine\textbackslash{}nscheme \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R\$ to be the topology whose closed sets\textbackslash{}nare exactly the sets of the form \$V(S)\$ for some \$S\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset R\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe have a scheme-theoretic version of the Nullstellensatz,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 311**. *Let \$R\$ be a ring.*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n*\$a)\$ For any closed subset \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R\$, we\textbackslash{}nhave \$V(I(X))=X\$.*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n*\$b)\$ For any ideal \$J\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}trianglelefteq R\$, we have \$I(V(J))=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}sqrt\{J\}\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nIn particular there is an inclusion-reversing bijection\textbackslash{}n\$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{equation*\}\textbackslash{}n        \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{closed subsets of \}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}xleftrightarrow\{1:1\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{radical ideals in \} R\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{equation*\}\$\$*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Eisenbud], Theorem \$I.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:1.6\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 45**. A particular property of schemes is that it allows points\textbackslash{}nthat are not necessarily closed, meaning that their closure is a bigger\textbackslash{}nsubscheme containing that point. We call non-closed point \$P\$ in a\textbackslash{}nscheme \$X\$ a **generic point** if its closure is the entire scheme.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe now cite a few topological properties of affine schemes :\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 312**. A topological space \$X\$ is called **reducible** if\textbackslash{}nit can be written as \$X = X\_1 \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cup X\_2\$, for closed subsets\textbackslash{}n\$X\_1,X\_2 \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subsetneq X\$. Otherwise it is called **irreducible**.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 313**. *An affine variety \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: R\$ is\textbackslash{}nirreducible if and only if \$R\$ is an integral domain.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#integral\_iff\_irr\_red .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 314**. *An affine scheme \$X\$ is said to be integral if and\textbackslash{}nonly if it is irreducible and reduced.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 315**. An affine scheme \$X\$ is called **disconnected** if\textbackslash{}nit can be written as \$X=X\_1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cup X\_2\$ for closed subsets\textbackslash{}n\$X\_1,X\_2\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subsetneq X\$ with \$X\_1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cap X\_2 = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}emptyset\$. Otherwise it is\textbackslash{}ncalled **connected**\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 316**. A topological space is called **Noetherian** if\textbackslash{}nthere is no infinite strictly decreasing chain of closed subsets.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThus an affine scheme \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: R\$ is Noetherian if and\textbackslash{}nonly if \$R\$ is a Noetherian ring.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 317**. The **dimension**\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dim X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{N\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cup \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}infty\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ of a non-empty topological space\textbackslash{}n\$X\$ is the supremum of the length of chains of strictly increasing\textbackslash{}nirreducible closed subsets of \$X\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proposition\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 318**. *For a ring \$R\$ and an element \$f\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in R\$, we call\textbackslash{}n\$D(f) := \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}backslash V(f)\$ the **distinguished\textbackslash{}nopen subset** of \$f\$ in \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: R\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 46**. The distinguish open sets form a basis of the Zariski\textbackslash{}ntopology of an affine scheme \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R\$ in the sense\textbackslash{}nthat every open subset \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R\$ is an\textbackslash{}narbitrary union of distinguished opens.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe now define the notion of morphism of schemes. Since schemes usually\textbackslash{}ncarry more structure than typical topological spaces, it is natural that\textbackslash{}nmorphism of schemes need to satisfy more conditions than just being\textbackslash{}ncontinuous. It does not just have to move points around, it needs to map\textbackslash{}nsections of structure sheaves in a meaningful way. This is defined\textbackslash{}nbelow.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 319**. A **locally ringed space** is a ringed space\textbackslash{}n\$(X,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X)\$ such that each stalk \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,P\}\$ for\textbackslash{}n\$P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$ is a local ring. A **morphism** of locally ringed spaces from\textbackslash{}n\$(X,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X)\$ to \$(Y,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_Y)\$ is given by a continuous map\textbackslash{}n\$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ and for every open subset \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset Y\$ a ring\textbackslash{}nhomomorphism \$f\^{}*\_U:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_Y(U)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow O\_X(f\^{}\{-1\}(U))\$ called\textbackslash{}nthe *pull-back* on \$U\$, such that the two following conditions hold :\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- The pull-back maps must be compatible with restriction (this implies\textbackslash{}n  there are ring homomorphism\textbackslash{}n  \$f\^{}*\_P:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{Y,f(P)\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,P\}\$ on the\textbackslash{}n  stalks for every \$P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$).\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- The ring homomorphism induced by \$f\^{}*\$ between the stalks of \$Y\$ and\textbackslash{}n  \$X\$ must be a local homomorphism, i.e. for every \$P\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$, we have\textbackslash{}n  \$(f\^{}*\_P)\^{}\{-1\}(I\_P) = I\_\{f(P)\}\$ where \$I\_P\$ and \$I\_\{f(P)\}\$ denote\textbackslash{}n  maximal ideals of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,P\}\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{Y,f(P)\}\$\textbackslash{}n  respectively.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAny affine scheme is a locally ringed space with its structure sheaf\textbackslash{}n(see Proposition \$II. \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:2.3.\$ in [@Hartshorne]). Let \$X\$ be an affine\textbackslash{}nscheme and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$ its structure sheaf. For any open subset\textbackslash{}n\$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$, then \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X(U)\$ is the ring of regular functions\textbackslash{}non \$U\$. This is not to be confused with the ring of *rational functions*\textbackslash{}non \$U\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 320**. A **scheme** is a locally ringed space that has an\textbackslash{}nopen cover by affine schemes. Morphisms of schemes are just morphisms as\textbackslash{}nlocally ringed spaces. This makes a category of schemes denoted\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}textbf\{Sch\}\}\}\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn the literature, there is often a distinction between separated and\textbackslash{}nnon-separated scheme (the notion corresponds to that of Hausdroff spaces\textbackslash{}nin topology). For sake of simplicity, all the schemes we consider are\textbackslash{}nassumed to be separated.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 47**. All the above topological concepts defined for affine\textbackslash{}nschemes immediately apply to schemes.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe can now define *open* and *closed subschemes* :\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: construction\textbackslash{}n**Construction 321**. Let \$X\$ be a scheme. We say that \$Y\$ is a **open\textbackslash{}nsubscheme** of \$Y\$ whose underlying space is the subspace \$Y\$ of \$X\$\textbackslash{}ntogether with an isomorphism of structure sheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_Y\$ with the\textbackslash{}nrestriction \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_Y\}\$. Similarly, an **open immersion**\textbackslash{}nis a morphism \$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ which induces an isomorphism of \$X\$ with\textbackslash{}nan open subscheme of \$Y\$.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nOn the other hand, \$Z\$ is a **closed subscheme** of \$X\$ if there is a\textbackslash{}nmorphism of locally ringed spaces \$i:Z\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ that is a closed\textbackslash{}nimmersion. This means it has to satisfy the following criteria :\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- the map \$i\$ is a homeomorphism of \$Z\$ onto its image,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- the associated sheaf map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow i\_*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_Z\$\textbackslash{}n  is surjective with kernel \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{I\}\$,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- the kernel \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{I\}\$ is locally generated by sections as an\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$-module.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThis is further explained in the next subsection.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nEven though they are an important class of schemes, we give a quick\textbackslash{}ndefinition of *projective schemes*.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: construction\textbackslash{}n**Construction 322**. Let \$R\$ be a commutative graded ring, where\textbackslash{}n\$R = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}oplus\_\{d\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}ge 0\} R\_d\$ is its gradation. The elements of\textbackslash{}n\$R\_d\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}backslash \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{0\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ are said to be homogeneous of degree \$d\$. An ideal\textbackslash{}nin a graded ring is called **homogeneous** if it is generated by\textbackslash{}nhomogeneous elements. The ringed space\textbackslash{}n\$(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: R, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R\})\$\textbackslash{}nis an **affine projective scheme** if \$R\$ is a graded ring as above and\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R := \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{P \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}trianglelefteq R \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{ with \} P \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{ a homogeneous prime ideals\} \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$,\textbackslash{}nwith the usual structure sheaf. Similarly as above, one define a\textbackslash{}n**projective scheme** \$(X,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X)\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 323**. Let \$X\$ be a scheme. The **ring of rational\textbackslash{}nfunctions** on \$X\$ is the ring \$R(X)\$ whose elements are rational\textbackslash{}nfunctions of \$X\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 48**. We can also define the residue field \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(P)\$ for \$P\$\textbackslash{}na point of a locally ringed space \$(X,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X)\$. It is defined as\textbackslash{}nfollows \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(P) := \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,P\}/\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\_P\$ where\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathfrak\{m\}\_P\$ is the unique maximal ideal of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,P\}\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#function\_field\_residue\_field .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 324**. *Let \$X\$ be an integral scheme, then the function field\textbackslash{}n\$k(X) = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_\{X,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta\} = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta)\$ for \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}eta\$ the unique\textbackslash{}ngeneric point of \$X\$ (see Lemma \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}ref\{irreducible\_generic\_point\}\$).*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Stacks][(Tag\textbackslash{}n01RV)](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01RV). ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 325**. Let \$X\$ be an integral scheme. The **function\textbackslash{}nfield** or **field of rational functions** of \$X\$ is the field \$R(X)\$,\textbackslash{}nthat we now denote \$k(X)\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nOne powerful aspects of scheme theory is that it allows us to consider\textbackslash{}nvarieties/schemes over particular fields. For example, we talk about a\textbackslash{}nscheme \$X\$ over a field \$k\$, when we consider the map\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:k\$. Over certain fields, schemes\textbackslash{}nmay have different properties which are called relative properties,\textbackslash{}nsince they are now relative to a base scheme. This was the case for most\textbackslash{}nconcepts presented in Section\textbackslash{}n[2.2](\#morphisms\_of\_schemes)\{reference-type=\textbackslash{}"ref\textbackslash{}"\textbackslash{}nreference=\textbackslash{}"morphisms\_of\_schemes\textbackslash{}"\}. In that sense relative properties of\textbackslash{}nschemes can be thought of as properties of morphisms of scheme.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 326**. A morphism of schemes \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ is said to\textbackslash{}nbe **quasi-compact** if \$Y\$ can be covered by open affine subschemes\textbackslash{}n\$(V\_i)\_\{i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\}\$ such that the pre-images \$f\^{}\{-1\}(V\_i)\$ are compact (in\textbackslash{}nthe usual topological sense) for all \$i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in I\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 327**. A morphisms \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ of schemes is called\textbackslash{}n**proper** if it is (separated) of finite type and universally closed.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nOne of the main important tool in that flavour is the ability to change\textbackslash{}nbase schemes.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 328**. Let \$X\$ and \$Y'\$ be schemes over a scheme \$Y\$, we\textbackslash{}ndefine the **fibre product** of \$X\$ and \$Y'\$ over \$Y\$ to be the scheme\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YY'\$ such that the following diagram commutes: \$\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}begin\{tikzcd\}\textbackslash{}n        X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_Y Y' \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[r,\textbackslash{}"p\_\{Y'\}\textbackslash{}"] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d, \textbackslash{}"p\_X\textbackslash{}"']\textbackslash{}n        \& Y' \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[d,\textbackslash{}"g\textbackslash{}"] \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}n        X \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}arrow[r,\textbackslash{}"f\textbackslash{}"']\textbackslash{}n        \&  Y\textbackslash{}n    \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}end\{tikzcd\}\$\$ If we consider the scheme \$X\$ over \$Y\$ and\textbackslash{}n\$g:Y'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ the change of basis, the **base change** of \$X\$ is\textbackslash{}nthe scheme \$X' :=X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_YY'\$ over \$Y'\$ and we call\textbackslash{}n\$p\_\{X'\}: X' \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y'\$ the **base change map**.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe say that a morphism of schemes is **universally closed** if for any\textbackslash{}nbase change, its base change map is a closed map.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 49**. The disjoint union distributes over the fibre product of\textbackslash{}na scheme, meaning that for any schemes \$X\_i\$ and \$Y\$ over a base scheme\textbackslash{}n\$Z\$, there is an isomorphism of schemes :\textbackslash{}n\$\$(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigsqcup\_i X\_i) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_Z Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bigsqcup\_i(X\_i\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_Z Y) .\$\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAn interesting use of the base change is the ability to consider\textbackslash{}n*geometric notions*. Usually, we want to work over algebraically closed\textbackslash{}nfields, but not all properties of schemes are invariant under base\textbackslash{}nchange. So we can \textbackslash{}"force\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}" a scheme to have a certain property over an\textbackslash{}nalgebraically closed field by considering it having that property over\textbackslash{}nits closure. As an illustration we give the following definition\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#geometrically\_integral .definition\}\textbackslash{}n**Definition 329**. A scheme \$X\$ over a field \$k\$ is said to be\textbackslash{}n**geometrically integral** if for all field extension \$L|k\$,\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_k \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: L\$ is integral, then of course\textbackslash{}n\$X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_k \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}overline\{k\}\$ is also integral.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nThere are many ways to define the fibre of a morphism in algebraic\textbackslash{}ngeometry\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 330**. Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a morphism of schemes, let\textbackslash{}n\$y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in Y\$ and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(y)\$ the residue field of \$y\$ with the inclusion\textbackslash{}nmorphism being \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}iota: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(y)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$.\textbackslash{}nWe define the **fibre of \$f\$ at \$y\$** to be the scheme\textbackslash{}n\$X\_y := X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}times\_Y \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}kappa(y)\$\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Quasi-coherent Sheaves \{\#annexe\_quasi\_coherent\}\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nSo far we have introduced schemes and morphisms between them without\textbackslash{}nmentioning any sheaves other than the structure sheaves, our review of\textbackslash{}nscheme theory would not be complete without mentioning sheaves of\textbackslash{}nmodules.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 331**. Let \$X\$ be a scheme and \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$ its\textbackslash{}nstructure sheaf. A **sheaf of modules** on \$X\$, also called a sheaf of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$-modules is a sheaf \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ on \$X\$ such that\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U)\$ is an \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X(U)\$-module for all open subsets\textbackslash{}n\$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$ and all restriction maps are \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$-modules\textbackslash{}nhomomorphisms in the sense that\textbackslash{}n\$\$(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi +\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_U = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_U + \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_U \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}text\{ and \}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: (\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lambda\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_U = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lambda\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cdot \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}vert\_U\$\$\textbackslash{}nfor all open subsets \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset V\$ of \$X\$, \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}lambda\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X(V)\$\textbackslash{}nand \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}psi\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(V)\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: examples\textbackslash{}n**Examples 332**.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Let \$X\$ be a scheme, then \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X\$ is a sheaf of modules on\textbackslash{}n  \$X\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Let \$f:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\$ be a morphisms of sheaves\textbackslash{}n  on a scheme \$X\$. For any open subset \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$, we set\textbackslash{}n  \$(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Ker\}\}f)(U):= \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}ker( f\_U : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(U) )\$.\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Ker\}\}f\$ is a sheaf of modules on \$X\$, we call it the\textbackslash{}n  **kernel sheaf** of \$f\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- For a morphism \$f:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\$ of sheaves on a\textbackslash{}n  scheme \$X\$ and any open subset \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$, we set\textbackslash{}n  \$(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Im\}\}' f)(U):= \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{im\}\}( f\_U : \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(U)).\$\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Im\}\}' f\$ defines a presheaf of modules but not yet a\textbackslash{}n  sheaf. We define its sheafification \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Im\}\}f\$ the\textbackslash{}n  **image sheaf** of \$f\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Let \$f:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\$ be a morphism of sheaves on\textbackslash{}n  a scheme \$X\$. We define the **tensor presheaf**\textbackslash{}n  \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\$ on \$X\$ by\textbackslash{}n  \$(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes'\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\})(U):= \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}(U) \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes\_\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X(U)\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}(U)\$\textbackslash{}n  for any open subset \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset X\$. We define its sheafification to be\textbackslash{}n  the **tensor sheaf** \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}otimes \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{G\}\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- Let \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ be a morphism of schemes and let \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$\textbackslash{}n  be a sheaf on \$X\$. Consider the direct image sheaf \$f\_*\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\$ on\textbackslash{}n  \$Y\$, it is a sheaf of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_Y\$-modules.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#exact\_at\_level\_of\_stalk .lemma\}\textbackslash{}n**Lemma 333**. *Let \$(X, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X)\$ be a ringed space. The category\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}bf\{Mod\}\}\}(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X)\$ is an abelian category.\textbackslash{}nMoreover a complex\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dots \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_1\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_2 \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_3 \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dots\$\textbackslash{}nis exact at \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_2\$ if and only if for all \$x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in X\$, the complex\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dots \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_1)\_x\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow (\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_2)\_x \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow (\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_3)\_x \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}dots\$\textbackslash{}nis exact at \$(\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{F\}\_2)\_x\$.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@Stacks] [(Tag\textbackslash{}n01AG)](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01AG) ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe now describe exactly how an \$R\$-module \$M\$ determines a sheaf of\textbackslash{}nmodules \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}widetilde\{M\}\$ on the affine scheme\textbackslash{}n\$X=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:R\$\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 334**. Let \$X=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}: R\$ be an affine\textbackslash{}nscheme, and let \$M\$ be an \$R\$-module.
