the cohomology of sheaves gives us powerful\textbackslash{}ninvariants, useful for the classification of schemes. Such as, the\textbackslash{}ncohomology groups themselves, the *Euler characteristics*, the genus of\textbackslash{}na scheme and much more.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n\#\#\# Analytification\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nA smooth scheme over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ can be seen as a complex manifold.\textbackslash{}nSince we can apply techniques of complex analysis and differential\textbackslash{}ngeometry to complex manifolds, provided we have a nice dictionary\textbackslash{}nbetween the language of abstract algebraic geometry and complex\textbackslash{}nmanifolds, we could translate those analytical results into results\textbackslash{}nabout schemes.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe first need to define what we mean by an analytic space (complex in\textbackslash{}nour case)\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 353**. Let \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\^{}n\$ be the Cartesian product\textbackslash{}nof open discs : \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{|z\_i| <1 \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid i=1,...,n\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$, let \$f\_1,...,f\_m\$ be\textbackslash{}nholomorphic functions on \$U\$ and let \$Y\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset U\$ be the closed subset\textbackslash{}n(for the usual Euclidean topology) consisting of the zero locus\textbackslash{}n\$V(f\_1,...,f\_m)\$, with its structure sheaf the restriction\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_Y = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_U/(f\_1,...,f\_m)\$ (for \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_U\$ the\textbackslash{}nsheaf of holomorphic functions on \$U\$).\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}nA **complex analytic space** is a locally ringed space\textbackslash{}n\$(X,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X)\$ which can be covered by affine open sets, each of\textbackslash{}nwhich biholomorphic (as locally ringed spaces) to a space \$Y\$ as above.\textbackslash{}n(Notice that \$Y\$ is open in \$X\$ but closed in \$U\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}subset \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\^{}n\$)\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nNotice that the sheaf structure is actually a structure of\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$-modules.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 50**. Theses spaces are called *analytic* because the topology\textbackslash{}non them is the topology induced from the usual one on \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\^{}n\$\textbackslash{}nopen sets are small, and compatible with analysis (limits, continuity,\textbackslash{}nholomorphic functions, \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}...)\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nSimilarly as in the algebraic case, complex analytic spaces are a\textbackslash{}ngeneralisation of complex manifolds, indeed, they also allow\textbackslash{}nsingularities. For example, let\textbackslash{}n\$X = \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\{(u,v)\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\^{}2 \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mid uv= 0\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\}\$ be a complex analytic space,\textbackslash{}nthen it is not a complex manifold since there is no neighbourhood at the\textbackslash{}norigin that is biholomorphic to an open subset of \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: definition\textbackslash{}n**Definition 354**. If \$X\$ and \$Y\$ are complex analytical spaces, a\textbackslash{}nmorphism \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ of locally \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$-ringed spaces\textbackslash{}nis called a **holomorphic map**.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nAs the name of this section suggests, the goal is to associate to an\textbackslash{}nalgebraic scheme \$X\$ over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ such a complex analytic space\textbackslash{}nthat we will denote by \$X\^{}\{an\}\$,\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: construction\textbackslash{}n**Construction 355**. Let \$X\$ be a scheme of finite type over\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$. Consider a covering of \$X\$ by affine open subsets\textbackslash{}n\$Y\_i=\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathop\{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathrm\{Spec\}\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:A\_i\$, recall that for all \$i\$, \$A\_i\$ is of\textbackslash{}nfinite type, so \$A\_i \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}cong \textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}[x\_1, ..., x\_n]/(f\_1, ..., f\_m)\$\textbackslash{}nwith \$f\_1,...,f\_m\$ polynomials in \$x\_1,...,x\_n\$. We can regard those\textbackslash{}npolynomials as holomorphic functions on \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\^{}n\$ and their zero\textbackslash{}nlocus form a complex analytic closed subspace \$Y\_i\^{}\{an\}\$ in\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\^{}n\$. Since the scheme \$X\$ is obtained by glueing the open\textbackslash{}nsets \$Y\_i\$, we can use the same glueing data to glue the analytic spaces\textbackslash{}n\$Y\_i\^{}\{an\}\$ into an analytic space \$X\^{}\{an\}\$. This is the associated\textbackslash{}ncomplex analytic space of \$X\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 51**. Notice that the above construction is functorial thus we\textbackslash{}nobtain a functor \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\_\^{}\{an\}\$ from the category of finite schemes over\textbackslash{}n\$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$ to the category of complex analytical spaces. There is also\textbackslash{}na continuous map \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}varphi : X\^{}\{an\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow X\$ of the underlying\textbackslash{}ntopological spaces, which sends \$X\^{}\{an\}\$ bijectively onto closed points\textbackslash{}nof \$X\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nIn his groundbreaking paper [@Serre], Serre proved a plethora of results\textbackslash{}nabout the relationship between a scheme \$X\$ ans its associated analytic\textbackslash{}nspace \$X\^{}\{an\}\$, we enumerate them below:\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#analytification\_space .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 356**. *Let \$X\$ be a scheme over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$, locally of\textbackslash{}nfinite type and \$X\^{}\{an\}\$ the associated analytical space. Then the\textbackslash{}nscheme \$X\$ is*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *non-empty,*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *discrete,*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *regular,*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *normal,*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *reduced, or*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *of dimension \$n\$*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n*if and only if the associated \$X\^{}\{an\}\$ is as well.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@SGA], Proposition \$XII.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:2.1\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: \{\#analytification\_morphisms .proposition\}\textbackslash{}n**Proposition 357**. *Let \$X\$ and \$Y\$ be two schemes over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$\textbackslash{}nlocally of finite type, \$f:X\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\$ a morphism of finite type and\textbackslash{}n\$f\^{}\{an\}: X\^{}\{an\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}rightarrow Y\^{}\{an\}\$ the associated analytical morphism\textbackslash{}ninduced by \$f\$. Then \$f\$ is*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *surjective,*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *a closed immersion,*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *an immersion,*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *proper, or*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n- *finite*\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n*if and only if \$f\^{}\{an\}\$ is as well.*\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: proof\textbackslash{}n*Proof.* See [@SGA], Proposition \$XII.\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}:3.2\$. ◻\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}nWe say that a complex analytical space \$(X,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathcal\{O\}\_X)\$ is actually a\textbackslash{}n*Riemann surface* if and only if it is \$1\$-dimensional and smooth (or\textbackslash{}nnon-singular). Thus, notice that the above notions also make sense for\textbackslash{}nRiemann surfaces when considering their structure sheaf of holomorphic\textbackslash{}nfunctions.\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n::: remark\textbackslash{}n**Remark 52**. It is interesting to note that in [@Serre], for \$X\$ a\textbackslash{}nprojective scheme over \$\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}mathbb\{C\}\$, Serre also showed that the\textbackslash{}nanalytification functor yields an equivalence of categories between\textbackslash{}ncoherent sheaves on \$X\$ and coherent analytic sheaves on \$X\^{}\{an\}\$.\textbackslash{}n:::\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}n"\\

\subsection*{summary (\texttt{claude-haiku-4-5})}
\begin{quote}\small\ttfamily\raggedright
\{\\
  "audience": "Graduate students in algebraic geometry, students of Galois theory, and mathematicians seeking to understand Grothendieck's conceptual innovations connecting topology and algebraic geometry.",\\
  "key\_contributions": [\\
    "Systematic exposition of the analogy between topological covering spaces and Galois theory, demonstrating how both encode symmetries through profinite groups.",\\
    "Construction and detailed study of the étale fundamental group for schemes, including comparison with the topological fundamental group via transcendental methods for complex varieties.",\\
    "Unified treatment of fundamental groups through Tannakian duality, showing how étale, topological, and motivic Galois groups arise naturally within a single categorical framework.",\\
    "Self-contained development of category-theoretic foundations (functors, limits, adjunctions, abelian categories) necessary for modern algebraic geometry."\\
  ],\\
  "plain\_language\_summary": "This thesis presents a systematic exploration of how fundamental groups---objects that capture the essential structure of spaces and their symmetries---appear across three major mathematical domains. The work begins with classical topological covering spaces, where fundamental groups classify how spaces can be continuously wrapped around themselves. It then follows Grothendieck's revolutionary insight that similar ideas apply to algebraic varieties, the geometric objects defined by polynomial equations. However, standard topological methods fail for varieties because they lack sufficient structure; the solution is the étale topology, a combinatorial framework where covering spaces are replaced by certain algebraic morphisms. Through this lens, the étale fundamental group emerges as the algebraic analogue of its topological cousin, and remarkably, the two coincide when the variety is complex---a deep connection bridging algebra and analysis. Finally, the thesis reveals that all three versions of the fundamental group---topological, étale, and motivic---are unified through Tannakian duality, a principle that recovers groups as symmetry groups of fiber functors on monoidal categories of representations.",\\
  "tldr": "A thesis developing fundamental groups as a unifying framework across topology, algebraic geometry via étale theory, and linear algebra through Tannakian duality."\\
\}\\
\end{quote}
